assets.topic: Scrub the Foundations: Why the Unspoken Dialogue Matters
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead drags across a timeline of human communication from cave walls to text chats; a myth-busting placard reading 93 PERCENT shatters over Mehrabian's lab, while a plane circles a remote Alaska camp, a baby grasps its mother's hand, and a press-room bookcase flashes by with the caption What you say is not as important as the bookcase behind you.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the chapter's opening case for nonverbal communication: why the unspoken dialogue is crucial to human relating despite Huxley's dismissal of it, why the famous 93 percent statistic overstates the case, and how the authors show the importance of nonverbal cues through their omnipresence, multifunctionality, their power to mislead as well as inform, phylogenetic, ontogenetic and interaction primacy, their ability to express what words cannot or should not, the trust people place in them, and their partial universality.
key_concepts: Humans are social creatures who spend most of their waking hours in contact with other people, and our ability to navigate the waters of daily living depends on the ways in which we and others communicate.

This textbook is about the unspoken dialogue: all those messages that people exchange beyond and alongside the words themselves, and human relating hinges on the ability to express ourselves nonverbally and to understand the nonverbal communication of others.

Although Aldous Huxley dismissed the study of nonverbal communication as trivial, the subject is belied by thousands of articles, books, documentaries, and investigative reports from disciplines including communication, psychology, psychiatry, sociology, anthropology, linguistics, semiotics, and biology.

The claim that 93 percent of all meaning is derived from nonverbal behavior is not an accurate general statement, because it grew out of early studies by Mehrabian and his colleagues whose designs, using a single word alongside changing voice and body cues, worked to overstate the importance of the nonverbal cues.
Nonverbal communication is consequential: nonverbal cues are key in bonding with partners and with babies, and they also play a role in bias against other groups, abuse, and sexual harassment.
Nonverbal cues pervade virtually every communicative act, with the body, face, voice, appearance, touch, distancing, timing, and physical surroundings all having a part in creating messages.

Even text-only communication can have nonverbal elements, as emails and text chats use font colors, punctuation, and capitalization to capture nonverbal nuances, a phenomenon Luangrath and colleagues call textual paralanguage.
Nonverbal communication is multifunctional, because the same cues can simultaneously be used for impression formation, sending relational messages, displaying identity, and exerting social influence.

Nonverbal communication can lead to misunderstanding as well as understanding, and misreadings can have a more profound impact than accurately exchanged messages, as when a young photographer in Alaska misread a pilot's signals with fatal consequences.

Nonverbal communication has phylogenetic, ontogenetic, and interaction primacy: it predated language in the evolution of the species, infants rely on it before learning language, and it precedes verbal behavior in the opening minutes of most human encounters.

When verbal messages contradict nonverbal ones, the bulk of research shows that adults usually believe the nonverbal message, because nonverbal cues are often seen to be more authentic, and young children do the same thing.
There is some universality to nonverbal cues and their meanings, as many cues have pancultural origins, yet cultural differences contribute to our use of and our misreading of nonverbal actions.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Definitions: Signs, Symptoms, Semblances, and Symbols
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table where semioticians face off: a smile card splits into signifier and signified halves, a monitor replays Hillary Clinton's eyes welling up while headlines scroll from she cares to crocodile tears, a sigh bubble drifts over a listener, and a gavel drops on the words other-directed and volitional.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue about how communication and nonverbal communication get defined: debate the semiotic machinery of signs, signifiers, and signifieds, weigh Goffman's given versus given off, follow Buck's two streams of symbolic and spontaneous communication, and then sort the three cue forms, spontaneous symptoms, arbitrary symbols, and pseudo-spontaneous semblances, before landing on the book's definition of nonverbal communication as other-directed and volitional sign exchange, with the polysemy puzzle and Clinton's tears as the closing exhibit.
key_concepts: Human communication is defined as the process of creating meanings between people through the exchange of signs, a complex enterprise involving encoding by senders and decoding by receivers.

In semiotics, a sign is anything that stands for something else, and the signifier is the thing that reflects something, a word, an object, or a posture, while the signified is the thing the sign represents.
A smile can be a sign or signifier for happiness, whereas the emotion of happiness is the signified, and the smile is itself not happiness but the way in which happiness is revealed to others.

The same cue or signifier can carry multiple meanings, a phenomenon called polysemy, as when Dr. Anthony Fauci's facepalm at a press conference during the COVID-19 pandemic was given different interpretations.

Using Goffman's terms, nonverbal behavior can be given off, meaning unconscious and not meant to be a message, rather than given, where given implies that a behavior is enacted with some level of consciousness to be sent to another.

Buck describes communication as proceeding in two simultaneous streams, one symbolic in which information is encoded into symbols and decoded by the receiver and one spontaneous in which emotion is displayed and picked up by pre-attunements in the receiver.

Spontaneous cues or symptoms, such as tearing up or a shaking hand, have an inherent connection between the signifier and the signified, and on their own they are not communication but just information about the person or the situation.

Symbols are signs that have an arbitrary relationship between the signified and the signifier, so nodding your head to show agreement or using a V sign to show victory is only meaningful because at some point people decided that those signs would have those meanings.

Pseudo-spontaneous cues, also called semblances or iconic cues, have at their base a natural connection to their signifier, but in the moments when they are used that natural tie does not exist, as when you sigh sympathetically in response to sad news even though you do not feel sad.
Nonverbal communication, then, is the exchange of signs, other than words, that are other-directed and used with some degree of volition as part of a message.

Most nonverbal expressions and patterns become well-learned habits that require little forethought or conscious awareness, so we perform many of our nonverbal behaviors without thinking much about them, as when we automatically smile and make eye contact when greeting a friend.

Manusov and Harvey's study of the mediated talk about Hillary Clinton's teary moment showed a range of meanings for the same cue, from showing that she cares to crocodile tears, reflecting the reality and complexity of the polysemy inherent in signs.

assets.topic: Audit Who Decides: Orientations, Communication Communities, and Cultural Codes
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger on a courtroom bench: four orientation tabs flip open while Christie's quote, it was just my face, prints out; a world map labels the same extended-hand gesture talk to the hand in the United States and mouthzah, a deep insult, in Greece; and a value pyramid rises with lauded accents at the top and tattooed and stigmatized cues near the bottom.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit who gets to decide what a cue means and whether it counts as communication: check off the source, receiver, interaction, and message orientations against the Chris Christie and Clinton cases, then inventory communication communities and their cultural codes, shared repertoires of meaning, plausible deniability, rule-governed and marked behavior, and the value hierarchy that ranks cues from lauded to stigmatized.
key_concepts: Researchers have taken a range of perspectives on who decides whether something counts as communicative and what it means, and their decision about where it is best to place the arbiter of meaning is known as their orientation.

A source orientation holds that whether something is communicative and what it means is up to the person engaging in the cues, as when Chris Christie told the press that his marked facial expression was just his face.

A receiver orientation holds that anything a receiver interprets as a message is communication regardless of source intent or awareness, an orientation that originated with the axiom that one cannot not communicate.

An interaction orientation, based on Stamp and Knapp, asserts that people in communication typically work together to determine the intent and meaning of a message, with shared meaning emerging jointly as they talk about what behaviors meant.

The message orientation moves the determination of meaning toward the larger communicative system in which behaviors occurred, viewing communication as arising from only those behaviors that form a socially shared coding system, and it forms the foundation for the social meaning model of nonverbal behavior.
Communication communities are any group of people who share a communication or cultural code, and such communities do not need to be based on national boundaries.
A communication or cultural code is defined as a historically enacted, socially constructed system of terms, meanings, premises, and rules pertaining to communicative conduct.

Within any cultural code, there are agreed-upon meanings for behavior, and usually for almost any behavior there are multiple possible meanings that are all legitimate, possible, or accepted within the community.

The same extended-hand gesture that can mean talk to the hand in the United States is called the mouthzah and is a deep insult in Greece, showing that the cultural code dictates which meanings are possible and which ones are not.

Because there are multiple, accepted meanings for behaviors, people can deny that another's interpretation of their behavior was accurate, an ability known as plausible deniability that can be part of deception or can be used to set the record straight.

Each speech community has a set of rules for the use of nonverbal communication, understood both as observable patterns of behavior and as what is taught about what people should or should not do, and behavior that deviates from norms is said to be marked.

The values of a speech community explain some of the use of behaviors and their repertoire of meanings, and the behaviors people use exist within a hierarchy from lauded and preferred at the top down to stigmatized, taboo, or against the law at the bottom.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Codes and Their Functions
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with code cards snapping into place beside icons of a body, a voice, two touching hands, and a clock; a fear signal splits into five channels, a direct gaze card lands in both the relational and influence cells, and a film strip unwinds with the caption Communication is a process, not a snapshot.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix that matches each nonverbal code to its channel: drop the body, kinesics, vocalics, haptics, proxemics, chronemics, and artifacts into their cells, then map the communication functions from identity display and emotion to relational messages, coordination, influence, and deception, testing the assumptions that one cue can serve many functions and one function many cues, a feat called equifinality, and that the codes only gain meaning as a dynamic, integrated process.
key_concepts: The term code is employed by nonverbal scholars to define the set of signals that is transmitted via one particular medium or channel, and nonverbal codes are often defined by the human sense or senses they stimulate and/or the carrier of the signal.

The body is a vehicle for conveying messages through physical appearance, adornments, and olfactics (or smells), including natural features of the body as well as grooming, hair styling, clothing, tattoos, personal objects such as jewelry, and fragrances.

Kinesics, known in the popular vernacular as body language, refers to body movements that are used to convey messages, including facial expressions, head movements, eye behavior, gestures, posture, and gait.

Vocal activity forms another category of performance codes known variously as paralanguage, prosody, or vocalics, and it includes dialect, pitch, tempo, resonance, pauses, dysfluencies, and intonation patterns.

Haptics refers to the use of touch as a communication system, whereas proxemics refers to the use of space and distance to communicate, and together these form what the authors call the contact codes.

Chronemics is the use of time to communicate, and artifacts (sometimes called objectics) and environment involve the use and arrangement of architecture and objects to communicate, together forming the time and place codes.

The various nonverbal codes simultaneously send forth a stream of information, and it is the totality of all the codes, or their juxtaposition to one another and their degree of congruence or incongruence, that produces meaningful patterns.

Nonverbal communication is a process: it is an ongoing, dynamic unfolding rather than just a static snapshot of cues, and the media's tendency to use photographs takes the cue out of the larger process and context in which it was embedded.
Functions are the purposes, motives, or goals of communication, and a single nonverbal cue may serve multiple functions while a single function may be accomplished through multiple nonverbal cues.

The ability of a single function to be accomplished through multiple nonverbal cues is known as equifinality, as when fear is expressed vocally, facially, posturally, proxemically, haptically, or through any combination of these channels.

Ekman and Friesen proposed five functions of nonverbal behavior as part of language: redundancy (duplicating the verbal message), substitution (replacing it), complementation (amplifying it), emphasis (highlighting it), and contradiction (sending opposite signals).

Coordinating interaction involves how nonverbal cues oversee conversations from the first hello to the last good-bye, including greeting rituals, turn-taking, departures, and patterns of matched or mismatched interaction.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Skills, Deficits, and the Streams of Evidence
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena built as a staircase: skill tokens labeled expressivity and sensitivity light the way up past a competence mirror and an emotional intelligence gauge; on one side a 3D virtual classroom trains youths with autism and a Möbius syndrome teen is coached to gesture; on the other side gates open onto a Paris Metro experiment, a doctor-patient gaze study, and a field ethnography tent.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss of the chapter's back half: level up on the skill system, from expressivity and sensitivity to communication competence, emotional intelligence, and social intelligence, then face the deficit conditions that make encoding and decoding hard, from autism spectrum disorder and nonverbal learning disorders to Möbius syndrome, and finally run the research gauntlet through the six heritages and the methods, experiments, observation, ethology, discourse, ethnography, and surveys, that ground every claim in the book.
key_concepts: Nonverbal skills encompass specific competencies that enhance the course of a social interaction so that the goals or functions of the interaction are more likely to be achieved.

Riggio grouped nonverbal skills into categories, the primary two of which are expressivity (or encoding skill) and sensitivity (decoding skill), with a third category of control and a fourth of interaction skills.

Nonverbal sending abilities or expressivity entail the capacity to encode and express oneself in ways that can be received and decoded accurately by others, and such skills can be improved, as when researchers trained adolescents in eye contact, facial expressions, gestures, and stance and the teens then encoded those cues in their job interviews.

Nonverbal receiving abilities, also called nonverbal sensitivity, entail the capacity to notice and/or accurately decode others' nonverbal cues, and people who are better at decoding facial and vocal cues are less likely to be depressed and more likely to have positive relationships.

Women are typically more expressive nonverbally than men are in public or social settings, their expressions are usually read more accurately by others, and women also tend to be better decoders of nonverbal cues than are men, with the advantage greatest for facial expressions.
Communication competence is knowledge of what behaviors are expected, appropriate, and effective in a given context along with specific skills to put that knowledge into practice.

Goleman proposes five dimensions of emotional intelligence, self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills, and Morand says a key part of emotional intelligence is the ability to decode others' emotions from their nonverbal cues.

Social intelligence is adaptive intelligence that relies substantially on nonverbal communication, and being competent at conventional intelligence tests does not guarantee that one can adjust to different environments and succeed in the real world.

Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by impairments in social interaction and atypical repetitive body movements, and people with ASD do not attend to others' faces as much as typically functioning people do.

People with nonverbal learning disorder tend to have strong verbal ability coupled with poor nonverbal cognition, while dyssemia is a more specific nonverbal learning disability that centers on decoding skills.

Teenagers with Möbius syndrome, who are not able to be facially responsive, were trained to increase their use of other nonverbal cues such as gestures, and doing so increased the perception of rapport in their interactions.

Manusov brought together six research heritages that have shaped nonverbal scholarship: the rhetorical, linguistic, sociological, cultural, ethological, and psychological heritages, and researchers in these traditions rely on methods from laboratory experiments and observation to ethnography and surveys.

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: Darwin, Natural Selection and the Fight to Survive
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over Darwin's 1859 volume and lands on a giraffe whose neck lengthens across generations, while a hunter-gatherer's brain lights up at the taste of sugar; a selection gauge stamps SELECTED FOR on advantageous traits and SELECTED AGAINST on others, and Perry's neural circuits link two figures in a handshake.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the origins of the bio-evolutionary paradigm: how behaviors like smiling, blushing and sweating were adaptive for our ancestors, why evolution is change in a species' characteristics over time, how Darwin's theory of natural selection explains why advantageous traits survive while disadvantageous ones die out, the four principles of natural selection, the giraffe-neck and sugar-preference examples, and how evolutionary psychologists apply selection pressure to the human mind, bonding, teamwork, smiling and touch.
key_concepts: A bio-evolutionary explanation suggests that behaviors such as smiling when happy, blushing when embarrassed, and sweating when nervous were adaptive for our ancestors and passed on to us.

Charles Darwin stated in 1872 that one of the most important adaptations humans can make is to learn to collaborate with others, because through human interaction, cooperation, and bonding we create the relationships needed to survive, reproduce, and protect each other.

The term evolution refers to changes observed over time in the physical characteristics of organisms, such as changes in the average length of the giraffe's neck or the average height of the adult human.
Contrary to popular belief, evolution was not discovered by Darwin, who instead offered his theory of natural selection as an explanation for how the process of evolution works.
Darwin's theory suggests that certain members of a species have traits that provide them advantages, relative to others in their species, with respect to survival and reproduction.
Many traits that provide advantages are at least partially heritable, which means they are passed from parents to their offspring genetically instead of through socialization.

Because organisms with advantageous traits are more likely than others to survive and reproduce, those advantageous traits will be passed on to future generations, whereas less advantageous traits will eventually die out.

The process of natural selection rests on four principles: more of a given species are born than can survive, individuals vary in cognitive, emotional, and physical ways, some of that variation is passed genetically from parents to offspring, and advantageous inherited characteristics are passed on with greater frequency.

Sugar doesn't taste sweet because it is sweet: sweetness is a sensation created by our brains, and the preference for sweets may have an evolutionary basis because sugar is an essential fuel that encouraged our hunter-gatherer ancestors to consume what they needed to survive.

Evolutionary psychologists argue that the human mind has been shaped by natural selection just as much as the human body has, so cognitive and emotional characteristics like intelligence, sensitivity, and even humor could also be advantageous.

According to Perry, some of the most powerful and complex neural systems in the human brain are dedicated to social affiliation and communication, because it is through interdependent relationships, families, clans, communities and societies that we survive and thrive.

Nonverbal behaviors related to liking and cooperation, including smiling and touch, may have evolved as key ways of connecting with group members and mates, since teamwork helped our ancestors hunt food, gather supplies, and protect each other from danger.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Body: Psychophysiology, Fear, Stress and Zoom Fatigue
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen debate: an evolutionary psychologist on one side argues WHY, a psychophysiologist on the other scans HOW, with a fear body map lighting up pupils, heart, sweat glands and the adrenal gland; a Zoom grid slides in where faces loom close, a voice meter reads 15 percent louder, and a fatigue gauge spikes while dopamine and oxytocin molecules drift from a face-to-face conversation.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between evolutionary psychology and psychophysiology: whether the why of a behavior can live apart from the how of the body, how fear's dilated pupils, racing heart and cortisol flood are survival machinery, how stress can debilitate yet also spark personal growth, and why videoconferencing rearranges our inborn proxemic, gaze, voice and neurochemical responses so that Zoom calls fatigue us.
key_concepts: The field of psychophysiology assumes that cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and social events are all reflected in the body's physiological processes.
Experiencing fear is associated with several hormonal reactions, nervous system activities, and muscular responses that distinguish it from other emotional experiences such as sadness or surprise.
Evolutionary psychology can often explain why a certain behavioral or emotional tendency is beneficial, but psychophysiology can explain how.

When you are afraid, your pupils dilate, increasing your visual acuity so you can better assess the threat, while increases in your heart rate and respiration provide extra fuel to your muscles in case you have to fight or flee.

When you are afraid you perspire more so your body doesn't overheat, and your adrenal gland increases production of the hormone cortisol, which suppresses nonessential bodily systems so that your energy can be used more efficiently.

Heightened and persistent stress can be debilitating, but physiological stress also indicates to us that we are in a state that requires repair and healing, and incidents that cause stress can lead people to find ways to benefit from it through personal growth.

Virtual forms of communication such as Zoom represent a dramatic technological disruption of our usual nonverbal communication, altering it in ways that cause cognitive and affective overloading, according to virtual communication expert Jeremy Bailenson.

With Zoom we are much closer than usual and need to maintain nearly constant eye contact or be seen as disinterested, whereas when we talk to people face to face we stand at a distance that gives us a proxemic buffer.

We also talk 15% louder than usual on Zoom, perhaps because we think people won't understand us as well if we speak at our normal decibel level, which again requires a higher output of energy than is typical of conversation.

As Bailenson puts it, Zoom smothers you with cues and they aren't synchronous, and it takes a physiological toll, because the sudden mass adoption of technology is disrupting the normal, instinctual, and fine-tuned way of communicating that developed to help humans survive.

Studies indicate that face-to-face conversation results in the release of neurotransmitters like dopamine, linked to feelings of pleasure, and the hormone oxytocin, so we get more biochemical bang for our buck during face-to-face contact because it offers a richer stream of social signals.

assets.topic: Audit the Face and Voice: Universal Displays, Pride, Tears and Pitch
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with a UNIVERSAL stamp over an eyebrow flash, a winners' podium where athletes raise their arms, tilt back their heads and puff out their chests while losers slump their shoulders, a tear drop magnified to show its extra protein, potassium and manganese, and a pitch meter swinging between a low dominant growl and a soft high affectionate murmur with a ballot box beside it.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the face and voice against the evidence: check off the eyebrow flash, the universal thesis of emotion displays, the Olympic portraits of pride and shame, the smiling and fearful faces of infants and of the blind, the facial feedback hypothesis, the chemistry of emotional tears, and the vocalics of pitch, dominance and affection.
key_concepts: The eyebrow flash, an almost imperceptible and fleeting raising of the eyebrows, appears to have an innate basis because of its universality, and it is used as a friendly greeting in a number of widely different cultures.

The universal thesis holds that if emotional displays are primarily rooted in bio-evolution, people around the world should encode and decode emotions such as joy, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and disgust similarly, and many investigations have supported it.

In Tracy and Matsumoto's study of athletes at the 2004 Olympic and Paralympic Games, winners from 36 countries, whether sighted or blind from birth, showed universal signs of pride including raised arms, fisted or outstretched hands, back head tilts, smiles, an expanded chest, and a pushed-out torso.

Tracy and Matsumoto suggest that pride displays may have evolved as a survival mechanism that allows people to telegraph to others that they are strong and powerful and therefore should not be challenged.

Infants begin smiling in response to external sights, sounds, and other stimuli around the end of their first month, and these expressions appear at about the same age for infants all around the globe.

Blind children tend to display facial expressions similar to those displayed by sighted children, and adults who had been blind since birth show virtually no differences from sighted adults in the expressions used to communicate happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, or disgust.

The facial feedback hypothesis suggests that merely engaging in a facial display of emotion will spark physiological changes that are consistent with that emotion, and in one experiment enacting fear, sadness, anger, surprise, and happiness increased heart rate while displays of disgust decreased it.

Human beings are the only creatures who genuinely cry in times of sorrow, and from the bio-evolutionary perspective crying contributes to our survival by signaling our distress and promoting prosocial behaviors in caregivers.
Many researchers now believe that we cry not because we're upset but because we're trying to recover from being upset, which is why you often feel a little better after having a good cry.

Emotional tears are quite different from basal and reflex tears chemically, containing up to 25% more types of protein and 400% more potassium than basal or reflex tears, and as much as 30 times more manganese than your bloodstream.

The pitch of your voice relates to how high or low it sounds and is determined by the length of your vocal folds, so the longer your vocal folds, the lower your voice, which is why men's voices are usually lower than women's and adults' lower than children's.

Loud, low-pitched voices are associated with perceptions of aggression and dominance, and studies have even shown that people are more likely to vote for a political candidate with a lower-pitched voice, a preference especially strong in a wartime scenario.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Touch, Pupils and the Signals That Bind Us
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix labeled TOUCH, AFFECTION and PUPILS; cards fly into place: an emperor's row of empty cribs, an orphanage ward, a joey in a kangaroo pouch, a massage table, an fMRI machine where a woman grips her husband's hand, a pair of eyes with a wide dilated pupil, a belladonna leaf, and a candlelit table where two diners' pupils open in the dim light.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of the body's bonding signals: drop the evidence cards into their cells, the emperor's doomed newborns, the orphanage babies, the Kangaroo Method and the Touch Research Institute into TOUCH, oxytocin's calm and the hand-holding fMRI study into AFFECTION, and Hess's pupils, the constrict-then-dilate pattern, belladonna and the candlelit dinner into PUPILS. Then close the ledger with what each cell says about survival, health and attraction.
key_concepts: Touch is the first of the five senses to develop and the most important sense for survival, because without the ability to feel touch one would constantly be susceptible to injury, extreme temperatures, and other environmental threats that could easily prove fatal.

Emperor Frederick II of Germany once put 50 newborn babies in the care of nurses who were told only to feed and bathe them but not to hold, comfort, or speak to them, and all the infants died before the emperor learned what language they would speak naturally.

Evidence from orphanages around the world showed that infants who were not touched tended to die before their first birthdays or develop psychological problems, whereas those who were cuddled frequently tended to thrive.

The Kangaroo Method, developed by Dr. Edgar Rey Sanabria, involves mothers holding their premature babies close against their chests with skin touching skin for long periods, and it reduces mortality rates among infants while having long-term positive effects on sleep patterns and reactions to stress.

Touch therapy has documented benefits for a huge range of conditions including anorexia, asthma, dermatitis, diabetes, HIV, hypertension, leukemia, nicotine addiction, Parkinson's disease, and sleep disorders, along with increases in the hormone oxytocin and decreases in heart rate and blood pressure.

The hormone oxytocin, released by the pituitary gland, has stress-alleviating effects on the body: it lowers blood pressure and heart rate, increases metabolism, suppresses pain, and promotes a feeling of calmness and pleasantness.

In one fMRI study, happily married women subjected to threats of electric shock experienced significantly less neurological arousal when holding their husband's hand than when holding no one's hand, and even holding a male stranger's hand was significantly better than holding no hand at all.

Affection behaviors, especially nonverbal ones, are thought to have evolved largely from maternal protective behaviors, as the protecting, cuddling, and attending that mothers gave infants for centuries gradually evolved into hugging, kissing, and caressing.

Besides being affected by light, pupil dilation is also affected by attraction: early research on pupil dilation showed that when people look at someone they find attractive, their pupils open up wider than normal because the nervous system becomes aroused.

A recent set of seven experiments challenged that finding, showing that the more attractive the face, the more pupils constricted at first, and only as people continued to look at the most attractive faces did their pupils begin to dilate.

All other things being equal, we find people with wide, dilated pupils more physically appealing than people with narrow, contracted pupils, and women in earlier centuries sometimes used a toxic herb called belladonna to dilate their pupils for cosmetic effect.

From the bio-evolutionary perspective, pupil dilation matters because attraction is often the first step toward developing a relationship, and dilated pupils allow us to take in more visual information about a person to help us decide whether they are a potential relational partner, all outside conscious control.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Beauty Code, the Nose's Mate Scan and the Grand Theory
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a judgment hall where a composite face morphs from 2 to 32 faces and grows more attractive, a symmetry dial, a waist-to-hip ratio gauge pinned at .70, a line of t-shirts being sniffed while an MHC ledger compares genetic pairs, and a three-tier tower labeled Emotion I, Emotion II and Emotion III with a scale weighing culture's obvious causes against biology's hidden ones.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the claim that beauty is in the eye of the beholder: walk the evidence that judgments of attractiveness are consistent across cultures and centuries, test symmetry, averageness, the .70 waist-to-hip ratio and the multiple fitness model against reproductive success, trace the nose's subconscious MHC mate scan through the t-shirt experiments, then enter Buck's grand theory of Emotion I, II and III and weigh the strength and the limitation of the bio-evolutionary perspective itself.
key_concepts: Contrary to the belief that beauty is in the eye of the beholder, people show strong agreement in what they find physically attractive, and many of our judgments about beauty are highly consistent across cultures and even across time periods.

Research suggests that we are most attracted to physical features that signal health and fertility, because from the evolutionary perspective the primary reason for forming romantic relationships is procreation and the production of healthy offspring.

Symmetry, the extent to which two sides of the body or face mirror each other, is an important marker of genetic quality, because genetic abnormalities and environmental stressors cause deviation and only the most genetically fit people can maintain symmetric development in the face of such challenges.

Sir Francis Galton stumbled upon the averageness effect when composite faces representing the average of known criminals turned out to be more attractive than individual faces, and later research found that the more faces that were morphed together, the more attractive the composite face was rated.

Some research suggests that averageness is an even more important ingredient in the recipe for an attractive face than is symmetry, especially for women, and the main appeal of symmetry may be that it is normative.

Across cultures, and even across time periods, the preferred waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) for adult women has been about .70, meaning that women are seen as maximally attractive when their waists are approximately 70% the width of their hips, no matter what the absolute measurements are.

Research found that women whose WHR was under .80 were more than twice as likely to get pregnant following 12 rounds of artificial insemination as were women with WHR over .80, supporting the idea that a WHR close to .70 corresponds to maximum reproductive success.

According to the multiple fitness model, people consistently prefer female faces with large eyes, prominent cheekbones, thicker lips, and a small nose and chin, preferences that are consistent across men and women, across different ethnicities, and across different age groups.

Each of us has a set of genes known as the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), which plays an important role in the health of our immune systems, and it is most adaptive to be sexually attracted to a partner with an MHC dissimilar to your own so that children inherit the strengths of both immune systems.

In Wedekind and Furi's t-shirt study, several men each wore the same t-shirts for a week without washing them, and both women and men rated the odor of each shirt as more pleasant if the man had MHC genes dissimilar to their own than if he had similar MHC genes.

Buck's general theory holds that nonverbal displays such as touches, pheromone releases, facial expressions, and vocalizations represent the publicly observable side of motivations, emotions, and cognitions, with sentic patterns like odors, touch, and vocalizations working best at close range and being innate, universal, and cross-cultural.

A key strength of the bio-evolutionary perspective is its ability to account for behaviors that are consistent across cultures and time periods, such as the preference for symmetry observed across cultures, centuries, and even species, but its limitation is that it deals with causes, like inherited genes for aggression, that are sometimes difficult to see.

assets.topic: Scrub the Cultural Code: Bowing, Co-Cultures, and Culture-Specific Studies
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides across a Japanese street where a salaryman bows 15 degrees to an acquaintance and 45 degrees to an elder, then lands on a Medieval courtier scraping his right foot while bowing; a flowchart grows branches for co-cultures and intersectionality while a map of Appalachia lights up with 1,612 collected tunes and a fortune chicken tied with a red ribbon rests in the corner.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the cultural foundations of nonverbal behavior: how most of our use of nonverbal cues is deeply ingrained in our larger culture despite the belief that cues are universal, how culture is a learned pattern of beliefs, values, and behaviors, how co-cultures and intersectionality shape differing norms, how the Japanese bow (ojigi) scales from the 15-degree eshaku to the face-down dogeza, how the Medieval European bow and scrape became ironic, how a nonverbal marker can signal a stigmatized identity, and what deep-dive culture-specific studies reveal about Finnish silence, the Taiwanese fortune chicken, and Cecil Sharp's hunt for the lost folk music of Appalachia.
key_concepts: Most of our use of nonverbal cues, and particularly the messages that we use them for, is affected by and deeply ingrained in our larger culture, even though people often think that nonverbal cues constitute a universal communication code.

Scholars in fields such as anthropology and communication often define culture as a learned and enduring pattern of beliefs, values, and behaviors that influence a large group of people, learned through interaction with one's family and friends, from the media, and from social and religious institutions.

A co-culture refers to a group of people within a given culture who share particular ways of thinking and behaving that may differ from the larger culture in which they live, and these sociological groupings can be tied to religion, ethnicity, age, social class, geographic location, physical ability, sexual orientation, and/or gender.
When co-cultures combine, as when someone is both Black and female, to create particular norms for interaction and identity, it is known as intersectionality.

A nonverbal marker is a cue that signifies that a person is a member of a group, and because not all co-cultures are valued equally within a larger culture, such markers can signify what is called a stigmatized identity, as when those with physical movement differences are viewed as a separate co-culture.

In some East and South Asian cultures, such as India, Taiwan, Vietnam, and Korea, bowing symbolizes much more than a simple greeting or departing behavior, as it can show respect, sincerity, humility, or remorse.

In contemporary Japan, bowing or ojigi is a fundamental part of social life, with the eshaku a 15-degree bow used around acquaintances for thanking or casually greeting, the keirei at 30 degrees used in business contexts, and the saikeirei at 45 degrees the most formal bow used to show respect to someone of very high status.

The least common Japanese bow is known as dogeza, and it is only used in extremely serious circumstances such as when a mistake is made that led to the death of another person, requiring the person bowing to get on their hands and knees and place their face to the ground.

Starting in Medieval Europe and continuing through the Renaissance, bowing was a purely masculine activity accompanied by a scrape, drawing back the right leg when bowing so the right foot scrapes the floor while the right hand presses horizontally across the abdomen and the left hand is held out from the body, though today the scrape and bow is done only ironically.

Carbaugh and colleagues identified terms in Finnish that refer specifically to quietude as a value, such as hiljaisuus, and found that in social scenes one can be identified as in one's thoughts and thus should be undisturbed, so people in Finland have crafted communicative practices that reflect the value of silence.

Huang and colleagues studied the fortune chicken, a common gift given to married couples by their parents in Taiwan that signifies family, fertility, and blessings, which originally took the form of a live hen and rooster tied to one another with a 9-foot red ribbon.

In the Sounds of Appalachia study, Cecil Sharp made three collecting trips to the Appalachians between 1916 and 1918, and fifty-two weeks spent in the field yielded 1,612 tunes, including variants, from 281 singers, altogether representing about 500 different songs.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Dimensions: Individualism vs. Collectivism and the Emotional Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table with an individualist on one side and a collectivist on the other while a projector shows Hofstede's bar chart of 40 nations, the Friesen film lab where a Japanese viewer smiles over a stressful film, two emoticon panels, horizontal open-mouthed versus vertical eye-oriented, and a closet split between self-expressive clothes and branded status clothes; a caption reads display rules apply.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between an individualist and a collectivist: debate the five cultural dimensions that connect to nonverbal communication, Hofstede's ranking of the United States as most individualistic, the value of privacy and spontaneous expression versus harmony and loyalty, the Friesen film experiment in which Japanese viewers replaced negative emotion with smiles, emoticon preferences in Twitter data from 78 countries, the Hispanic values of personalismo, simpátia, confianza, respeto, and familismo, and how independent versus interdependent self-construals show up in smiles, neutral faces, and clothing purchases. Then weigh the cultural display rules that govern when emotions may be shown at all.
key_concepts: Five cultural dimensions in particular are connected to nonverbal communication: individualism/collectivism, immediacy/non-immediacy (contact/noncontact), low/high power distance, low/high context, and feminine/masculine orientations, and although sometimes described as competing characteristics, they are best seen as ends of continua with cultures falling toward one end or the other.

In Hofstede's study of 40 nations, the United States rated the highest in terms of individualism, followed by Australia, Great Britain, Canada, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Italy, Belgium, Denmark, and France.

People in individualistic cultures are likely to value personal space, autonomy, privacy, freedom, and the right to express themselves verbally and emotionally, and these values become manifest in the rules and meaning for nonverbal cues.

People in collectivist cultures tend to value harmony among people and between people and nature, emphasize togetherness, loyalty, and tradition, and inhibit expressions of negative emotions that could upset the balance of harmony within one's family or broader social group.

Researchers have found that individuals from collectivistic cultures have a harder time recognizing and identifying other people's facial expressions of negative emotion than do people from individualistic cultures.

In Friesen's study, when people from Japan and the United States viewed highly stressful films alone they expressed emotions such as fear, disgust, anger, and sadness similarly, but when they were in the presence of another person, people from the United States tended to express negative emotions whereas people from Japan tended to inhibit them and replace them with smiles.

Using Twitter data from 78 countries, Park and colleagues found that people from cultures labeled as individualistic preferred horizontal and open-mouthed emoticons, whereas people in countries labeled collectivist favored vertical and eye-oriented emoticons.

According to García and colleagues, the primary values of Hispanics who live in the United States include personalismo (preference for warm relationships), simpátia (preference for smooth relationships free of criticism), confianza (trust), respeto (respect in all interactions but particularly with the elderly, educated, and people in authority), and familismo (emphasis on family, loyalty, cooperation, and interdependence), all reflecting a greater collectivist orientation.

Self-construals are conceptualized as a constellation of thoughts, feelings, and actions concerning one's relationship to others and the self as distinct from others, with individuals in any culture having a more independent (self-oriented) or interdependent (relationally oriented) self-construal.

Matsumoto and Kupperbusch found that the US white women they studied exhibited similar facial expressions when alone, but interdependent women tended to smile or display neutral facial expressions when watching a film with someone else more than did those with more independent self-construals.

Millan and Reynolds found that those with independent construals were more likely to buy clothes that helped them express themselves, whereas people with interdependent self-construals favored branded clothes that showed status relative to others.

Cultures develop cultural display rules that guide how, when, and with whom cultural members are to show emotion, and in Izard's study people from some parts of Africa had difficulty decoding facial expressions of disgust/contempt, probably because the Africans they studied had display rules that discouraged them from showing this emotion.

assets.topic: Audit Contact, Power, and Context: Immediacy, Power Distance, and the Context Continuum
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger stretched over a world map: a contact/noncontact column stamps the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Northern Europe, a pedestrian crosswalk counter ticks 2% versus 25% for smiles and nods, a coffee pot pours with the left hand and is accepted with the right, a boss towers over a seated employee labeled power distance, and a context slider runs from a Japanese rock garden on one end to a US television spot on the other.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit three more dimensions against the evidence: check off Edward Hall's contact and noncontact cultures and the pedestrian study showing 1% to 2% of Japanese versus 9% to 25% of US passersby smiling, nodding, or speaking, stamp the expressive Arabs with their expansive gestures and coffee rituals, tick the climate gradient of touch, log the abrazo hug and cheek-kissing greetings, then audit power distance from Hofstede's index to Matsumoto's theory of which emotions flow up and down the hierarchy, and close the books on high- and low-context cultures, from Japanese rock gardens and Dubai's nonverbal refusals to the Russian suspicion of smiles.
key_concepts: Edward Hall identified different nations as contact or noncontact cultures based on how much people from various countries touched as well as how close people stood to each other during conversation, focusing on proxemics patterns in and across cultures in his book The Hidden Dimension.

The Middle East, the Mediterranean area of Europe, Eastern Europe and Russia, Northern Africa, Central America, and South America are generally characterized as contact cultures, whereas Northern Europe, Great Britain, and most Asian countries have been classified as primarily noncontact cultures.

In Patterson's pedestrian study, only 1% to 2% of Japanese passersby smiled, nodded, or spoke to a research confederate compared to 9% to 25% of people from the United States, and Japanese passersby tended to respond with low levels of immediacy regardless of what the confederate did.

People from Arab countries tend to display emotions in a largely expressive manner through facial expressions, expansive gestures, touch, and loud, animated voices, consistent with Arabic cultural values that include living life to the utmost and showing pride in oneself and one's culture.

Serving and receiving coffee in traditional ways, including pouring with the left hand but serving and accepting with the right, drinking no less than two and no more than three cups, and filling the cup to specified heights, are all part of traditional Arabic coffee rituals that likewise reflect respect and hierarchy.

Pennebaker and colleagues found that within many countries, such as Croatia, Italy, Japan, Serbia, Switzerland, and the United States, people living in southern regions were more expressive than people living in northern regions.

People in South American countries often engage in a hug called the abrazo when greeting one another, which involves putting one's arms fully around another person and then patting their back heartily two or three times, while people in some Asian countries greet one another by bowing, with the lowest and longest bows reserved for the most highly respected.

Power distance refers to the degree of social inequality or hierarchy that exists within a given culture, and Hofstede coined the term power distance index to refer to the degree to which a co-culture or individual member of a culture is separated from another in terms of power.

In high power distance cultures, communication often functions to reinforce status differences, with people of lower status likely to engage in submissive nonverbal behavior and to hide negative emotions, especially when in the presence of high-status others.

Matsumoto theorized that individuals in cultures characterized by high power distance are likely to display positive emotions to higher-status others as a way of showing respect, while high-status individuals should feel freer to express negative emotion and criticism to lower-status others.

In high-context cultures, information is found in the physical environment or within people rather than in messages themselves, so there is a heavy reliance on nonverbal forms of expression, whereas people in low-context cultures find the majority of information needed to interpret a message within the message itself.

Russians tend to view smiling as inauthentic and so withhold smiles in conversation, whereas US Americans tend to smile freely as a sign of friendliness, and in societies where corruption is high, smiling may signify distrust.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Emblems, Gaze, Time, and the Global Gesture Chart
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled EMBLEMS, AFFECT AND GAZE, TOUCH and TIME; cards fly into place, a waving hand labeled come here flips its meaning from hello to good-bye as it crosses borders, a veiled woman gestures expressively, a monochronic road-clock splits into segments while a polychronic diffuse clock pools, and a world map blazes with the O.K. gesture labeled zero in France, money in Japan, and obscene in South America.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix matching cross-cultural evidence to its cell: drop the emblem definitions and the come here gesture with its good-bye meaning in Italy, China, and Colombia into EMBLEMS, place the expansive Arab gestures, the veiled woman's gesturing hands, the Middle East's extended eye contact, the African rule of averting eyes from high-status speakers, and the Arab preference for loud speech into AFFECT AND GAZE, file the Bush-Abdullah hand-holding into TOUCH, and sort the monochronic and polychronic clocks, the US future orientation, and the O.K., thumbs-up, V sign, and hang loose gestures onto the global chart, including the Nixon O.K. scandal in South America.
key_concepts: Emblems are gestures that substitute for language, and because emblems have literal translations and are tied to language, it should not be surprising that emblematic gestures are used differently across cultures, just as different words make up different languages.

The come here gesture used in the United States, which involves moving one's fingers and palm back and forth toward one's body, means good-bye in countries such as Italy, China, and Colombia, and it means hello and good-bye in Algeria.

In Mexico and the Caribbean the hang loose gesture is associated with alcohol, and in parts of Asia it means 6 when counting (5 for the thumb plus 1), showing that even a gesture adopted from Hawai'i takes on new meanings as it travels.

Arabs are likely to use expansive gestures as a way to show involvement and to express themselves, and for Arab Muslim women who are wearing veils that cover their faces, gesturing can substitute for facial expression as a way of conveying emotional information.

People from the Middle East generally engage in more frequent and extended eye contact than do North Americans, whereas people in some parts of Africa are taught to avoid eye contact when listening, especially when the person speaking is of high status.
Arab cultures are characterized by louder speech than most cultures, presumably because loudness connotes strength and sincerity to Arabs, whereas softness communicates weakness and deviousness.

Hand-holding between Arab men in public is the warmest expression of affection and does not have sexual meaning, which is why President George W. Bush walking hand in hand with King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia was un-Texan to Americans but a sign of friendship and equal status in the Middle East.

In monochronic cultures people tend to focus on one task at a time and to adhere to schedules, seeing time like a road that extends from the past to the future and can be divided into segments, whereas people in polychronic cultures tend to focus on multiple tasks simultaneously and see time as flexible and diffused, with more focus on human interaction than on adhering to schedules.

Gonzalez and Zimbardo found that only 9% of people from the United States reported being primarily oriented toward the present and only 1% reported being oriented toward the past, with most people reporting either a balanced orientation or an orientation focused primarily on the future.

The O.K. gesture means money or coin in Japan, worthless or zero in France and parts of Switzerland, and an obscene gesture in various countries, and when then-US Vice President Richard Nixon displayed it in South America in the 1950s it was considered obscene there because it symbolized the female genitalia.

The thumbs-up gesture means speak up or turn up the volume in parts of South America, 1 when counting in parts of Central Europe, 5 when counting in parts of Asia, and an insult in Iran and parts of South America.
The V sign made with the open palm toward one's face is an insult in Australia, Great Britain, and South Africa, where it means that you are acting like an animal with horns.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Intercultural Minefields, Bias, and the Cultured Mind
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a courthouse corridor: a judge's gavel freezes above a laughing Chinese woman, then shifts to a world stage where Rabin hesitates and Arafat reaches out, a negotiation table splits between relaxed Canadian postures and Chinese space-occupying stances, a clock-gift card flips from friendship in Malaysia to short life in China, and a wall of falling masks labeled stereotypes, microaggressions, and ethnocentrism crashes down as two teenagers in Paris and Miami reach toward each other through a COVID-19 glass partition.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the challenge of interpreting across cultures: walk the court case where a judge mistook a Chinese woman's nervous laughter for mockery, negotiate the Arafat-Rabin handshake where Rabin hesitated before accepting, read the Canadian and Chinese dominance displays at the negotiation table, then defeat the traps of equifinality and polysemy with the Chinese clock gift that wishes a short life, harness convergence and divergence and the textism followers of the powerful, and finish by storming the walls of the challenges: stereotypes that made Arab and US students mistrust each other, nonverbal race bias and racial microaggressions, haptic norms that change over time from Paris and Miami teenagers to COVID-19 social distancing, and the ethnocentric lens that makes each culture prefer its own behaviors.
key_concepts: In Vargas-Urpi's study of immigration workers in Catalan, Spain, Chinese patterns of smiling and laughing were often misinterpreted, as when a judge got mad at a Chinese woman who laughed while being told off because she was in a difficult situation and her culture lets her laugh then.

At their 1994 meeting, Yasser Arafat was reportedly comfortable with a high-contact greeting such as a hearty handshake accompanied by cheek kissing, while Yitzhak Rabin agreed to the handshake only after being assured there would be no cheek kissing, and most Israelis interpreted Rabin's hesitation before accepting the handshake as a reluctant willingness to negotiate rather than as an insult.

Adair and Semnani-Azad found that in negotiations between Canadians and Chinese, Canadian negotiators used more relaxed postures and displayed more negative emotion than their Chinese counterparts, whereas the Chinese negotiators occupied more space at the negotiation table, showing that although all the negotiators displayed dominance, the particular form of the displays varied by culture.

Equifinality is the principle that a given end state can be reached by many potential means or that a goal or communicative function can be achieved in many ways, so people in one culture will learn one set of ways to communicate something that may not be the same as what people from another culture learn.

Polysemy is the idea that the same behavior or set of cues can potentially mean different things, as when presenting the gift of a clock to someone from China amounts to telling the receiver that the giver wants him or her to have a short life, whereas in Malaysia a clock given as a gift symbolizes friendship.

According to communication accommodation theory, developed by Howard Giles to explain why accents change, people often accommodate their own communication style to the style of others in an effort to either converge or diverge, and individuals generally exhibit more convergence when they are with in-group members and people they like.

Adams and colleagues found that most people converged to the amount of textisms they received from others, and those lower in power were particularly likely to converge toward the greater use of textisms by those more powerful than them.

Watson found that because Arabs prefer closer conversational distancing than do people from the United States, Arab students came to regard students from the United States as condescending and aloof, whereas US students regarded Arab students as arrogant and overbearing.

Nonverbal race bias is the nonverbal expression or communication of race-based judgments, and Meadors and Murray found that people used a more closed posture when viewing a photograph showing a person acting inconsistently with their racial stereotype.

Sue and colleagues define racial microaggressions as brief and commonplace daily verbal, behavioral, or environmental indignities, whether intentional or unintentional, that communicate hostile, derogatory, or negative racial slights and insults toward people of color, and many of them are nonverbal, including avoidance behavior.

Haptic and proxemic norms change over time, as shown by Field's finding that teenagers in Paris touched one another significantly more than did teenagers in Miami at McDonald's restaurants, and the United States has been moving toward becoming a more contact-oriented society since Hall's and Jourard's early observations.

When we judge someone from another culture or co-culture through the lens and evaluative frame of our own group, it is called ethnocentrism, and Endrass and colleagues found that people from Germany and Japan each preferred the behaviors generated to resemble their own background.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Visual and Auditory Codes: Kinesics and Vocalics

assets.topic: Scrub the Visual Code: The Scope and Power of Kinesics
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a medical facility where a consultant scans a body; counters tick up an estimated 700,000 physical signs and 20,000 facial expressions while an eye resolves a 1/50-second flash; Emerson's quotation hangs over a nod, a smile, two thumbs up and fists shaken overhead, all signaling approval.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the most powerful of the nonverbal codes: define kinesics, the visible code of body movement that excludes physical contact, and weigh the sheer wealth of its inventory, from Pei's 700,000 physical signs and the face's 20,000 expressions to Krout's 7,777 classroom gestures and Hewes's 1,000 postures. Then test the receiving side: vision's 80 per cent share of sensory perception, movements caught in 1/50 of a second, brain-registered flashes of 125 microseconds, Emerson's ocular dialect, the equifinality of approval signals, and why people rely on kinesic cues more than any other code.
key_concepts: Kinesics is what we commonly (but problematically) know as 'body language,' and it includes all the ways we use the body to express and interpret messages, making it the most elemental wordless way we communicate with one another.

The term kinesics derives from the Greek word for 'movement' and refers to all forms of body movement, excluding physical contact with another's body, including facial, eye, head, trunk, limb, hand, and foot movements as well as postures and gait (how people walk).

Billions of years before written language was developed, humans were using kinesics and vocalics to communicate (Givens, 2020), and they occupy a central place in the assemblage that is nonverbal communication.
Ralph Waldo Emerson opined that '[t]he eyes of men converse as much as their tongues, with the advantage that the ocular dialect needs no dictionary but is understood the world over.'

The face and eyes are commanding because they are always visible and always 'on'; even in repose or in solitude, the body still presents useful information and can reveal internal mood states or emotions (Cohn & Ekman, 2008).

An estimated 700,000 different physical signs can be produced by humans (Pei, 1965), and physiologists have estimated that the 30 or so muscles in the face are capable of displaying 20,000 different expressions (Birdwhistell, 1970).
Krout (1971) observed 7,777 distinct gestures in classroom behavior and 5,000 hand gestures in clinical situations, while Hewes (1957) reported that 1,000 steady human postures are possible.
Vision accounts for around 80% of our sensory perception; the remaining 20% comes from hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling.

Observers can distinguish movements as short as 1/50 of a second, and even fleeting facial expressions and body movements of 125 microseconds that seem to escape conscious observation may still be registered by the brain (McLeod & Rosenthal, 1983).

Because of equifinality, you might approve of something a friend has done with a very brief, almost imperceptible head nod, a vigorous nod, a smile, two thumbs up, or shaking both arms overhead with hands clenched in fists, each transmitting a slight variation on that theme of approval.

People rely more on kinesic cues than any other code to derive meaning from nonverbal messages (Burgoon & Hoobler, 2002), as a result of the innate tendency for those that are sighted to orient to others visually and the overtly noticeable, attention-getting characteristics of kinesics.

assets.topic: Dialogue in Silence: The Zen Parable and the Origins of Kinesics
assets.visual_frame_description: A shrine room where two monks sit in silence while one finger, two fingers, three fingers and a clenched fist float between them; each finger is captioned twice, once Buddha's enlightenment and once the younger monk's insult; beneath them, an infant reaches for a caregiver and Michael Jordan's tongue shows at a basketball game.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage the silent debate between the one-eyed younger monk and the wandering traveler in the temple of northern Japan, then replay both wildly different interpretations of the same raised fingers and clenched fist. Then trace the origins of the kinesic code: Darwin's evolution-wired expressions, the innate tongue display of Michael Jordan, the newborn's Moro reflex and 72-hour-old imitation, intermodal matching, the first-year pointing gesture, gaze fixated on the caregiver's eyes at birth, and the three routes, innate, common-experiential, and culture-specific, by which kinesic expressions are acquired.
key_concepts: In a temple in the northern part of Japan two brother monks were dwelling together, and the elder, who was learned, told the younger, who was stupid and had but one eye, to take his place and 'request the dialogue in silence' when a wandering monk challenged them to a debate.

In the traveler's account of the silent debate, his one finger represented Buddha, the younger monk's two fingers signified Buddha and his teachings, three fingers meant Buddha, his teachings and his followers living the harmonious life, and the clenched fist shaken in his face indicated that all three come from one realization, so he concluded the younger monk had defeated him.

In the younger monk's account, the traveler's one finger insultingly insinuated that he had only one eye, his own two fingers congratulated the stranger on having two eyes, the three fingers suggested that between them they only had three eyes, and he got mad and started to punch the traveler before he ran out.

Charles Darwin, in The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872), noted similarities between the emotional expressions of humans and those of primates and other species, and believed that facial expressions were programmed into the brain in the course of human development due to their importance to survival.

Tongue showing is a kinesic behavior with innate origins: when people are intensely involved in activities requiring concentration, are under stress, feel a loss of control, or are being reprimanded, they often display their tongue, as Michael Jordan was known for doing while playing basketball.

As early as 72 hours old, infants imitate adults' tongue protrusions and head movements, and infants imitate facial gestures as early as two months, an imitation reflex that is innate for most infants, requires little cognitive function, and helps newborns maintain social interaction before their control of gaze, head, and mouth movements develops.

Newborns display many kinesic reflexes in the first few months of life, including a ritualized Moro reflex in which they reach for caregivers who, in turn, respond by lifting them up (Rousseau et al., 2017), and within the first three months infants smile, stare at faces, make eye contact, and display distress, delight, and excitement.

The pointing gesture usually emerges in a child's first year and provides a bridge between nonverbal and verbal expression as children acquire more language skills, with children often looking at a caregiver before pointing, as if first checking that the caregiver is paying attention.

Within a few days of birth, infants appear to fixate on the caregiver's eyes, and simply seeing the eyes of a caregiver is sufficient to produce a smiling reaction, with the distance at which newborns focus best being the distance from the infant to the mother's eyes when breast-feeding (Argyle & Cook, 1976).
Eye contact is necessary for proper maturation of infants, and the lack of mutual gaze impairs infant interaction and perceptual and social development (Andersen, 1985).

Kinesic expressions are acquired in three ways: from innate neurological processes passed on genetically and developed through evolution, from experiences common to all humans as they interact with the environment (such as eating with the hands and witnessing death), and through culture-specific tasks and social interactions that vary across cultures.

Mothers are generally children's 'expert' tutors in emotional expressions, and the affective environment created by mothers, their role as models of expressive behavior, and their responsiveness, especially to children's expressions of distress, are particularly important influences on the socialization of emotional expressions (Denham & Grout, 1993).

assets.topic: Audit the Savvy Traveler's Emblems: Cataloguing Gestures With Precise Meanings
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger on a world map: six checkboxes for the emblem's functions stamp past, three exhibit cards count 200 Persian, 50 Israeli and fewer than 100 US emblems, a Roman cab freezes a driver with arms flat against his sides, Berlusconi pinches his fingers at the G20, and a trading floor shows a palm inward for buy and a palm outward for sell.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the emblem, the gesture with a clear symbolic meaning that stands alone as a speech act: check it against the six criteria, tick off what emblems do from the wave hello to the throat-slashing death sign, and count the ledger from Iran's 200 Persian emblems to Israel's 50 and America's fewer than 100. Then take the audit to Rome, where a taxi driver freezes in astonishment, Berlusconi serves Obama a va-va-voom, Poggi counts 250 conversational gestures, and Sraffa's chin-brush rewrites Wittgenstein, and close the books on the Chicago grain traders' buy-and-sell palms and Kita's four cultural dimensions of iconic gestures.
key_concepts: Emblems are gestures that have a clear symbolic meaning and can stand alone as a speech act, meeting criteria that include having a direct verbal translation, having a precise meaning known by most or all members of a social group, being most often used intentionally to transmit a message, and having clear meaning even when displayed out of context.

Emblems do such things as express greetings (a wave hello), requests (the 'come here' beckoning gesture), insults (the cuckold horns), threats (the pistol shot gesture with forefinger and thumb), physical states (stomach rubbing to signal hunger or satiation), death (slashing the throat), and promises ('cross my heart' or crossed fingers to nullify a promise).

Emblems serve the same functions in all cultures, but the number, forms, and meanings of particular emblems differ from culture to culture, as there are 200 Persian emblems in use in current-day Iran but only about 50 in Israel.

Ekman reported that emblems perform six functions in all cultures: insulting others, giving interpersonal directions like 'come here' or 'be quiet', greeting others, signaling departure, replying positively or negatively to requests, and commenting on physical or emotional states.

All cultures seem to use emblems in similar places in conversations: at the beginning or end of a turn, in filled pauses, and preceding or accompanying the words they repeat, though most emblems have unique meanings in each culture.

Some cultures, like middle-class US culture, have less than 100 emblems, whereas others, like Israeli student culture, have over 250, so the savvy traveler should learn in advance what a culture's emblems mean and may consult Desmond Morris's Bodytalk (2015) for the country-specific meanings of various gestures.

Isabella Poggi, a professor of psychology at Roma Tre University and an expert on gestures, has identified around 250 gestures that Italians use in everyday conversation, and the only thing differentiating them from sign language is that they are used individually and lack a full syntax.

When former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi greeted then-President Obama and his wife, Michelle, at a meeting of the Group of 20 leaders in September 2009, he extended both hands, palms facing toward himself, and then pinched his fingers as he looked Mrs. Obama up and down, a gesture that might be interpreted as 'va-va-voom.'

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein overhauled, or at least refined, his theory that language was used to establish truth and inform after the Italian economist Piero Sraffa responded to his theory with a single gesture: fingers brushing the chin, indicating 'I don't give a damn,' the classic antiauthority brushoff.

Davidson (1950) documented emblems used by grain traders on the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade, where the palm of hand held up and inward meant 'buy,' the palm held outward meant 'sell,' fingers held vertically indicated quantities traded (5,000 bushels per finger), and fingers held horizontally indicated price.

Kita (2009) identified four dimensions along which iconic gestures vary across cultures, including culture-specific conventions for associations between form and meaning, such as the cut-off gesture that is more common in Asian than Western cultures and showing modesty by covering one's mouth when laughing.

Emblems are more likely to be displayed when communicating across a noisy room that prevents verbal communication, and many groups, like businesses and professions, develop their own emblems that carry meaning only among members of those groups, such as those used on the floor of the Chicago Board of Trade.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Structure Meets Function, From Birdwhistell's Kinemes to the Duchenne Smile
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with STRUCTURE on one side and FUNCTION on the other; cards fly into place, a notated face divides into Birdwhistell's eight regions, two smiles face off with lip corners versus eye corners highlighted, five gesture-type cards spread out, a pencil-tapping object adaptor, and a video frame where an ellipse labeled Quadrant 2 tracks a gesturing hand.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a two-sided matrix for the kinesic code: drop the structural cards into place, Birdwhistell's 50 to 60 culturally universal kinemes across eight body regions, the kines and allokines like the 23 eyelid positions that reduce to four meaningful ones, the kinemorphs that build sentences, and parakinesic markers, stress, and juncture that work like syntax, then file the Duchenne smile against the posed social smile with its zygomatic major and orbicularis oculi. Then fill the functional cells with Ekman and Friesen's five gesture types, the eight illustrator categories, the three adaptor targets, the regulators' turn-taking gaze norms, and a computer-vision blob that finds the hands in Quadrant 2.
key_concepts: In Birdwhistell's system, the smallest meaningful unit of behavior is the kineme, and Birdwhistell identified 50 to 60 kinemes that he considered culturally universal, meaning that cultural differences in kinesic behavior come from variations within kinemes, not from the use of different kinemes.

Kinemes are equivalent to morphemes and can be broken down further into kines, which are equivalent to phonemes, while variations in the intensity, duration, or extent of these behaviors are called allokines or kine variants, as when trained observers note as many as 23 different eyelid positions but only four positions appear to change the meaning of gaze behavior.

Birdwhistell divided the body into eight regions, each with its own set of kinemes: total head, face, neck, trunk, shoulders/arms/wrists, hand and finger activity, hips/legs/ankles, and foot activity (including walking).

According to Birdwhistell (1970), kinemes-in-use are combined into kinemorphs, which are similar to words in the linguistic system, and kinemorphs often occur in concert with other kinemorphs to produce complex kinemorphic constructions similar to sentences, the level at which the meaning of kinesic behavior becomes fully understandable.

Parakinesics, similar to syntax in language, include kinesic markers, stress, and juncture, so that subtle head movements serve as markers, such as gesturing backward slightly with the head when talking in past tense and nodding forward when using future tense to describe future plans.

Two muscle groups are involved in smiling, the zygomatic major (lip corners) and orbicularis oculi (eye corners), and experiments, perceptual observations, EMGs, and automated facial image analyses show that the Duchenne (spontaneous/genuine) smile differs from deliberately posed ones in terms of the onset, offset, duration, and possibly asymmetry of the muscle groups that are engaged.
