Posed smiles, also called semblances or social smiles, when compared to spontaneous smiles (symptoms), are 'turned on and off' more quickly but are longer in duration, are 'bigger,' tend to be more lopsided, and are less likely to engage the corners of the eyes.

Ekman and Friesen (1969) proposed five distinct types of gestures, emblems, illustrators, regulators, affect displays, and adaptors, each of which performs different functions or displays different meanings, and these categories are not mutually exclusive, as a single gesture may serve more than one function at the same time.

Illustrators (also called gesticulations) are kinesic acts accompanying speech that aid in the description of what is being said, trace the direction of speech, set the rhythm of speech, and gain and hold a listener's attention, with the Ekman and Friesen (1969) taxonomy including pictographs, kinetographs, ideographs, spatial movements, emblematic movements, deictic movements, batons, and rhythmic movements.

There are three types of adaptors, self-adaptors (such as scratching your arm, playing with your hair, working your jaw, biting your lip, or picking your nose), alter-directed adaptors (movements directed toward another person during interpersonal interactions), and object adaptors (such as tapping a pencil while concentrating or playing with your phone), distinguished by the target of the behavior.

Regulators are kinesic behaviors designed to manage or regulate turn taking between two or more interactants, learned at a very early age, displayed at a low level of awareness, and produced almost automatically, with the normal amount of gaze in an interaction ranging from 28% to 70% of the time, increasing when listening and decreasing when speaking.

A 'blob' is what computer vision experts call the ellipses their techniques superimpose on human body parts: computers scan the pixels in a video, use color look-up-tables that match skin colors, form a bounding box and then an ellipse around the head, and use the head's position along with knowledge of the body's geometry to infer where the hands, forearms, shoulders, trunk, and legs are likely to be located within the frame.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Voice, Vocalics, and the Power of Sound
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a sound wave: a spectrogram towers as the boss while an ear receives 16 to 20,000 Hz, a voice print freezes mid-analysis next to a fingerprint, Trager's voice set forms the backdrop, 'uh-huh,' 'shh' and 'tsk-tsk' float as emblems, a silent table of wait staff disappears into the background, and a newscaster's BBC English broadcasts from a monitor.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss of the auditory code: defend why the authors prefer the label vocalics over paralanguage, prosody, and noncontent speech, then unlock the machinery, the ear's 16 to 20,000 Hz range, the voice print that rivals the fingerprint, and a voice ranked second only to kinesics in communicative power. March through Trager's voice set, the eight elocutionary features plus dialect and fluency, the vocal emblems and alternants, the silences that make a person a 'nonperson,' Poggi's mind markers and cognitive state indicators, the acoustics of anger, the attractive voice, BBC English, and the leakage that gives liars away.
key_concepts: The authors prefer the label vocalics because it encompasses any vocal-auditory behavior except the spoken word, while 'paralanguage' is in some usages unnecessarily broad (encompassing kinesics) and in other respects too narrow, 'prosody' is usually linked to the words that are spoken, and 'noncontent speech' inaccurately implies that vocal aspects have no content.

The human ear is capable of perceiving frequencies ranging from 16 to 20,000 Hz, and humans can recognize incredibly minute variations in sound, to the point that law enforcement and speech scientists have worked to perfect a voice print that would rival the fingerprint in producing reliable identification of people.

The voice is probably second only to kinesics in the ranking of nonverbal codes on their communicative power, it is thought to have preceded formal language as a means of communication and been retained throughout evolution, and it has primacy in human development, since an infant begins to communicate with vocal cues long before words appear.

In Trager's (1958, 1961) structural classification system, analysis begins with voice set, which consists of the mental, physiological, and physical characteristics of a speaker, including sex, age, state of health, body build, mood, bodily condition, and geographic location, against which all vocalic and speech behaviors are judged.

Proponents of the elocutionary movement identified vocal features that a good speaker was expected to master, including pitch and pitch variation, inflection (the tonal patterns of the voice), loudness, emphasis, time or tempo, pauses, voice coloring, and voice quality such as clear, harsh, mellow, tremulous, or nasal.

To the eight elocutionary vocal features, 20th-century researchers added dialect (the presence of accented speech) and fluency (the presence or absence of dysfluencies), the latter subdivided into the filled-pause variety, the 'ums' and 'ahs' that substitute for where a silent pause would occur, and other dysfluencies like unfilled pauses, repetitions, stutters, and garbled or incoherent sounds such as clicks and snorts.

Vocalizations that stand alone and have well-understood symbolic meaning within a culture are considered vocal emblems, such as Trager's 'uh-huh' and 'hun-uh' for yes and no, and paralinguistic alternants like the rapid trilling of the lips that expresses delight from a child but disappointment or disgust from an adult, 'shh' to hush someone, and 'tsk-tsk' to chide someone.

Silences are a particularly powerful symbolic message: they can be used to express negation without having to say 'no,' establish a sense of being aligned or in harmony with another, or transform the recipient into a 'nonperson,' as when teenagers subject a disliked classmate to total silence or a person stops speaking to a former friend as a forceful message that they have been 'excommunicated.'

Poggi (2002a) introduced the concept of 'mind markers,' indications through voice, gesture, and other nonverbal signals that reveal a speaker's thoughts, goals, plans, and emotions, such as a 'hrmpp' that reveals disgruntlement at a proffered solution or a cooed 'oooh' that reveals pleasure in response to exciting news.

Acoustically, anger is displayed through higher intensity, higher mean fundamental frequency, greater F0 range and variability, downward contours, higher-frequency energy, and clearer articulation, showing that emotional states can be described in terms of acoustic-prosodic combinations.

Zuckerman and Miyake (1993) found that voices perceived as the most attractive had higher articulation and resonance, low to moderate shrillness, moderate pitch, small to medium pitch range, and low nasality.

In the twentieth century, accent training became an unofficial requisite of the British educational system, and many newscasters for the British Broadcasting Corp. adopted the accent of their Oxford masters, which connoted intelligence and distinction and acquired the nickname BBC English, while newscasters in the United States are trained to remove any sign of an accent and speak general American dialect.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Contact Codes: Haptics and Proxemics

assets.topic: Scrub the Skin: Touch as the First Sense and the Engine of Human Development
assets.visual_frame_description: A womb of warm light where a fetus floats against a beating heart rhythm, then a laboratory with a baby monkey clinging to a terrycloth mother beside a wire mother holding a bottle, an orphanage crib with a rocking child, an MRI scan of a brain 20 percent smaller fading in, a dark room door labeled Genie, and a nurse massaging a premature baby while a heart-rate monitor slows.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through why touch matters from the very first moments of life: how the skin is the first sense to develop and the last to leave us, how the fetus is soothed by the mother's rhythms in the womb, why Harlow's infant monkeys chose the terrycloth mother over the wire mother that fed them, how nineteenth-century orphanages lost 90% to 100% of their infants to marasmus for want of being held, how Spitz's cuddled babies thrived while tactile deprivation shrinks the brain, how Genie's emotional and cognitive development was irrecoverably harmed by her isolation, and how touch shapes attachment, social skill, health, and even the cardiovascular benefits of expressing affection.
key_concepts: Haptics refers to the perception and use of touch as communication, while proxemics refers to the perception, use, and structuring of personal space as communication, and the two codes form a continuum from physical contact to its absence.

Touch utilizes our largest sense organ, the skin, which is the first sense to develop, probably the last sense to leave us when we die, and the most intimate and nuanced of our senses (Hansen, 2007; Reite, 1990).

The first sensory experience of the fetus is through the skin, and in the womb the fetus is pleasantly stimulated by the heartbeat and rhythms of the mother and coordinates its own rhythms to hers (Crucianelli & Filippetti, 2020; Field, 2014).

In Harlow's (1958) classic studies, infant monkeys spent up to 18 hours a day clinging to warm terrycloth-covered surrogate mothers and visited the wire mothers who supplied food only long enough to get nourishment, showing that contact comfort is a primary need in higher-order mammals.

Montagu (1978) summarized evidence from orphanages and children's hospitals in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries showing a mortality rate among infants of a staggering 90% to 100%, many dying from marasmus, or wasting away, because although they received adequate food they were seldom held.

Spitz (1945, 1946) reported that when children were not touched they tended to die before their first birthdays and develop psychological problems if they survived, yet babies thrived in orphanages where women from the community came to cuddle them on a consistent basis.

Tactile stimulation during the first year and a half of life is essential for healthy brain development, and children who fail to receive adequate stimulation have underdeveloped pathways in the parts of the brain that process social and emotional information (Gerhart, 2004; Perry, 2002).
People who suffered from tactile deprivation during early childhood have brains that are about 20% smaller than children who have received average or high levels of stimulation (Honig, 2005).

Genie, who was locked up in a dark room for over 10 years with virtually no social interaction, was able to learn words but never able to string them together into sentences, and scientists concluded that her emotional and cognitive development was irrecoverably harmed by her lack of early social interaction (Rymer, 1994).

In the first few months of life, touch is a key active ingredient in the development of secure attachment and the formation of family bonds (Cascio et al., 2019), and premature babies gain weight more quickly and go home earlier when nurses massage them frequently (Honig, 2005).

Dunbar (2010) hypothesized that social grooming releases a neuroendocrine cascade of oxytocin and endorphins that cement the process of social bonding in primates and nonprimates, making intimate touch a mechanism for social bonding that undergirds reproductive success.

People who express affection to others show quicker physiological recovery from stress and have better cardiovascular health, and expressing affection is related to being happier, having less fear of intimacy, and feeling less depressed (Floyd et al., 2005, 2007).

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Dimensions and Functions of Touch
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table where two debaters argue over a pat on the shoulder that shifts from comforting to condescending as a rival says better luck next time, a touch dimensions dial with sliders for intensity, duration, location, frequency, and instrument, and a wall of function cards flipping: a doctor's exam, a two-handed handshake, a criss-cross hug, a consoling pat, a congratulatory high five, an intimate embrace, a playful tickle, a boss's shoulder tap, and a violent shove.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue about what a touch means: debate how the same pat on the shoulder can comfort or condescend, how intensity, duration, location, frequency, and the instrument of touch change interpretation, and how the functions of touch - instrumental, socially polite, affectionate, comforting, appreciative and congratulatory, sexual, playful, control, negative affect, and hybrid - each carry different relational messages, from the handshake most patients want from doctors to the criss-cross hug that outranks the engulfing hug, from high fives that bond teammates to the 20 domestic partners abused per minute in the United States.
key_concepts: The same type of touch can send different messages because touch is polysemous: a pat on the shoulder can be comforting when given by a good friend providing social support, or condescending when it comes from a rival who says better luck next time after being promoted instead of you.
People interpret tactile behavior based on dimensions that include intensity, duration, location, frequency, and the instrument of touch (Hertenstein, 2002; Weiss, 1979).

A study showed that elderly residents in a nursing home evaluated touch above the wrist by nurses more positively than touch below the wrist, and students evaluated male professors especially negatively when depicted as touching a student's thigh (Hollinger & Buschmann, 1993; Lannutti et al., 2001).

Instrumental touch is typically one-sided and task oriented and has little if any personal meaning, such as when a doctor examines a patient, an usher guides people to their assigned seats, or a parent puts a child in a high-chair.

Jones and Yarbrough (1985) identified seven main types of touch based on diary entries that included nearly 1500 descriptions of actual contacts, and Guerrero and Ebesu (1993) found that young children used many of the same types of touch as adults.

Socially polite touches are relatively formal and governed by social norms and rules of politeness, and across two studies between 61% and 78% of patients reported that they prefer having a doctor who shakes their hand when greeting them (Davis et al., 2007; Makoul et al., 2007).

Jones and Yarbrough (1985) found that people tend to greet or depart from others verbally before or during a touch rather than after, so people typically introduce themselves right before or during a handshake at a business meeting.

Affectionate touch reflects general friendship, warmth, and intimacy without necessarily conveying sexual attraction, and common forms include hugs, hand holding, and some forms of kissing (Derlega et al., 1989; Floyd & Morman, 1998).

Floyd (1999) found that the criss-cross hug was perceived as the most intimate, followed by the neck-waist hug, while the engulfing hug was rated as conveying the least intimacy because it was perceived as more one-sided.

In Dolin and Booth-Butterfield's (1993) study of comforting behaviors, the most common behavior students mentioned for comforting a distressed roommate was hugs, with 41.9% saying they would hug their roommate by either engaging in a full-body hug or hugging them around the shoulders.

Sexual touches, which Heslin and Alper (1983) referred to as the most intense and intimate form of physical contact, are usually concentrated in more vulnerable areas of the body such as the mouth, thigh, or genitals and typically involve multiple kinds of touches occurring together in sequence.

Control touches direct the behavior, attitude, or feeling state of another, as when a boss touches an employee on the shoulder and says could you get this done by 5 o'clock, while 2020 statistics show that 20 domestic partners per minute are abused in the United States, with 1 in 3 women and 1 in 4 men abused by intimate partners over their lifetimes.

assets.topic: Audit the Moderators: Sex, Personality, Culture, and the Touchy Issue of Contact
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger stamped SEX, PERSONALITY, CULTURE: in the sex column a man initiates a touch at a movie theater line while a woman reaches for her husband at home, in the personality column a Social Touch Questionnaire fills itself in while an avoidant couple keeps their distance, and in the culture column a map glows from the Mediterranean to Scandinavia, a Finn waves his hands, a Japanese card is offered with two hands, and a Trinidadian medical student hesitates before a doctor's outstretched hand while an elder looks away.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit what changes the meaning of touch: check off how sex and gender shift who initiates touch in public versus private settings, why men touch more at the start of romantic relationships and women more in marriage, how the Social Touch Questionnaire ties touch avoidance to anxiety and how the Big Five personality traits predict touch perceptions better than sex does, why avoidant attachment styles avoid touch, and then stamp the cultural ledger: high-contact Latin America and the Mediterranean versus low-contact Scandinavia, the touchy Finns, Japan's two-handed business cards, and how Western-based health guidelines collided with local mores in doctor-patient interviews in Trinidad.
key_concepts: In public settings, men may initiate touch more often than women, but in private settings women appear to initiate touch just as much or more than men (Henley, 1973; Major et al., 1990; Stier & Hall, 1984).
Burgoon and Bacue (2003) concluded that, in general, women touch and are touched more than men.

Three observational studies demonstrated that men are more likely to initiate touch in the beginning stages of romantic relationships, whereas women are more likely to initiate touch in marriages, possibly because men use touch as social control early on while women use touch to communicate affection once relationships are established (Guerrero & Andersen, 1994; Willis & Dodds, 1998).

In the United States, women friends touch each other considerably more than men friends, with the exception of sports, when men pat, hug, and bang against one another because the masculine context of a sporting event makes man-to-man touch socially appropriate (Floyd, 2000).
Russo et al. (2020) conducted a meta-analysis that confirmed that, on average, women perceive affective touch as more pleasurable than men, regardless of sex distribution, age, or number of touches.
According to the Social Touch Questionnaire, people who score high on touch avoidance also score high on measures of anxiety (Lapp & Croy, 2020).

In a study of whether the Big 5 personality traits affect perceptions of touch, Dorros et al. (2008) found that personality was a bigger predictor of positive perceptions of touch than biological sex or satisfaction with the toucher, with openness strongly correlated with positive reactions to nonintimate touch.

Individuals with an avoidant attachment style avoid touch and are less comfortable with it, and in married couples, attachment insecurities predicted reactions to touch (Chopik et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2020).

In high-contact regions like Latin America, southern Europe, and the Mediterranean, people touch each other more often, adopt closer interpersonal distance, make more eye contact, and speak louder, whereas low-contact cultures or regions include Western Europe, Scandinavia, and the United States.

Despite most Northern European cultures being on the low-contact side, Finns are frequent touchers, and although Chinese adults are more tactile than Japanese, Asian cultures have been classified as either high or low contact depending on the study.

Many cultural rituals involve touch: business cards in Japan are to be handed and received with two hands and placed carefully face up, in South Korea handshakes should be two-handed, orthodox Jewish men in Israel do not shake hands with women, and touching the top of the head, acceptable in the United States, is taboo in many parts of Asia.

In the doctor-patient interviews in Trinidad described in Box 5.6, Barbadian students said touch is a necessary part of the doctor-patient encounter, students from the other islands believed it should be restricted to task-oriented touching only, Muslims and some Hindus said all forms of touch needed to be carefully regulated, and in communities such as those in Tobago it is considered disrespectful to look into the eyes of an elder.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Territory, Personal Space, and the Four Distances
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-cell wall matrix labeled TERRITORY, PERSONAL SPACE, CROWDING, DISTANCE: cards fly in showing a defended house, an invisible bubble around a body, Sika deer and rats in a pen, and a measuring tape stretching from 0 to 18 inches to 4 feet to 10 feet, while a nightclub crowd gleams in excitement and a crowded dorm room dims in stress.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of space: drop each evidence card into its cell - the definition of territory as a fixed defended domain, the personal space bubble as a body-buffer zone, Lyman and Scott's body, home, interactional, and public territories against Altman's primary, secondary, and public categories, Goffman's territories of self, the neighborhood bar that is secondary territory to regulars but home territory to employees, and Hall's four conversational distances from intimate 0 to 18 inches through personal-casual to social-consultative and public 10 feet and beyond - then weigh the crowding evidence: the Sika deer that died with enlarged adrenal glands, Calhoun's cannibalistic rats, crowded dorms and high-rise apartments, and Altman's distinction between density and the feeling of being crowded.
key_concepts: A territory is a fixed geographic area that is occupied, controlled, and defended by a person or group as their exclusive domain, and territories often house valuable resources or possessions such as food, diaries, computers, jewelry, or money (Hall, 2003; Hediger, 1961).

In contrast to territory, personal space is an invisible, adjustable bubble of space that people carry around with them, actively maintained as a way to protect themselves from physical harm and emotional discomfort (Ciolek, 1983; Sommer, 1966).

Personal space can be thought of as an individual's perceived self-boundary or body-buffer zone in that it provides a buffer against physical and emotional threats, and it has been extended to include all the senses, being violated by loud noises, unpleasant smells, or someone staring at you in an elevator (Rosenbloom, 2006).

Shy people generally have stronger needs for personal space than do outgoing people, and women generally require less space than men, while people generally require less space in informal settings with close relational partners than in formal settings with strangers (Andersen, 2008).

The two most popular systems for categorizing territory were developed by Lyman and Scott (1967), who discussed body, home, interactional, and public territories, and Altman (1975), who distinguished among primary, secondary, and public territory.

Of all types of territories, Lyman and Scott (1967) argued that body territory is the most private and is defended the most vigorously when invaded, and in most societies laws protect people's body territories by punishing those who assault or rape others.

Goffman (1971) defined territories of self that revolve around environmental structures or stalls, social norms, tasks, and adornments, so people expect work cubicles, confessionals, and showers to be private, expect others to wait their turn in line, and expect objects like clothing, jewelry, briefcases, purses, and cell phones not to be touched without permission.

Primary or home territories include places like houses, bedrooms, offices, and cars where people spend a great deal of time, and people use these territories as a place to retreat both physically and psychologically, letting down their guard in ways they would not in public.

Secondary or interactional territories are semipublic with somewhat loose rules, and the same territory can be used differently by various people: the regular patrons in a neighborhood bar treat the bar as a secondary territory, the employees treat it as a home territory, and the occasional customers treat it as a public territory.

Hall (1966, 2003) proposed that there are four perceptual categories of conversational distance - intimate, personal-casual, social-consultative, and public - which affect the overall tone of an interaction by influencing how the senses are engaged and how intimate and formal the interaction is.

The intimate distance range stretches from 0 to 18 inches, the personal-casual zone ranges from 18 inches to 4 feet, the social-consultative zone ranges from 4 to 10 feet, and public distance encompasses 10 feet and beyond, with the zones created based on data from North America and possibly not generalizable to other cultures.

Christian et al.'s (1961) study of Sika deer showed that overcrowding on James Island caused the population to suddenly decrease from 300 to 80 deer with greatly enlarged adrenal glands, and Calhoun's (1962) rat studies found that overcrowding led to destructive behaviors such as sexual dysfunction, cannibalism, hyperactivity, and vicious attacks.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Space Moderators, Virtual Touch, and the Modern World
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a city sidewalk at rush hour with invisible bubbles shifting size as strangers pass, a virtual room where avatars shake hands through haptic joysticks while a vibration runs between two keyboards, an airport boarding line where a firm handshake glows while an overweight traveler is left untouched, and a nightclub where dimmed lights and a happy crowd beat back the crowding stress meters.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the modern collision of space, culture, and technology: hold the line on how sex, personality, and culture moderate personal space - women's closer interaction distance, the anxious and introverted who need more room, violent offenders' rear buffer, Anglo Saxon versus Latin spacing, colder versus warmer climates - then face the virtual frontier: joystick handshakes men prefer when mirrored back, haptic devices that build immediacy and trust across cyberspace, the firm grip that wins first impressions, and the subtle discrimination of less casual touch directed at overweight individuals, and finish in the modern world: airline legroom, Second Life avatars, iPods, dimmed lights, road rage, and the dual needs for privacy and closeness.
key_concepts: A meta-analysis by Hall and Gunnery (2013) showed that women adopt closer interaction distance, along with other behaviors showing more nonverbal immediacy, than men, consistent with women engaging in more touch and being more comfortable than men with crowded situations.

Cozby (1973) found that people with high self-esteem are more likely to approach others closely because they expect to be liked, whereas people with high social anxiety want larger distances from others, and there is evidence that introverts and those who score high on neuroticism need more distance from others.

McGurk et al. (1981) found that violent offenders, especially those with psychotic tendencies, had a high need for personal space from the rear, and an fMRI study by Schienle et al. (2015) found that women with borderline personality disorder showed higher brain activation with personal space intrusions in social situations involving disgust.

Beaulieu's (2004) study of employees and students from 11 countries showed that Anglo Saxons used the largest zone of personal space, followed by Asians and then Caucasians, while people from Latin cultures used the shortest distances.

Høgh-Olesen (2008) found that people living in the three colder climates of Denmark, Finland, and Greenland used larger distances when interacting with strangers than did those from the warmer climates of Cameroon, India, and Italy, and within countries people living in warmer areas tend to have smaller personal space zones.

Although cultures differ in their tolerance for being close together and what they perceive as crowded, all groups experienced about the same level of distress due to crowding, as shown by a study in which African Americans and White Americans perceived a sharper increase in psychological crowding but all groups ended up with similar distress (Evans et al., 2000).
In a study by Bailenson and Yee (2007), a joystick was used to simulate a handshake in a virtual environment, and men liked the handshakes that mimicked their own handshake more than women did.

Virtual interpersonal touch may revolutionize computer-mediated communication by creating a greater sense of immediacy, togetherness, and trust, and people who engage in collaborative tasks or play games in virtual environments perform better and feel closer to one another if haptic devices are utilized (Basdogan et al., 1998; Sallnas et al., 2000).

People who shake hands with a firm, complete (but not hard) grip while giving eye contact are rated more positively than people who offer a weaker handshake, and individuals who are extraverted and open to new experiences are more likely to have firm handshakes (Chaplin et al., 2000; Holmes, 2005).

Research suggests that overweight individuals receive less casual touch, such as handshakes and pats on the arm, than do other individuals, and this discrepancy in tactile behavior is a subtle, but powerful, form of discrimination.

The high five originated in a variety of places and times, studies have found that its use can increase bonding among teammates and it emerged among baseball and basketball players, and its many variations include the up high, the down low, the baby five, the air five, the double high five, the fist bump, and the self-high five.

Haptic and proxemic cues are instrumental in helping people manage their dual needs for privacy and closeness, because there are times when we want to put as much distance between ourselves and another person as possible and other times when it may seem impossible to get close enough, and these two codes help us achieve both of these goals.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Body as a Code: Appearance and Adornment

assets.topic: Scrub the Static Code: Why Appearance Arrives Before Words
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead sweeps across a first-impression corridor where a job candidate and a dater are seen before a word is spoken; a freeze-frame splits the screen into static appearance cues (face, height, weight, coloring) versus dynamic adornment cues (clothes, perfume, jewelry, makeup), while a ticker shows the 1.5 trillion dollar fashion market and a counter tallies three selfies a day on a phone screen.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the body code itself: how appearance cues such as facial structure, height, weight, and coloring differ from adornment cues such as clothing, perfume, jewelry, and makeup, why the code is limited because it is static and inflexible, and why adornment cues more closely conform to the definition of communication. Then weigh the evidence that appearance matters: the 82% of men and 93% of women oriented toward looking attractive, the 1.5 trillion dollar global fashion market, preschoolers pointing out the better-looking kids, infants turning toward beautiful faces, the 1957 yearbook study linking looks to later well-being, and the five hours a week young women spend taking selfies.
key_concepts: Appearance cues include physical features such as facial structure, height, weight, and coloring, while adornment cues such as clothing, perfume, jewelry, and makeup are worn on the body.
Because appearance and adornment cues are generally static and unchanging, they constitute a somewhat inflexible communication channel once an interaction has begun, unlike kinesic and vocalic cues.

Adornment cues are message vehicles that are selected and modified by their senders and interpreted as communicative by receivers, so they more closely conform to the definition of communication than do static appearance cues.
Because appearance cues have interaction primacy and are noticed before any other nonverbal or verbal messages have been exchanged, they have great power to set the stage for any human interaction.

One study showed that 82% of men and 93% of women are actively oriented toward developing and maintaining an attractive appearance, and 40% of college students believe themselves to be perfectionists when it comes to their physical appearance.
In 2020 the global fashion market alone was valued at 1.5 trillion dollars, and the global perfume and fragrance market was projected to hit 64.6 billion dollars by 2023.
Even in preschool, children are able to point out who the better-looking kids are, and these children are often the most popular in their classes.
Infants react positively to beautiful faces and look away from ugly faces, suggesting that children are born with a sense of what is physically attractive.

In one study, high school yearbook pictures from 1957 were rated for physical attractiveness, and the students rated more attractive tended to report high levels of psychological well-being and low levels of distress and depression decades later.

Young women between the ages of 16 and 25 spend, on average, about five hours a week taking selfies, posting an average of three selfies a day across social media platforms such as Instagram and Snapchat.
The overall goal for posting selfies is to manage one's impression, and the two main ways to do that are to post pictures that emphasize your physical attractiveness and show you are happy.
Businesses that help people look their best often continue to thrive when economic times are hard, because even when money is tight people still want to look and feel their best.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Beauty Bias: Halo Effects, Meat Markets, and the Matching Game
assets.visual_frame_description: A debate stage where two sides argue beautiful is good versus beautiful is conceited while a halo and a narcissist mirror hover overhead; a speed-dating wheel rotates 25 suitors with yes and no cards tallying 34% and 49%, a measuring tape pins weight in proportion to height as the deciding factor, and a heart monitor shows a couple rating each other more attractive after a warm laugh.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on how beauty is perceived: defend the halo effect and the what is beautiful is good hypothesis against the what is beautiful is conceited hypothesis and the presumption that good-looking people are sexually experienced, promiscuous, and unfaithful, then show why these are perceptual biases rather than facts and how a self-fulfilling prophecy makes attractive people more confident. Then walk the HurryDate meat market where the market model beats the matching model, the deception people use to land dates, the matching hypothesis, the 25% aspirational ceiling in online dating, and the interaction appearance theory that good interactions literally make people look better.
key_concepts: The halo effect, or the what is beautiful is good hypothesis, associates an outwardly attractive appearance with positive internal characteristics such as friendliness, ambition, likeability, and intelligence, and it is present from childhood through older adulthood.

According to the what is beautiful is conceited hypothesis, attractive people are sometimes perceived as materialistic, self-centered, snobbish, and vain, a bias reflected on social media where people who post a lot of selfies are rated as narcissistic.

Good-looking people are often presumed to be sexually experienced, promiscuous, and more likely to be unfaithful than average-looking people, and they may be held to different standards that make it harder to meet people's high expectations.
These are perceptual biases rather than facts, and there is no evidence showing that physically attractive people are actually nicer or have more or less integrity than average-looking people.

Attractive people are often more confident because of a self-fulfilling prophecy, as positive feedback from others fuels and sustains their self-confidence and helps them develop social skills and communication competence.

In the HurryDate speed-dating study of 2,650 participants, the most important factor determining how many yeses one got was weight in proportion to height, while personality, religion, education, and income did not seem to matter much, and the market model won because the same people were consistently deemed desirable.

In one study, over one third of women and nearly 46% of men admitted to deceiving someone to initiate a date, with men exaggerating their success and sincerity and women enhancing their appearance with tactics such as covering blemishes with makeup.

The matching hypothesis holds that people search for partners who are at about the same level of physical attractiveness as themselves, and it applies to various types of relationships, including friendships and marriages.

In online dating, most people pursue aspirational partners who are up to around 25% more desirable than they consider themselves to be, but they tend not to seek relationships when potential partners exceed that 25% mark.

According to interaction appearance theory, having a positive interaction with someone can enhance people's perceptions of their partner's physical appearance, while a negative interaction can make even an attractive person seem less attractive.

People in happy relationships perceive their partners to be especially attractive and also derogate the physical attractiveness of potential alternative partners, which helps them stay loyal and maintain healthy relationships.

Physical appearance is one of the best predictors of romantic attraction, passion, intimacy, and commitment in relationships, and it was the most common primary characteristic that initially attracted college students to their current dating partner.

assets.topic: Audit the Universal Face: Koinophilia, Neoteny, and Symmetry
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger across a face: a checklist stamps KOINOPHILIA next to a composite of 32 averaged faces, NEOTENY next to a young woman's wide eyes and full lips with a high cheekbone marker, and SYMMETRY next to left-left and right-right mirror faces that a crowd rates below the natural photograph; a balance scale tips averageness above symmetry.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the three features universally associated with facial attractiveness: tick off koinophilia with the computer-generated average faces that beat the real ones, facial neoteny with the ideal woman's face of fuller lips and wider eyes and the right mix of babyish and sexually mature features, and symmetry with the mirror-image faces people actually judge as worse than the natural ones. Then close the books on men's faces, where the most attractive are neither too masculine nor too feminine, and on the finding that averageness matters more than symmetry.
key_concepts: Counter to the popular saying that beauty is in the eye of the beholder, some features of physical attractiveness are universal in that people from around the globe agree that certain features are attractive.

The three features universally associated with facial attractiveness are koinophilia, facial neoteny combined with sexual maturity, and symmetry, all of which are static features that cannot be readily encoded as a message.

Koinophilia is the tendency to perceive faces with average features as attractive, which makes sense because features that are overly large, small, or close together detract from the aesthetic beauty of a face.

In the first major study of average faces, composite faces created by mathematically averaging the features of 96 college-aged men and 96 college-aged women were rated as more attractive than individual faces, with composites of 16 or 32 faces rated most attractive.
Facial neoteny refers to having facial features that are youthful or baby-like, such as large eyes, full lips, and a small nose, and such features are also regarded as more feminine.

In one study, a composite of the features people liked best produced an ideal woman's face with more neotenous features, including fuller lips, wider eyes, small chins, shorter distances between the eyes and nose, and larger distances between the eyes and hairline.

Men rated women as most attractive when they had neotenous features such as full lips, a big smile, and large wide eyes combined with high cheekbones, a sexually mature feature, and they expressed more interest in dating and having sex with those women.
A face that is too babyish looking can be seen as immature, so to be viewed as optimally attractive faces often have a combination of neotenous and sexually mature features.

Men's faces are judged as most attractive when they combine some moderately masculine features with some androgynous or feminine features, and men with highly masculine faces are rated lower in warmth, honesty, and cooperativeness but higher in dominance.
Facial symmetry refers to how similar the two sides of a person's face are, and the larger the differences between the two sides, the more likely the face will be judged as unattractive.
People rated natural faces as more attractive than the perfectly symmetrical right-right or left-left mirror versions, and the research suggests that a face can be too symmetrical.

A review of the literature on facial attractiveness showed that koinophilia had a larger effect on facial attractiveness than did symmetry, so if facial features are not attractive, making them symmetrical is unlikely to do much to improve attractiveness.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Somatotypes, Waist-to-Hip Ratios, and the Scarcity of Coloring
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled BODY TYPE, BODY ECONOMICS, COLORING, and BODY IMAGE: somatotype silhouettes parade under stereotype tags, a dollar sign lifts tall men above a weight scale, a tanning sun and an Indian parasol trade places across a world map, and a color swatch from very light to very dark slides past a 126% discrimination marker.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of body and coloring cues: drop the endomorph, mesomorph, ectomorph, ecto-meso, and endo-meso somatotype cards with their stereotype labels, the dad bod, and the hourglass preference into BODY TYPE; the tall men earning more and the overweight penalty, the .70 waist-to-hip ratio, and the online dating height rules into BODY ECONOMICS; the tan in fair-skinned cultures versus light skin in India, the rare blue eyes, and the blue-eyed man's paternity logic into COLORING; and the 11.8% weight over-perception, the 70% thinner media women, and Monk's 126% colorism figure into BODY IMAGE.
key_concepts: In the United States there are stereotypes associated with five general types of bodies, also called somatypes: endomorphs, mesomorphs, ectomorphs, ecto-mesos, and endo-mesos.

Endomorphs, who are heavy in comparison to their height with round bodies and often underdeveloped muscles, are most commonly stereotyped as introverted, insecure, humorous, caring, sad, unenergetic, and friendly.

Mesomorphs, who have a strong muscular body with weight proportional to height, are stereotyped as immodest, athletic, energetic, extraverted, secure, strong, and goal-oriented, but also as selfish, insensitive, and controlling.

Ectomorphs, who are thin compared to their height with a lean body type and small muscles, are most commonly associated with traits such as being introverted, intelligent, afraid, tense, insecure, and quiet.

The dad bod, a term made famous in 2015 by college student Mackenzie Pearson, is an example of an endo-meso body, and women report that men with a dad bod seem more genuine and modest and more likely to be faithful than men with more perfect mesomorphic bodies.

In a study comparing women's preferences across five body types, 50% of White women and almost 60% of Black women favored hourglass-shaped forms over all other types, with Black women preferring a curvier hourglass shape than White women did.

Tall people, and especially tall men, generally make more money than shorter people, while overweight and obese people, especially women, make even less money, with a healthy weight in proportion to height associated with higher salaries and better positions.

Men from various countries around the world prefer women with waist-to-hip ratios of about .70, a ratio associated with health and fertility, and Marilyn Monroe and Audrey Hepburn both had ratios close to .70 despite being very different in overall size.

According to the scarcity principle, people often like coloring that conveys status or is scarce within their ethnic or co-cultural group, which is why tanning is valued in fair-skinned cultures while people in India prize light skin and carry parasols to prevent tanning.

Blue-eyed men are drawn toward blue-eyed women because choosing a partner with the same recessive eye color can provide reassurance that the woman's babies are theirs too, and blue-eyed men are indeed more likely to be romantically involved with women of the same eye color.

Colorism means that lighter-skinned African Americans and Mexican Americans enjoy substantial privileges still unattainable to their darker-skinned counterparts, and Black Americans with the darkest skin tones perceive themselves as discriminated against at a rate of 126% more than do those with the lightest skin tones.

Mass media perpetuate the thin is good assumption with women on television and in movies around 70% thinner than average, and people tend to make more upward than downward comparisons, so those who compare themselves to better-looking others tend to be less satisfied with their bodies.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Adornment Arsenal, Cosmetics, Tattoos, Clothing, and Perfume
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a glamour workshop: a makeup table with a kosmos label where a woman's face morphs more attractive, a highway with 1600 cars stopping for the made-up hitchhiker, a tattoo parlor wall where inked arms rise from 5% to 30%, an interview room where a manager stamps REJECT on a facial piercing, and a perfume counter where one spray is crowned and five sprays are sprayed away.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of how people intentionally dress, decorate, and scent the body: hold the cosmetics up to the light and trace the Greek kosmos, the professional makeup boost, the hitchhiking and tipping payoffs, the sexual harassment downside, and the rise of men's makeup, then run the tattoo gauntlet from 5% to 30% of Americans inked, the ankle versus arm placement, the promiscuity stereotype, and the managers who will not hire visible ink. Finish with the clothing ledger of status over physique display and the perfume trial where a light spray wins and five sprays lose.
key_concepts: The word cosmetics comes from the Greek word kosmos, which means adornments, and women are judged as more attractive when they wear an appropriate amount of makeup, especially when it is applied professionally, with smooth, clear skin known as a sign of health.

For women within the average range of facial attractiveness, wearing makeup has just as powerful an impact on attractiveness ratings as do structural features, in part by exaggerating contrasts that make them look more feminine, such as fuller lips and longer, darker eyelashes.

Wearing makeup has real-life consequences: male drivers were more likely to stop for hitchhiking women wearing makeup, waitresses wearing makeup received more tips, and women wearing makeup were approached more by men in a bar in France.

There is a downside to makeup: women wearing a lot of makeup were perceived as more likely to be victims of sexual harassment, and in resume studies women wearing a lot of makeup were viewed as less competent and assigned lower starting salaries.

Both men and women overestimate the amount of makeup they think people prefer, with a moderate level regarded most positively, and increasing numbers of men have started using beauty products, including James Charles, named the first male spokesmodel for CoverGirl in 2016.

Body modifications were relatively rare in Western cultures until they became popular in the 1980s, and the percentage of the US population with at least one tattoo has increased from about 5% in the early 1990s to around 30% in 2019.

Women are more likely to get softer, smaller, and more personal tattoo images in discreet places such as the ankle or lower back, whereas men are more likely to get larger, more macho images on highly visible parts such as the arms, upper backs, and shoulders.

Compared to untattooed people, individuals with tattoos are more likely to be perceived as adventurous, artistic, creative, impulsive, independent, open, politically liberal, sexually liberal, and unique, and less likely to be perceived as agreeable or conscientious.

In one beach study, women with temporary tattoos on their lower backs were approached more by men than were women without tattoos, and men rated their likelihood of having sex on a first date as higher with the tattooed women, who were rated as more promiscuous but not more physically attractive.

Some studies estimate that between 82% and 87% of managers would be unlikely to hire someone with visible tattoos or body piercings, and facial piercings are associated with negative characteristics such as untrustworthiness, incompetence, and lower moral character in the workplace.

In a study that manipulated dress, both men and women found models wearing high-status clothing most appealing across all four types of attractiveness, physical, dating, sexual, and marital, while physique display only enhanced sexual attractiveness.

Perfume can be used as a means of attracting others, but too much can be a turn-off: men rated women interviewers as most physically attractive wearing light perfume while women preferred none, the excessive five to six spray condition was rated least positively, and perfume boosted casually dressed women's attractiveness but decreased it for formally dressed women.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Place and Time Codes: Environment, Artifacts, and Chronemics

assets.topic: Scrub the Code: What Environment and Artifacts Are, and How We Acquire Their Meanings
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a Stonehenge rock circle, then sweeps into a Japanese rock garden, a health spa with soothing colors and soft surfaces, and a split globe where a high-context speech bubble packs meaning into the physical context while a low-context bubble spells everything out explicitly.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the origins of the environmental and artifactual code: define the code as the physical objects and environmental attributes that communicate directly, delineate the communication context, or guide social behavior, and see how the natural environment becomes a code only when humans act upon it. Then trace acquisition through socialization and culture, weigh Hall's high-context versus low-context distinction, spot the innate, survival-based foundations beneath the learned specifics, and end with Mehrabian's three dimensions of emotional response to environments and the health spa that stages pleasure, dominance, and arousal.
key_concepts: The environment and artifacts code can be defined as the physical objects and environmental attributes that communicate directly, delineate the communication context, and/or guide social behavior.

The natural environment is not in itself a code and only becomes a potential element in our nonverbal coding system when we as humans act upon it, as when we create formal or informal gardens or arrange rocks in a symbolic form like at Stonehenge.

Unlike with other nonverbal communication codes, we don't really acquire the environmental code in any direct sense; rather, we acquire reactions to the environment by learning to interpret meaning from the environment, that certain contexts prompt different kinds of interaction, and that particular environment cues imply sets of rules and guides for behavior.

Our reactions to the environment are learned primarily through socialization, and the meanings we ascribe to it are heavily influenced by our cultural background, as when Westerners may not draw much meaning from a formal Japanese rock garden whereas people from Japan may draw quite important meanings from it.

Hall's distinction holds that a high-context communication is one in which most of the information is either in the physical context or internalized in the person while very little is in the coded, explicit part of the message, whereas in low-context communication the mass of the information is vested in the explicit code.

High-context cultures, which include the Japanese, Iranian, and French cultures, use messages with implicit meanings that communicators are presumed to know, so context and environment assume a very important role in helping people interpret a communicator's behaviors accurately.

Low-context cultures, including the German, Swiss, and US cultures, are more likely to use explicit verbal messages that depend very little on the environment or context for their meaning, and ambiguity in communicative behavior is undesirable.

Although the specifics of the environmental code are learned, its fundamental basis is more innate and consistent with evolutionary premises, since humans have long altered the environment for their purposes, imbued it with meaning, and relied on environmental cues for guides to behavior, all adaptations that have survival value.

Mehrabian proposed that there are three basic dimensions along which we respond emotionally to environments, namely pleasure-displeasure, dominance-submissiveness, and arousal-nonarousal, and these kinds of reactions may be inborn.

Health spas give attention to every detail from the landscaping of grounds and gardens to soothing colors and soft rather than hard surfaces, meant to communicate that this is a place for relaxation and rejuvenation, high in pleasure, moderate in dominance, and low on arousal.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Space: Fixed and Semifixed Features and the Norms They Set
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table where one side argues fixed features and the other semifixed features: a scale model shows right-angled US rooms, a courtroom dais looms high, a Harkness oval table gathers students, a tidy office glows beside a color wheel ranking blue first, and a door swings shut between two selves as a fire symbol flares beside it.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the fixed and the semifixed features of the environment: pit floors, ceilings, walls, spatial organization, size, linear perspective, and materials against the arrangement of objects, sociofugal and sociopetal seating, the Harkness table, tidy offices and the halo effect, light, and color. Then settle the norms of the code: Schwartz's doors as a human event equal to the discovery of fire, and the home as an extension of the self.
key_concepts: Hall offered that environmental and artifactual features can be classified into three distinct categories: fixed-feature elements, semifixed-feature elements, and non-fixed-feature elements, with the last of these categories, which Hall called informal elements, largely coinciding with proxemics.

The category of fixed-feature elements consists of everything that is relatively permanent or slow to change in an environment, such as floors, ceilings, and walls, and the spatial organization of such elements may communicate something about the people who inhabit an environment or those who designed it.

Small spaces with low ceilings invite intimate and informal communication, moderately sized spaces are appropriate for a wide range of social and task-oriented interactions, and large-scale spaces are used for public events such as rallies, public addresses, or large banquets.

In US society there is a heavy and almost exclusive use of right angles and straight lines in design, and rooms like the Oval Office in the White House or the rotunda of the US Capitol are notable partly because of their departure from this pattern.

Soft, plush, and textured materials may create a relaxed atmosphere that is more inviting for conversation, whereas hard surfaces and bright, angular objects may create feelings of energy or anxiousness, and materials may also have symbolic value reflecting one's social class and interpersonal style.
One might think of the home as an extension of the self, and personal artifacts perform the same function, so homes and the objects within them carry significant symbolic meaning.

Sociofugal arrangements direct people away from each other, and people may seek them when they need a sense of safety, whereas sociopetal arrangements bring people together, and people may feel more connected within them.

The Harkness Method of teaching involves arranging up to 12 students and a teacher around an oval table, an arrangement meant to de-emphasize the separation between students and teachers and to encourage students to interact with each other in an open, engaging way.

In a study by Teven and Comadena, participants who visited a high aesthetic office rated the instructor as significantly more trustworthy, more authoritative, and friendlier than those who visited a disorganized and untidy low aesthetic office, an example of the halo effect.

Lower levels of light are conducive to social conversation whereas higher levels of light set a task tone, which is why you often find lower levels of lighting in a restaurant or bar than in an office or classroom.

Cool colors such as blues and greens have calming effects on people, whereas warm colors such as red, orange, and yellow are more arousing, and Eysenck, summarizing 21,060 participants, found a consistent rank order of color preferences in which blue was preferred, followed by red, green, purple, orange, and yellow.

Schwartz refers to doors as a human event of significance equal to the discovery of fire, because they can be used deliberately and selectively to regulate physical and social intrusion and because they contribute to psychological self-definition.

assets.topic: Audit the Chronemic Ledger: Origins, Physical and Biological Cycles, and the Systems of Time
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger unfolds along a timeline: bone scratches from 20,000 years ago, a Babylonian abacus dividing the hour into 60, an atomic clock ticking 9,192,631,770 periods, a day-night dial spinning toward a 25-hour cycle, a chart of six chronotypes, and a column of stamps labeled TECHNICAL, FORMAL, and INFORMAL.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the chronemic code as it is defined, invented, and acquired: count off Fisher's claim that time is the most neglected variable of communication, then check the human invention of time from ice-age bone markings and Babylonian base-60 counting to the caesium-133 atomic second. Tick off the physical cycles of day, month, and year, the circadian rhythm with its zeitgebers and 25-hour drift, ultradian and circalunar rhythms, and the six chronotypes. Then audit acquisition from infants to Piaget's age 12, and close the books on displaced versus diffused point patterns and the three systems of technical, formal, and informal time.
key_concepts: Chronemics is how humans perceive, structure, and use time as communication, and it concerns its semiotic or meaningful aspects as well.
Fisher's comment that time is, without a doubt, one of the most crucial, yet most neglected, variables of communication is still true more than 40 years later.

Time is a human invention, and although naturally occurring events such as the development of a child or the changing of the seasons provide a basis for the concept and measurement of time, they are indicators of time, not time itself.
Ice-age hunters in Europe gouged holes and scratched lines in bones and sticks over 20,000 years ago, possibly to count the light-dark cycles, or days, between phases of the Moon.

Since 1967, the International System of Units has defined a second as the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two energy levels of the ground state of the caesium-133 atom, a cycle that forms the basis of the atomic clock.

We have 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour because the Babylonians used a counting system with a base of 60, and had the British invented time with a base-10 system we would likely have hours composed of 100 minutes and minutes composed of 100 seconds.

The circadian rhythm, also known as the diurnal rhythm, is a biological cycle that governs changes in sleeping and waking patterns, eating behaviors, hormone and catecholamine levels, body temperature, blood sugar levels, and cognitive and mental alertness.

Many circadian processes are ordered by cues in the physical environment, such as the alternation of light and dark, and by human-made signals such as clocks and schedules, and when these zeitgebers are removed people's circadian processes actually approximate a 25-hour cycle.

Ultradian rhythms, such as your breathing pattern, the beating of your heart, or your alternation between REM and non-REM stages of sleep, govern processes that begin and end multiple times every day, and circalunar rhythms influence processes that transpire approximately monthly.

Infants have no sense of time other than their awareness of their own biological cycles, and by around age 6 children have learned such formal time categories as the days of the week, while by age 12 they have typically mastered the key elements of their culture's time system, consistent with Piaget's suggestion that a mature sense of time requires reaching the higher stages of cognitive development at around age 12.

People who follow a displaced point pattern see appointed times as a fixed end point and would show up for a 1:00 pm meeting anytime between 12:45 and 1:00, whereas those who follow a diffused point pattern view appointed times as rough approximations and might arrive anytime between 12:45 and 1:15.

At the sociocultural level, time can be organized according to technical time, the scientific and precise clock time to which all computers and cell phones can now be synchronized; formal time, the traditional, consciously taught system in which western cultures order time in a highly segmented, linear, and hierarchical fashion; and informal time, the implicit system learned through experience with a culture that has no pancultural rules about acceptable wait time or punctuality.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Time Orientations, Monochronic versus Polychronic, and Relational Messages
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with columns labeled PAST, TIME-LINE, PRESENT, and FUTURE, then rows labeled MONOCHRONIC and POLYCHRONIC: cards fly into place showing a retirement investor, a genealogy tree, a siesta beach, and a teardown of historical buildings, while a clock-that-is-a-commodity confronts a never-ending river, and a snail mascot crawls past a kiva and a Hawaiian beach at 'three Hawaiian time.'
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for reading chronemic culture: drop the past, time-line, present, and future orientations of psychological time into their cells with their cultural homes from the US to France, Germany, Japan, and Spain, lay the space metaphors for time across the second row, and then pit monochronic Germany, Switzerland, and the US against polychronic Latin America, the Arab Middle East, and sub-Saharan Africa. Finish by placing the co-cultural cards, the Navajo here and now, Haole versus Hawaiian time, and the Slow Food snail, then run the three relational message rows of politeness, value, and power through the grid.
key_concepts: Research suggests that there are four basic psychological time orientations: individuals with a past orientation dwell on events in the past and see events as recurrent and time as circular, those with a time-line orientation see time as a continuum integrating past, present, and future, those with a present orientation focus on the here and now, and those with a future orientation focus on anticipating and planning for future events.

Many European and Asian societies, including France, Germany, Japan, and Indonesia, emphasize a past orientation that encourages behaviors such as preserving oral histories, valuing genealogy and social traditions, and keeping rather than replacing historical sites.

Time orientations can affect the content, urgency, and structure of communication: people with past or present orientations may see little need for punctuality or adherence to others' time pressures, whereas those with a time-line or future orientation may see schedules, calendars, and deadlines as necessities.

Gonzales and Zimbardo showed that people gravitate to jobs with matching time orientations and that job success and satisfaction depend on intensifying that time orientation, with children of skilled and professional parents acquiring the kind of time orientation that allows them to succeed in skilled and professional occupations.

When people reason about something abstract they have a tendency to imagine something concrete that the abstract entity is similar to, and for many people that thing is space, which is why English speakers say that the future is in front of us and the past is behind us.

Societies that have a monochronic concept of time, such as Germany, Switzerland, or the United States, present time as a commodity, treating it as something of value, believing that time is money, and talking about making time and losing time.

People with a polychronic orientation think of time as more holistic, more fluid, and less structured than their monochronic counterparts, conceiving of it more like a never-ending river flowing infinitely into the future, and because they see time as infinite they aren't as obsessed with it.

In polychronic societies schedules are more fluid and flexible: a business may not open at an appointed time but opens whenever the proprietor chooses, and a professor and students would arrive to class over a period of time and begin whenever the professor was ready.

For traditional Navajo, time and space are very much the same, only the here and now is real, and the future is a foreign concept, while Native Hawaiians operate under two time systems, Haole time, which resembles the mainstream culture's time system, and Hawaiian time, which is very lax.

The Slow Food movement was founded in Italy in 1986 by Carlo Petrini as an organization promoting long, leisurely dining experiences that encourage conversation and appreciation of the food being eaten, and its mascot is the snail.

Arriving for an appointment or an event at the appropriate time signals politeness and acknowledges the value of other people's time, but what constitutes being on time varies across cultures, and people in polychronic societies would be unlikely to take offense if you showed up at noon for an 11 am class.

Even within a monochronic society such as the United States, being on time for a business appointment most often means literally arriving at the appointed time and arriving more than five minutes late requires an apology, whereas arriving on time at a friend's 8:00 pm party may mean showing up at 8:30 or 9:00, possibly later.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Waiting, Punctuality, and the Communication Potential of Chronemics
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a waiting room: a clock ticks past five minutes with an apology bubble, a doctor's door swings after three minutes while a child's calendar counts twenty minutes of quality time, Harry Truman's office clock shows 45 minutes remaining, a lecture hall fills with students waiting 30, 20, or 10 minutes for their professors, and a text message reply speed meter flashes QUICK = IMMEDIACY while a fog of ambiguity swirls over the informal time system.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of what time really says about us: hold the politeness, value, and power messages up to the light, weigh the five-minute rule and the regional rules for parties and dinners, count the value ledger from quality time and Galinsky's children to the Family Medical Leave Act and the two weeks of US vacation, then face the power gauntlet of Harry Truman's 45 minutes and the professor's waiting ladder of 30, 20, and 10 minutes. Finish with the six chronemic variables, response speed and the quick reply, and the encoding and decoding potential that makes the informal time system so hard to read.
key_concepts: In monochronic societies, the way people use their time sends signals about what and whom they value, because as time is seen as a finite commodity, giving your time to a person, an activity, or a cause implies that you believe that person, activity, or cause is valuable to you.

Many child development experts have opined that it is not so much the quantity of time parents spend with their children but rather the quality of that time that matters, and some suggested that giving children 20 minutes a day of undivided attention was just as beneficial as five hours of divided attention.

In a national representative sample of over a thousand third through twelfth graders in the United States, Galinsky found that 60% of children felt they spent enough time with their parents whereas 40% did not, and older children were more likely than younger children to express a desire for more time, especially with their fathers.

In the United States, the Family Medical Leave Act allows up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave to care for a newborn, newly adopted, or foster child, whereas federal law in Sweden allows full parental leave at 80% salary until a new child is 18 months old.

The United States is the only industrialized country in the world that does not guarantee paid vacation time, nearly 25% of US workers receive no paid vacations or holidays at all, and every nation in Europe has collective bargaining agreements guaranteeing between 20 and 36 days of paid vacation annually.

At least in monochronic cultures, the use of time, and the ability to dictate how others use their time, sends signals about power and status, and we generally do not find waiting for a doctor, a professor, or a supervisor to be violations of our expectations because we expect that people of higher status have the right to make us wait for their time.

The story is told about Harry Truman that when he was president a newspaper editor who had waited 45 minutes in the outer office was told, when I was a junior senator from Missouri, that same editor kept me cooling my heels for an hour and a half, so the son of a bitch has 45 minutes to go.

Many US American university students have repeated the unwritten rule that students must wait 30 minutes for a full professor who is late for class, 20 minutes for an associate professor, and only 10 minutes for an assistant professor, with the implicit message that the further removed one is from you in status, the more legitimate it is for them to make you wait.
Among the chronemic variables that can be encoded and decoded as messages are punctuality, wait time, lead time, duration, simultaneity, and response speed.

When communicators intend to send messages with the chronemic code, they can find the code's encoding potential limited because the number of identified elements in the code is relatively low and it is not always clear which forms of time manipulation qualify as messages in a given culture.

Accuracy in the perception of chronemic cues varies: the formal and technical elements of this code tend to be perceived quite accurately, but the informal time system, which contains the elements most likely to affect behavior, tends to be perceived less accurately.

The message sent by the chronemic cue of a quick reply to a text or email is generally greater immediacy, at least among people who are relationally close, and cell or mobile phones have shortened the time we expect it to take to get a chance to talk with someone.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Displaying Identities, Managing Images, and Forming Impressions

assets.topic: Scrub the Origins: Identity Display, Impression Management, and the Markers We Wear
assets.visual_frame_description: A split screen where one side shows hospital staff in color-coded scrubs labeling their occupational identities while another doctor in black scrubs makes a social-justice statement; a curator's wall of identity cards marked SYMPTOM, SEMBLANCE and SYMBOL pinned to a human silhouette, with an intersection grid of a young urban male of Pakistani descent lighting up at the center.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the three related communicative functions that open this chapter: how we reveal ourselves through nonverbal codes in identity display, how we reflect or pretend to have particular characteristics in image or impression management, and how others decode who we are in impression formation or person perception. Then weigh the building blocks: markers as cues that indicate group membership, symptoms as biological features like skin tone, semblances and symbols learned through socialization, the multiple and intersecting identities our cues reflect, and the hospital scrubs and #BlackLivesMatter black-scrub examples that show identity display and impression management combined in real life.
key_concepts: The process of revealing ourselves to others by showing our identities through nonverbal codes is referred to as identity display, while using nonverbal cues to reflect or pretend to have particular personal characteristics is known as impression or image management.

Impression formation or person perception is largely a decoding process in which others attend to cues like our gait to see if we are easy-going or action oriented and hear our vocal qualities to discern our cultural background.

Identity display, image management, and impression formation are intimately related, as our ability to project a certain image depends on our knowledge of how others will interpret our behaviors, making identity displays and impression formation two sides of the same coin.

In US hospitals, the clothing or scrubs that different staff wear represent their occupational identity, but a group of doctors who chose black scrubs to show their alignment with the #BlackLivesMatter movement turned that clothing into an impression management action.
Cues that help reflect particular identities are called markers because they mark or indicate a particular group that we are in or a characteristic that we have.

Some identity markers are symptoms, which are characteristics such as skin tone and eye shape that are part of our biological makeup, while others, either semblances or symbols, are learned through socialization processes.

Social learning theory emphasizes that children learn ethnic and racial socialization messages through living and observing salient messages in context, transmitted either knowingly through cultural artifacts or unknowingly through everyday childrearing practices.

Identity displays are complicated because we have multiple aspects to our identity, and our nonverbal cues can often only be understood from the intersection of these identities, such as being a young urban male of Pakistani descent.

The term identity refers to several foci in the literature, including the culture of a people, common identification with a collective or social category, the creation of a common culture among social movement participants, and the meanings people attach to the multiple roles they play in differentiated societies.

Identity displays remain central to our communicative lives, though they can be the site of personal and social challenges as people work with their own sense of self and sometimes try to change the ways others define and evaluate their groups.
Identity display and image or impression management count as encoding processes that we do both consciously or unconsciously, and they are at once both simple and complex accomplishments.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Identifiers: Culture, Ethnicity, Sex and Gender in Nonverbal Markers
assets.visual_frame_description: A world stage with five spotlighted figures, each labeled with a different identifier: a Japanese woman performing the face-cutoff gesture, a Kuna woman in a mola blouse beside a hijab-clad Muslim woman, a Yoruba jewelry display, and a pair of men in a Latin American arm link; behind them a café clock ticks touch counts from 180 to 0, and a bar chart contrasts men's and women's smiling, touch, and talking time.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the identity categories our nonverbal cues mark: walk the national culture identifiers, from the nonverbal accent and culture-specific emblems and illustrators to display rules, the face-cutoff gesture of Japanese women, and the café touch counts that ranged from 180 touches per hour in San Juan to zero in London. Then defend the ethnic and racial identifiers, from physiognomy and the contested social construct of race to the hijab, Kuna molas, Yoruba jewelry, and the gait patterns of New Millennial African Americans. Finish by weighing sex and gender identifiers: primary, secondary and tertiary differences, expressivity demand theory, why women smile more, vocal pitch, touch, space, and talking time.
key_concepts: Physical appearance and vocal cues are two large categories that may affect how our cultural identity is portrayed, and different cultures may use facial expressions and body movements in somewhat diverse ways that act as a nonverbal accent reflecting our cultural membership.

The facial cut-off gesture, used by some Japanese women particularly those adhering to traditional sex roles, communicates shy femininity, caution, coyness, and self-consciousness, and less frequent and less varied cutoff gestures appear in European, African, South American Indian, and Indonesian flirting behavior.

Cultures have unique display rules dictating what facial expressions can and cannot be displayed and what objects or events elicit an emotion, such as Japan's eyelid position rule for expressing the intensity of anger.

It is expected that US Americans, particularly women, will respond with a smile from a stranger and failing to do so is considered socially incompetent, whereas there is no norm for returning the smile among Israelis.
