Jourard observed that couples in cafés in San Juan, Puerto Rico, averaged 180 touches per hour, those in Paris averaged 110, those in Florida averaged only 2, and those in London made zero contacts.

The most prominent physical appearance identifier of race, and to a lesser extent ethnicity, is physiognomy and accompanying differences in skin and hair color or texture and facial features, though the idea of race itself is contested and may best be seen as a social rather than a biological construct.

In Droogsma's study, US American Muslim women who voluntarily veil reported that wearing the hijab helped them express their Muslim identity and commitment to Muslim principles, far from signifying oppression, and functioned as an empowering symbol of their identity.

Molas are distinctive blouses made and worn by Kuna women in Panama that serve as identifiers of the Kuna people specifically and of people from Panama more broadly, and the Yoruba ethnic group can be identified in part through the particular jewelry that they create.

African American youth in Greene and Stewart's focus groups said the walks from the late 1960s pervaded the community as symbols of coolness, togetherness, and sociopolitical defiance, whereas the New Millennial generation walks in more subdued, conspicuous struts dictated by outfits, shoes, situations, and destinations.

Women are expected to be more expressive and will often meet those expectations, but when status and power differ, both women and men smile more when in a lower-power position and smile less when in the higher position, per expressivity demand theory.

Overall, women tend to smile more than men regardless of the emotion they feel at the moment, a pattern that is common across cultures and co-cultures, and communicators expect women to smile more frequently than men even when they may not do so in actuality.

Men's voices tend to have a lower pitch than women's partly because men have a larger larynx and longer, thicker vocal folds due to physiological changes at puberty, and girls and boys are socialized into different speaking styles at a very early age.

assets.topic: Audit the Image: Goffman's Stage, Stigma, and the Tactics of Impression Management
assets.visual_frame_description: An auditorium stage seen from the wings: a spotlighted actor performs behind a lectern while cards stamped INVALIDITY scatter the floor marked sneeze, stumble, hiccup, and the Dean Scream waveform; a ledger with columns DEFENSIVE/ASSERTIVE and STRATEGIC/TACTICAL opens into a 2 by 2 matrix, and a stigma shelf holds three jars labeled Abominations of the Body, Blemishes of Character, and Tribal Stigma.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the image management ledger: check off the four principles that underlie the process, the multiple selves we project, cause-and-effect knowledge, the generalized audience, and the single encoder. Then walk Goffman's dramaturgical stage, ticking off the performance, the audience, the stage, the front region, props, and poise, and audit the performance violations that invalidate an image, from the Dean Scream to stage fright and over- or underdressing. Close the books on stigma's three categories of abominations, blemishes, and tribal stigma, and on Tedeschi and Norman's defensive or assertive by strategic or tactical taxonomy, plus the finding that interviewers are only marginally affected by impression management attempts.
key_concepts: Impression management, variously called image management or self-presentation, is related to identity displays but is connected to specific attributes and is often more purposeful or strategic.

Schlenker defines impression management as goal-oriented activity that involves controlling information to influence the impressions formed by others, and Keating discusses it as how the silent self speaks volumes.

The fact that we manage multiple images does not necessarily mean we are being inauthentic, because the Self is really a collection of multiple, smaller selves, each representing a portion of who we are but none representing us completely.

Successful image management relies on knowledge about which behaviors and characteristics foster which impressions, that is, on understanding the cause-and-effect relationships between behaviors, characteristics, and impressions consistent with our larger cultural code.

Image management is inherently social, as others must recognize and affirm the image you are trying to project in order for your image management to be successful, though the process is primarily focused on the encoder.

Goffman's dramaturgical theory, presented in The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, builds upon analogies between theatre and everyday human interaction, holding that people present themselves in daily life through the roles they adopt and perform.
The front region of the stage encompasses the areas the communicator customarily uses to present the performance, and it may involve props or artifacts and clothing that complement the role.

Goffman considers poise extremely important to maintaining a successful line, because temporary loss of coordination and muscular control, such as sneezing in the midst of silence or hiccupping while proposing marriage, can divert attention from the performance and raise questions about an actor's self-control.

When then-Senator Howard Dean made a noise meant as an encouraging yell at the end of a 2004 speech, the amplified Dean Scream made people think he did not have adequate emotional control to be president, even though the people at his event did not hear his vocal cues in the same way.

Goffman described stigma as any attribute that is deeply discrediting within a particular social interaction, arguing that a person with stigmatized attributes is reduced in our minds from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one.

Tedeschi and Norman's taxonomy of image management rests on two basic distinctions, so that techniques can be either defensive or assertive and either strategic with long-term goals or tactical with short-term ones, crossing into a 2 by 2 matrix of possible image management behaviors.

In a meta-analysis, Barrick and colleagues found that interviewers are only marginally affected by interviewees' impression management attempts, and there is little relationship between people's use of verbal and nonverbal impression management in interviews and their job performance.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Selection, Organization, Interpretation, Thin Slices, Stereotypes and Expectancies
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-column wall matrix labeled SELECT, ORGANIZE, INTERPRET and EVALUATE; into it fly a Twitter bird tweeting at a candidate's blink rate, a schema deck with four cards, a scowling friend across a street, a stopwatch showing 30 seconds and then 6 seconds predicting teacher ratings, a blonde stereotype chain, and a calibration meter showing violations as enhancing credibility rather than harming it.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build the perception matrix: drop the three tasks of perception into their cells, selection with the Twitter debate study and the noticeability of unusual, frequent, and intense stimuli, organization with the four perceptual schemas and the online chronemic and eS ET cues, and interpretation with the polysemous scowl and immigrant versus non-immigrant patients. Then fill the heuristics row with thin slicing, from Ambady's 30-second and 6-second teacher predictions to the traits, status, pathologies, and citizenship it can predict, the three-part stereotyping process and the IAT, and finish the grid with EVT's expectancies, communicator valence, and the finding that positive violations can actually enhance credibility and attraction.
key_concepts: The perception process involves three separate but related tasks, selection, organization, and interpretation, which we engage so quickly and unconsciously that we think of our perceptions as objective reflections of the world.

In a study of Twitter responses during US presidential debates, Shah and colleagues found that responses went up just as much when candidates used certain nonverbal cues such as facial displays, expressive gestures, and blink rates as when they said something memeworthy, showing that tweeters were selecting nonverbal cues.
Several things make a stimulus more noticeable, including how unusual or unexpected it is, how frequently you are exposed to it, and the strength or intensity of the stimulus.

People use four specific types of schema to classify information about others: physical constructs emphasizing appearance, role constructs focusing on social position, interaction constructs emphasizing behavior, and psychological constructs centering on thoughts and feelings.

In a study of asynchronous text-based online teaching, students perceived chronemics, silence or no communication, electronic style effort and tone (eS ET), and 2D visual cues such as photographs and emojis as forms of nonverbal communication.

Ambady and colleagues use the term thin slicing to describe forming impressions on the basis of small amounts of information, and in one study participants who watched only 30 seconds of silent videotape of college instructors accurately predicted the evaluations those teachers received from students at the end of the semester.

Observing the nonverbal behaviors of a college instructor for only six seconds gives a person enough information to predict with significant accuracy the evaluations that instructor will receive from students who observed him or her all semester long.
Thin slices of information provide adequate bases for forming accurate impressions of certain personality traits, status, pathologies, sexual orientation, and citizenship.

Stereotyping is a three-part process that begins by identifying a group you believe a person belongs to, next involves recalling a generalization made about people in that group, and finally involves applying that generalization to the individual.

The Implicit Association Test tracks response times and accuracy when pairing faces with evaluative words, and results demonstrate that many of us carry negative stereotypes subconsciously even if we believe at a conscious level that we do not.

People hold expectancies, enduring patterns of anticipated nonverbal and verbal behavior, which are grounded largely in social norms based on our cultural code but also take into account knowledge of another's unique behavioral patterns.

EVT predicts that positive violations enhance credibility and attraction while negative violations reduce them, so violations can lead to more positive impressions for the violator than if the violator had done what is normative or expected.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Beating the Biases, Sizing Up Accuracy, and Reading Credibility Cues
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a courtroom where six bias cards flash across the bench, the Asch adjective list reorders itself, a rose-colored lens floats over a couple, and a red X stamps one negative fact onto an otherwise green interview file; on the witness stand a white-coated physician speaks while a tempo gauge sweeps fast, a pause meter ticks one to three seconds, and a loudness dial rises to moderately high.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the cognitive biases that twist our impressions: catch the primacy effect with Asch's adjective-order study, the recency effect with entertainers' final impressions and IRC openings and closings, the confirmation bias with gaze aversion judgments, the visual bias with the third of the brain devoted to sight, the positivity bias with rose-colored glasses, and the negativity bias that lets one piece of negative information spoil a job interview. Then weigh accuracy versus consensus, the traits we judge accurately, Berry's three explanations, and the forms of impressions from age and sex through the voice to sociocultural class signals, uniforms, regional accents, vocal attractiveness, and the credibility cues of tempo, pauses, and loudness.
key_concepts: According to the primacy bias, first impressions are critical because they form a baseline for all future impressions, and in Asch's early study a person described as intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, and envious was judged more positively than one described in the reverse order.

The recency bias suggests that the most recent impression we have of someone can be more influential than our earlier impressions, and both the primacy and recency biases can operate because each is more influential than any impressions that come between them, as shown in an analysis of Internet Relay Chat interactions where both the opening and closing phases were critical for the impressions people formed.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice or interpret evidence such as behaviors you observe in ways that support what you already believe, and observers in one study judged interviewees they were told were lying as more gaze aversive.

Researchers call our tendency to give more weight to visual information a visual bias, and one of its most pronounced effects is leading us to rely heavily on physical appearance when forming impressions, partly because nearly a third of a sighted person's brain is devoted to visual ability.

The positivity bias is the tendency for perceptions to be influenced more heavily by positive information, exemplified by people in love looking at each other through rose-colored glasses by overestimating positive characteristics and underestimating faults.

According to the negativity bias, even one piece of negative information can spoil your perception of someone you would otherwise like, and it appears to be particularly strong in competitive situations such as a job interview or graduate school admissions.

Accuracy means an impression reflects a person's true characteristics, while consistency means the impression is shared by several people who know the same individual, and the two are separate issues since an impression can be accurate even if others do not share it.

Judgments of physical characteristics such as sex, age, or ethnicity are typically accurate because the characteristic is largely manifested physically, whereas judgments of psychological characteristics such as attitudes, values, beliefs, and some personality traits tend to be less accurate.

Berry offered three explanations for high judgment accuracy: direct links between some features of personality and behavior, self-fulfilling prophecies in which we treat someone as having a characteristic they then develop, and repetitive expressions of affect becoming permanent features of appearance such as frown wrinkles from frequent scowling.

Kraus and colleagues assert that social class signals are a frequent, rapid, and accurate component of person perception, and observers make consistent status distinctions on the basis of clothing cues such as uniforms, with patients rating physicians as most credible when they wore a white lab coat over hospital scrubs.

A vocal attractiveness stereotype exists whereby people with attractive voices are perceived as more honest, warm, dominant, likeable, and likely to achieve, while adults with babyish voices are perceived as warmer and more honest but less powerful and less competent than those with mature voices.

Most studies show that faster speaking enhances credibility perceptions such as intelligence, objectivity, and knowledge, while pauses of one second or less may be best for appearing competent, pauses of one to three seconds may be best for appearing trustworthy, and increasing vocal volume up to a moderately high level improves impressions of dominance, boldness, competence, and extraversion.

assets.topic: Scrub the Experience: What Emotion Is, From Precipitating Events to Affect, Physiology, Cognition and the Seven Basic Emotions
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead slides over a chain of events: a report card triggers pride, an unfair supervisor triggers anger, a physician's good news triggers relief; a thermometer and pulsing heart icon mark physiological change, while a three-column display shows the seven basic emotions as photo tiles, a family tree of emotions anchored by LOVE, and a circular plot with Active and Passive on one axis and Pleasant and Unpleasant on the other.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the nature of emotional experience: how researchers split emotion into internal emotional experience and external emotional expression, how emotions arise as adaptive responses to precipitating events, and how they are characterized by positive or negative affect, physiological changes such as accelerated heart rate or tense muscles, and cognitive appraisal. Then catalogue the three approaches scholars use to describe emotion: the basic emotions approach with its seven universal, discrete and adaptive emotions, the prototype approach with its emotion families anchored by love, joy, anger, sadness, fear and surprise, and the dimensional approach with its activity, valence and intensity dimensions.
key_concepts: Researchers distinguish between emotional experience, which is the internal, intrapersonal part of emotion, and emotional expression, which is the external, interpersonal part of emotion that is particularly relevant to understanding the importance of nonverbal cues.

Emotions are the feelings people have in response to precipitating events, so parents feel proud when their children get good grades, employees feel angry when supervisors treat them unfairly, and patients feel relieved when physicians tell them they will recover from a serious injury.

Affect refers to the positive or negative feelings that characterize emotion, with people generally experiencing positive affect when something is consistent with their goals and desires and negative affect when something blocks or interferes with those goals.

Physiological change refers to the biological or internal changes in one's body that occur when a person experiences an emotion, including increased or decreased arousal, warmer or cooler body temperature, and tighter or more relaxed muscles.

Across different cultures, anger is associated with an accelerated heart rate, warm skin temperature, and tense muscles, sadness with tense muscles and a lump in the throat, and fear with an accelerated heart rate, tense muscles, and a cold sweat.

According to the cognitive appraisal theory of emotion, people label their feelings as particular emotions by considering how personally relevant the event is, how pleasant or unpleasant they feel, how much control they have, whether the event helps or interferes with a goal, and who or what is responsible.

According to the categorization view of emotions, cognitive processing is essential to the experience of emotion because emotions do not exist in nature; they are created in people, who use learned knowledge to label their feelings under socially constructed categories such as angry or sad.

The basic emotions approach is centered on the universal thesis, the proposition that people around the world are hardwired to experience and express certain basic emotions similarly, and emotions qualify as basic only if they are discrete and evolved to be adaptive.
Based on the criteria of discreteness and adaptiveness, there is evidence for seven basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust, and contempt.

Non-basic emotions are considered blends of the basic emotions or broader mental states that include emotion, so hurt may be a mixture of sadness and anger, disappointment a combination of sadness and surprise, and jealousy a blend that includes anger and fear.

Russell's circumplex model includes an activity dimension, which refers to how aroused or relaxed a person is compared to normal, and a valence dimension, which refers to the degree to which people experience pleasant or unpleasant feelings with the emotion.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Expression: Spontaneous Symptoms Versus Strategic Semblances, Action Tendencies, Contagion and Display Rules
assets.visual_frame_description: A stage with two speakers: one represents the spontaneous symptom, giggling and furrowing a brow against the speaker's will, and the other holds a rehearsed I love you script; a bowler at an alley smiles only after turning to face his group, emotion particles fly from one person to another labeled MIMICRY, FEEDBACK, CATCH, and a wall chart lists the five cultural display rules with Katelyn, Jack, Isabella, Gustavo and Jordan as their example faces.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between the spontaneous and the strategic sides of emotional expression: debate how much of our emotional expression is involuntary symptom-like output we cannot hide versus planned semblances we craft to send a message, weigh Darwin's action tendencies and the timing of infants' first smiles, then trace how expression turns social as bowlers hold their smiles until they face their group, how people catch each other's emotions through the three-stage contagion process, and how cultural display rules simulation, inhibition, exaggeration, minimization and masking govern what we show, ending with emotional labor in jobs from customer service to 911 dispatch.
key_concepts: Much of our emotional expression is spontaneous and nonverbal, taking the form of symptoms or natural signs that represent a causal relationship between how you are feeling and what you are expressing, and sometimes people cannot hide cues such as giggling or furrowing one's brow.

Other times emotional expression is strategic, as when we plan how we will say I love you for the first time or try to hold back tears to look tough during a sentimental movie, and nonverbal cues of this kind often take the form of semblances, or posed expressions meant to convey a particular message.

Action tendencies are innate, biological impulses that prompt people to respond to specific emotions in adaptive ways, so the action tendency associated with anger is to attack and the action tendency for happiness is to smile and approach someone, although people rarely act on these instincts directly.

Some emotions are present at birth, including distress, disgust, and interest, most infants display their first social smile between six and ten weeks old, and by six or seven months most babies show anger, surprise, shame, fear, and joy, while more complex emotions such as contempt and guilt emerge later.

People are more likely to display certain emotions when with others than when alone, and in a classic study bowlers tended not to smile after making a spare or strike until they turned to face their group.

The process of catching another person's emotions is called the emotional contagion effect, and it occurs in three stages: people mimic the nonverbal emotional expressions of others, the act of expressing emotions provides feedback to the brain that activates the emotion, and people then catch the emotion of those with whom they are interacting.

Emotional contagion appears to be a universal phenomenon, with people in both Western and Eastern cultures exhibiting it, although the effect may be stronger in collectivist cultures where people value group cohesion and harmony.

In one social media study, when Facebook users' feeds contained less negative emotional content, people posted more positive content and less negative content, and the reverse pattern held when positive content was reduced.

The term cultural display rule describes how people manage emotional communication to be socially appropriate within a given situation or culture, so in the United States boys are taught to hold back tears on the football field and women may learn they will face negative consequences at work if they display negative emotions too aggressively.

Researchers have identified five types of display rules: simulation, inhibition, exaggeration, minimization, and masking, with masking the most complex because it is the only rule that involves substituting a felt emotion for a very different emotion.

Emotional labor is the effort people make to display emotions in ways consistent with job expectations, and it occurs at three levels: surface acting, deep acting, and genuine expression, such as when customer service workers must put on a pleasant face while tired or frustrated.

assets.topic: Audit the Theories: Universalistic, Neuro-Cultural and Behavioral Ecology Accounts of the Experience-Expression Link
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with three column headings; under Universalistic, a world map of flags tags faces from Argentina to the United States with recognition percentages, under Neuro-Cultural a diagram of Emotional Elicitors feeding an Affect Program crossed by Cultural Display Rules with a circled X, and under Behavioral Ecology a table of facial signals in which a felt smile means readiness to play, a poker face means declaration of neutrality, and a sad face means elicitation of support.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit three competing theories of the link between internal emotional experience and external emotional expression: check the universalistic claim that expressions are innate, inherited hardwired reactions with the face as the primary channel, ledgering recognition rates from happiness near 90 percent down to fear, anger and sadness in the 60 to 80 percent range, the in-group advantage, and nonverbal accents and dialects such as the Gabon and Quebec contempt finding; stamp the neuro-cultural model with its emotional elicitors, affect program, and the circled X where display rules modify pure read-outs, using Mario at his wife's company picnic; then close the books with the behavioral ecology perspective's minimal universality, its social motives, and Fridlund's table of facial signals from felt smiles to poker faces.
key_concepts: The universalistic perspective is the traditional position that emotional expressions are innate and inherited, with Darwin describing how adaptive actions which were at first voluntary soon became habitual, and at last hereditary, performed even in opposition to the will.

According to the universalistic perspective, the face is the primary channel used to express the basic emotions, and facial expressions of basic emotions evolved so that infants, adults, and people from different cultures all display them the same way.

Infants display facial expressions of positive emotions, such as joy, interest, and surprise, in ways highly consistent with adults, and even newborns display pain expressions using the same specific nonverbal behaviors as adults, but infants and adults do not match when displaying anger, disgust, fear, and sadness.

In typical cross-cultural studies, people shown photographs of facial expressions identify basic emotions well beyond chance levels, with happiness recognized at a rate of 90 percent or higher in most cultures, surprise from around 82 to 92 percent, and fear, anger, and sadness ranging from the 60 percent to the 80 percent range.

Most researchers believe people have an in-group advantage when decoding emotions from facial expressions, meaning they may decode emotion better in the faces of people from the same cultural or ethnic group, as when Chinese individuals decode Chinese faces better than people from the United States do.

Nonverbal accents are subtle differences in how people express emotions that vary based on culture, while nonverbal dialects are a subset of accents that impede accurate decoding, and when strong nonverbal dialects exist it is more difficult for people from other cultures to identify the emotion someone is experiencing.

In a study comparing faces from Gabon and Quebec, nonverbal dialects were relatively strong for contempt but weak for fear, so people from Quebec had a harder time decoding contempt than fear when judging Gabonese faces, and the stronger the dialect, the less accurate cross-cultural decoding became.

Ekman's neuro-cultural theory extends the universalistic perspective by arguing that cultural display rules can alter the way an internal emotion is expressed, with the process beginning with emotional elicitors, moving through the affect program of basic universal emotions, and then being modified or blocked by cultural display rules.

According to the neuro-cultural model, the nonverbal and verbal expression of emotion often represents a combination of one's true feelings and the feelings one wishes to project, as when Mario puts a polite smile on his face at his wife's company picnic even though his first reaction is surprise followed by dread.

The behavioral ecology perspective holds that nonverbal expressions of emotion are influenced by social motives and should be interpreted within the context of interpersonal interaction, so Mario's smile was not false but a natural reaction to the competing desire to please his wife and act socially appropriate in front of her colleagues.

Behavioral ecologists believe the case for universality has been overstated, arguing for a pattern of minimal universality in which facial expressions display more than emotional states, also reflecting people's thoughts, intentions, and physical states, and they prefer to call a smile a facial signal rather than an expression.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Channels of Emotion, From Face and Voice to Body, Activity and Physiological Cues
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with five columns labeled FACE, VOICE, BODY, ACTIVITY and PHYSIOLOGICAL; cards fly in showing a face divided into three regions with action-unit diagrams, a waveform with volume and pitch arrows, a striding angry man beside a slumped sad figure, a curtain behind which a hand touches an arm while emotion labels swing, shake, stroke and squeeze appear, and a flushing cheek with sweat drops and a pulsing heart.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a five-cell matrix of the nonverbal channels of emotional expression: drop static, slow and rapid facial signals into the FACE cell with the nasolabial fold, the three face regions, microexpressions lasting a fifth of a second, and the mouth-versus-eyes scanning pattern; place loudness, tempo and fundamental frequency in the VOICE cell with the acoustic patterns of Table 9.6 and the newborn cry-to-laugh repertoire; file gait, posture and positioning under BODY with the angry stride, sad slump and happy bounce; slot solitary and interpersonal actions under ACTIVITY with the curtain study of touch; and mark the PHYSIOLOGICAL cell with sweaty palms, blushing, pupil dilation and the most noticed cues of crying and changes in breathing.
key_concepts: People typically take at least four channels of communication into consideration when determining what emotion someone is experiencing, and people report relying most on facial and vocal cues, least on physiological cues, and more on nonverbal than verbal communication when judging others' emotions.

Ekman and Friesen focused on three types of facial cues: static facial cues such as bone structure and skin color, which provide the canvas on which other facial expressions occur; slow facial signals such as wrinkles; and rapid signals, the facial movements made while expressing emotion, which are the most important.

Rapid facial signals occur in three regions of the face: the eyes, eyelids, and bridge of the nose; the eyebrows and forehead; and the cheeks, nose, mouth, chin, and jaw, and a happy expression is often marked by the nasolabial fold, the creases that form diagonal lines from the nose to the corners of the mouth.

Expressions of surprise and fear tend to be especially fleeting, with the initial surprise expression rapidly replaced by another emotion, and facial signals that unfold rapidly are likely to be interpreted as happiness or surprise, whereas those that unfold slowly are likely to be viewed as sad.

Microexpressions, or micromomentary facial expressions, were first identified when Haggard and Isaacs slowed down films of therapy patients and found that fleeting emotional expressions lasting 1/5 of a second or less were not noticeable until the film was slowed down, and they can provide tell-tale cues about what people are actually feeling.

When looking at a happy face, people tend to focus their attention on the mouth, but when looking at sad or angry faces they fixate more on the eyes, and people can reliably decode sadness, anger, surprise, disgust, and fear from the eyebrows alone.

Outwardly positive emotions such as happiness and excitement tend to be interpreted more accurately when expressed with direct eye contact, whereas inwardly negative emotions such as sadness and anxiety tend to be interpreted more accurately when gaze is averted.

The voice is one of the most important channels for communicating emotion, with loudness and speaking rate especially important for decoding, hostile emotions such as anger and contempt often communicated with loud voices, and supportive emotions such as affection and empathy with soft voices and pitch variation.

The fundamental frequency of the voice indexes the number of sound-wave vibrations produced per second, so the more vibrations a voice produces, the higher its pitch, and Johnstone and Scherer compiled synthetic acoustic patterns showing that fundamental frequency rises for anger, fear, and joy but falls for sadness.

Newborns have an amazing repertoire of crying and cooing behaviors, babies follow a similar pattern of vocalic behavior in the first year moving from crying to speech sounds to varied intonation, and children from different parts of the world learn to laugh at around the same time, with deaf and blind children producing laughter without ever having heard or seen it.

Gait is an especially potent indicator of emotion: angry people walk stronger and heavier with longer strides, a sad gait is characterized by less arm swing, and a happy gait is characterized by bouncier steps and a faster pace, while anger is also linked to erect posture and clenched fists and sadness to a slumped posture with lowered head.

Activity cues include solitary actions such as going for a walk, eating, drinking, smoking, and throwing things, as well as interpersonal actions such as kissing, hugging, tickling, hitting, and touching, and touch is the most important nonverbal cue used to show love and affection as well as empathy and comfort.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Encoding and Decoding Emotion, From Emotional Intelligence to Display Rule Mastery Across the Lifespan
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena styled as a brain circuit board with four glowing nodes labeled RECOGNITION, UNDERSTANDING, MOTIVATION and MANAGEMENT; a gauntlet of faces flashes past with a happy face scoring 90 percent while an angry face pops out of a crowd, a pen held between teeth plays a cartoon, and a developmental timeline runs from a crying two-year-old exaggerating pain to a teenager learning masking, with a scale tipping slightly toward women on decoding and toward men on emotional control.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, emotional skill itself: first master the four components of emotional intelligence, recognition, understanding, motivation and management, including emotional flooding, perceptual nonverbal dominance, and the facial feedback hypothesis with the pen-between-the-teeth cartoon study; then run the decoding gauntlet, where happiness is the easiest face to read, an angry face stands out in a crowd of happy faces, intense and posed emotions decode more accurately than mild and spontaneous ones, and women are slightly better decoders than men; and finish on the encoding side, where expressing positive emotion brings popularity and health, stifling emotion brings cardiovascular and memory problems, women smile more and men control more, and children learn the display rules in order, exaggeration first and masking last.
key_concepts: Emotional intelligence refers to the ability to understand, manage, and utilize your emotions to inform thoughts and actions, meet goals, and understand the emotions of others, and emotionally intelligent people are more successful in their careers and personal lives.

There are four essential components of emotional intelligence: recognition, understanding, motivation, and management, and emotionally intelligent people avoid the trap of believing they can always read the emotional expressions of others, continuing instead to look for nonverbal and verbal cues that affirm or change their initial impression.

Emotionally intelligent people are better able to decode the emotions of others in part because they practice perceptual nonverbal dominance, the tendency to rely more on nonverbal than verbal information when interpreting emotional situations.

The most commonly noticed physiological cues of emotion in everyday life are crying and changes in breathing, and outward manifestations such as sweaty palms, blushing, pupil dilation, shaky hands, and a quivering lip can accompany internal changes in arousal, blood pressure, heart rate, muscle tenseness, and skin temperature.

Gottman used the term emotional flooding to describe what happens when people become so overwhelmed with emotion during interpersonal conflict that they become defensive and stop communicating effectively, and when emotions are intense it is often better to postpone talking about your feelings until you can think more rationally.

The facial feedback hypothesis, also called self-perception theory or efference and first proposed by Charles Darwin, holds that facial expressions send signals to the brain that produce feelings, and in support of it people who held a pen between their teeth, which activates the smiling muscles, rated cartoons as funnier.

People who are able to decode the emotions of their friends and romantic partners accurately tend to have happier relationships, and socially competent men tend to be especially good at decoding facial expressions of positive emotion while socially competent women are especially good at decoding negative emotion.

Happiness is perhaps the most easily recognizable of all emotions when judging faces, it is easier to pick an angry face out of a crowd of happy faces than a happy face out of a crowd of angry faces, and intense and posed expressions are easier to decode than mild and spontaneous ones.

Decoding vocal expressions of emotion can be difficult, with one study showing accuracy rates of about 50 percent, and mistakes often occur when people confuse fear with nervousness, love with sadness or sympathy, pride with happiness, surprise with happiness, anger with contempt, or interest with pride or happiness.

In general, women are slightly better than men at decoding emotional expressions, a difference that appears early in life, partly because women tend to focus on more details when decoding emotions while men focus more generally, and people gain decoding accuracy with age from about age 5 to age 25 or 30.

People who are good at decoding emotional expressions are not always skilled at encoding them, and encoding emotions appropriately is critical: people who express too much negative emotion are perceived as less likeable, while people good at expressing positive emotions are more popular, have better relationships, and are physically and mentally healthier.

Children learn display rules in a sequence, first exaggerating emotions as when a two-year-old cries loudly to get attention even if only a little hurt, next inhibiting or minimizing emotions, while masking, which substitutes a different emotional expression for the emotion a child is feeling, is usually learned last.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Relational Messages: Developing and Expressing Closeness

assets.topic: Scrub the Foundations: Relational Messages, Intimacy, and the Seven Dimensions
assets.visual_frame_description: A seven-panel wall of dials labeled intimacy, dominance, similarity, task orientation, formality, composure, and arousal behind two people facing one another in a hallway of mirrors, where each mirror shows a different version of the same gesture; a tag on one panel reads equifinality while a speech bubble shows a gesture meaning liking to one person and intimacy to another.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the scaffolding of relational messages: how nonverbal cues reflect the nature of a relationship, how two people may be negotiating the relationship nonverbally when they disagree about it, Burgoon and Hale's seven fundamental themes of relational communication, and why intimacy/non-intimacy and dominance/submission are called the most important dimensions. Then weigh the definition of intimacy as both a psychological state and a communicated behavior, separate closeness from liking, and trace how immediacy and positive involvement cues, equifinality, and the polysemous nature of cues leave room for misinterpretation.
key_concepts: A primary function that nonverbal cues serve is to reflect the nature of the relationship that exists between people, and the messages people imply nonverbally about what their relationship is are known as relational messages.
When two people display different understandings of what a relationship is, their different behaviors can be seen as a form of nonverbal negotiation for what the relationship will be.

Burgoon and Hale identified seven key dimensions underlying relational communication: level of intimacy, dominance/submission, degree of similarity, social-task orientation, formality/informality, degree of social composure, and level of emotional arousal.
Some scholars have argued that intimacy/non-intimacy (or affiliation/disaffiliation) and dominance/submission are the most important of the relational message dimensions.

Most researchers agree that intimacy is experienced as an internal state and expressed using nonverbal and verbal behaviors, making it both psychological when it is felt and communicative when it shows up in behavior.
People experience intimacy when they share knowledge about one another and feel liked, accepted, understood, cared for, or loved.
Nonverbal communication is often considered the primary mode for expressions of intimate feelings, and a person can feel closeness without expressing it or express closeness without feeling it.
Whereas intimacy is akin to closeness, affection is more about liking, so we sometimes like people with whom we are not close and sometimes do not like people even if we are close to them.

Immediacy or positive involvement cues, such as leaning in toward someone, giving eye contact, smiling, and speaking in a warm vocal tone, help people communicate intimacy and closeness, and highly involved positive interactions may lead to greater feelings of intimacy.
Because of equifinality, the same meaning or outcome can come about in a number of ways, so intimacy, affection, and immediacy can each be expressed through a range of nonverbal cues.

Because the same cues can be a part of all of these sub-functions (e.g., high levels of gaze can reflect intimacy, affection, and immediacy), their use in interactions may not always be recognized as an encoder intends, which can lead to perceptions of sexual harassment or of a power message.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Cue Lexicon: Proxemics, Touch, Voice, Time, Gaze, Smiles, and Posture
assets.visual_frame_description: A circular stage with six stations: a couple standing inside a glowing intimate zone ring, a pair linking arms under a tie-sign banner, a hand fixing a collar tagged mutual grooming, two heads leaning together over a whisper line, an hourglass marked punctuality and time together, and a smile ripple spreading from one face to the next while a pair of open body silhouettes face each other.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the cue vocabulary of closeness: defend the intimate zone of proxemics and the vulnerability it creates, walk the ledger of touch from inclusion touches and body contact tie signs through mutual grooming and comforting touch, and then tune the voice channel with warm, animated, soft voices and the silences that mean harmony. Argue the chronemic rules of punctuality, time spent together, and monochronic focus, arbitrate the gaze debate over moderate versus very high eye contact, and close with how smiling spreads through emotional contagion while open body positions and direct orientation create closeness.
key_concepts: Hall defined the nearest distances people may be to one another as the intimate zone, a close proxemic distance typically reserved for intimate relationships such as those between family members, romantic partners, and close friends, where people make themselves vulnerable because the partner can easily touch and smell them.
People who sit or stand close together are usually rated by observers as more intimate than are those who are farther apart from one another, as are those who touch versus those who do not touch.
Positive and welcomed forms of touch can send strong messages of intimacy by communicating inclusion, drawing attention to the act of being together and suggesting psychological closeness.

Body contact tie signs, such as holding hands, linking arms, and putting arms around someone's waist or shoulder, signal that a couple is to be treated as a bonded pair, and posting on a partner's social media sites can also act as a form of nonverbal tie sign.

Mutual grooming behaviors, such as moving a strand of hair out of someone's eyes, wiping a tear off another's cheek, or fixing someone's collar, are a special type of touch used to communicate caregiving and attachment rather than flirtation or attraction.

When people described how they would comfort a roommate going through a romantic relationship breakup, hugs and pats to the shoulder or arm were the most commonly reported forms of comforting, and the invention of the elbow-to-elbow greeting shows that people find physical contact essential even when regular touch is not encouraged.

Intimacy may be communicated by voices that are warm, animated, moderately relaxed, resonant, rhythmic, and punctuated with relaxed laughter, and soft voices draw people closer together proximally as they lean near one another to hear.
Silences may be associated with complete harmony: when people are comfortable and intimate in a relationship, there is no need to talk.

Violations of chronemic rules of punctuality and consideration may signal non-intimacy through a lack of respect and equality, while the amount of time that people spend together is another important intimacy cue and a key way of showing relational closeness.

In the United States and some other cultures, having a monochronic focus on a partner tends to communicate interest and attention, though younger people may not see cell phone use while interacting as a lack of focus in the way older people do.

Reed found that moderate eye contact was rated as better at conveying genuineness and empathy than were high levels of eye contact, and gaze is most likely to communicate closeness only when it is used alongside other intimacy cues such as smiling.

Both the frequency and intensity of smiling help predict how much intimacy people feel toward one another, and because of emotional contagion a smile may spread from one person to others, creating an overall more intimate interaction climate.

assets.topic: Audit the Affection Ledger: Direct and Indirect Ways of Showing Liking
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-column ledger book: the direct column stamps hugging, kissing, hand-holding, arms around shoulders, and a voice meter reading higher pitch, while the indirect column stamps a casserole delivered to a door, a quick supportive text, and a scratch of the eyebrow that only two prisoners understand; a photo card in the center shows face touches and handholding rated most affectionate and a handshake rated least affectionate.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how affection gets expressed: tick off the critical incidents and nonverbal turning points that mark the development of intimacy, weigh the three reasons nonverbal affection expressions matter more than verbal ones, and run the gaze and smiling entries that signal liking, including the 9.7-times warmth finding. Then split the ledger into direct behaviors, affectionate touch, hugs, tie signs, baby talk, and vocal pitch, versus the indirect entries of social support, support gestures, and the private idioms couples invent, closing the books on the Affectionate Communication Index.
key_concepts: In newly forming relationships, expressions of affection frequently serve as critical incidents that denote the development of intimacy, romantic partners often remember their first hug or kiss, and Docan-Morgan et al. referred to behaviors that bring about a change toward greater or lesser closeness as nonverbal turning points.

Nonverbal expressions of affection are often more important than verbal ones because they may be enacted with less conscious control and reflect genuine emotional status more accurately, because their intended meanings may be easier to deny or downplay if the receiver does not share the feelings, and because nonverbal codes are uniquely suited for conveying subtle and complex analogic meanings.

People engage in more eye contact when they like one another, increased gaze typically sends messages of liking and friendliness, averted gaze may signal disliking and hostility, and patients report liking and trusting their therapists more when the therapists use high levels of eye contact.

In one study, speakers who smiled were 9.7 times more likely to be rated as showing interpersonal warmth compared to when they did not smile, and when avatars were modified to have larger smiles, people had more positive feelings and felt greater social presence after the interaction.

Researchers separate nonverbal affection behaviors into two categories: direct expressions whose meaning is overtly affectionate within a communication community, like hugging, kissing, and hand-holding, and indirect expressions whose link to affection is more covert, like doing a favor for someone.

In Burgoon's study of photographs depicting different types of touch, face touches, handholding, and arms around shoulders were generally perceived as the most affectionate touches, while hand shaking was rated as the least affectionate but still more affectionate than not touching at all.

Hugs vary on a number of dimensions: longer hugs are often used to express more intense affection than shorter hugs, romantic partners may engage in intense full-body-contact hugs, and casual friends might prefer lighter hugs that are restricted to upper-body contact.
Tie signs are used more frequently in dating relationships than in platonic friendships, and the most common tie signs in both relationships are haptic: pats, shoulder embraces, and handholding.

Adults use baby talk, which involves speaking at a high pitch with lots of pitch variance and exaggerated, highly simplified speech sounds, as a means of expressing affection with their romantic partners and, to a lesser extent, their platonic friends.

In Floyd and Ray's study, observers thought confederates were being the most affectionate when they used higher-pitched voices, women were seen as most affectionate with higher pitches while men were seen as most affectionate with lower pitches, and both were rated highest in affection when their voices had lots of pitch variation.

One of the most common indirect ways of expressing affection is providing needed social support, and providing a resource such as money, time, or effort is often seen by the recipient as a significant and genuine gesture of affection, even though the affectionate message is indirect.

Idioms are behaviors that have a specific meaning only to people in a particular relationship, allowing partners to express affection secretly whenever they want and in situations where more overt affectionate displays are inappropriate, as when two prisoners in the movie Bent decided that scratching an eyebrow would signal affection.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Immediacy, Involvement, and the Dyadic Patterns of Similarity, Reciprocity, and Synchrony
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four cells: a classroom where a teacher smiles, gestures, and walks the room while a grading chart tilts, a clinic where a doctor leans toward a patient and patients check five outcome boxes, a mirror where two people adopt the same posture while a frowning pair throws frowns back and forth at a 1:1 ratio, and a metronome where two figures fall into step under a banner reading rapport.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for closeness in action: drop the classroom immediacy card with its halo effect, affective learning, and online variants into the first cell, the doctor-patient immediacy outcomes and the involvement behaviors like direct body orientation, positive reinforcers, and motor mimicry into the second, and the interdependent patterns into the third and fourth, sorting behavioral similarity and reciprocity from compensation, and synchrony with its rapport and mirror-image postures, before arguing how the Golden Rule and negative reciprocity spirals play out in intimate relationships.
key_concepts: Teachers who smile, use eye contact, gesture, walk around the room, and have an open, relaxed body position are rated more favorably by their students than are teachers who use less immediacy.

Perceptions of a teacher's nonverbal immediacy are related to positive affective learning, and because immediacy behaviors are associated with positive emotions that produce a halo effect, students like immediate teachers more and rate them as more competent, trustworthy, caring, and credible.

In online teaching, nonverbal immediacy cues take different forms, such as emoticons, color, cohesion, visual imagery, response latency, and message frequency, and using these teacher-immediacy cues increased student engagement.

When physicians show more nonverbal immediacy, their patients trust them more, talk to them more about symptoms and concerns, understand and retain more medical information, are more motivated to follow medical advice, and are more generally satisfied with their doctor visits.

Direct body orientation reduces distraction and allows two people to see one another's facial expressions better, and head nods can act as positive reinforcers by signaling agreement and showing liking.

Motor mimicry reflects facially that we understand what a person is saying, as when you shut your eyes while listening to a story about a bad dust storm, and it reflects a person's engagement in the conversation.
Behavioral similarity occurs when both people interacting with one another use the same cues, and reciprocity occurs when one person uses similar behavior in response to another's actions.

Married couples' levels of touch were more similar to one another than were the behaviors of serious or casual daters, suggesting the role of relational closeness, and university students tend to be attracted to other students who dress similarly to themselves.

The Golden Rule perfectly encapsulates the principle of reciprocity, and in close relationships patterns of positive reciprocity are essential for developing and maintaining intimate relationships, so immediacy often begets more immediacy.

Negative reciprocity patterns are common in intimate relationships, particularly when couples engage in conflict, and recurrent patterns of negative reciprocity can result in conflict spirals that become increasingly hostile.

In contrast to reciprocity, compensation occurs when a person responds to another person's change in behavior with the opposite behavior, as when you pull back if your romantic partner tries to hug you while you are mad at them.

Interactional synchrony is the coordination of physical movements or similarity in the rhythm of behavior, and when people's behaviors are in synchrony with one another, the pattern often brings about a feeling of rapport or the harmonious connection that involves common understanding.

assets.topic: Boss Level: From Courtship Stages to Escalation, Maintenance, and the End of Relationships
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a staircase that rises and then falls: a couple ascends through five labeled courtship gates where a smile dial reads friendliness, flirtation, then seduction, and five flirting-style cards fly past; at the top a handshake morphs into touch and a phone screen glows Facebook official; on the descent four horsemen labeled criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling charge while a hug restores the pair to acting normal again.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the full life cycle of romantic relating: climb Knapp's dual staircase through the escalation stages, then run the five courtship stages from attention and recognition through positioning, sexual arousal, and resolution, sorting the five flirting styles and the perils of quasi-courtship and misinterpreted friendliness. Then hold the line through the principle of escalation, the maintenance stage with its drop in immediacy cues, satisfied couples' 5-to-1 positivity ratio and trust, and finally survive the de-escalation markers, Gottman's Four Horsemen, and the nonverbal routes to forgiveness.
key_concepts: Knapp's dual staircase model holds that relationships escalate, stabilize, and often descend in intimacy over time, with escalation stages of initiating, experimenting, intensifying, integrating, and bonding, and de-escalation stages of differentiating, circumscribing, stagnation, avoidance, and terminating.

Courtship tends to progress in stages, and the first stage requires attracting another's attention, with heterosexual women in particular tending to engage in behaviors such as giggling and tossing their hair back as attention-getters, though no cue is an always-reliable sign of attraction.

In the recognition stage, women signal availability and interest through subtle behaviors such as darting glances, smiling, primping, nodding, and tossing their head or hair, and women are more sensitive to nonverbal signals of rejection, such as reduced eye contact, yawning, and frowning, than are men.

In the positioning stage, people place themselves in close face-to-face positions that shut others out, and Perper found that courtship behavior often follows a fairly consistent pattern, with approach followed by turning and direct body orientation, first touch, and then increased synchronization of body movement.

Hall et al. define flirting as a form of communication that directly or indirectly signals attraction, and in the context of courtship small amounts of smiling typically signal friendliness, moderate levels of smiling tend to signal flirtation, and constant smiling often signals seduction.

Hall and Xing described five types of heterosexual flirters, the physical, traditional, sincere, polite, and playful styles, each associated with particular nonverbal cues such as nodding, lean in, flirtatious gazes, higher or lower pitch, and self-touch.

When people flirt without intending to develop a sexual relationship, their flirting behaviors are classified as quasi-courtship, and heterosexual men in particular may overestimate the extent to which friendly behaviors are intended to show sexual interest, which can lead to serious consequences including date rape and sexual harassment.

The principle of escalation is based on the idea that nonverbal cues related to intimacy, affection, and immediacy tend to increase in frequency as a romantic relationship escalates, so people in serious dating relationships touch more than do couples who are casually dating, and an important contemporary marker of relational stage is to go online and announce the relationship, such as becoming Facebook or Insta-official.

The maintenance stage is typically the longest lasting, and although there is a drop in immediacy and flirtation-type cues, Hinkle found a strong correlation between how much immediacy married couples engaged in and how much they liked one another, and everyday touch in dating couples helped partners feel happier and more intimate with lasting effects on well-being.

Gottman and Gottman reiterate the finding that happier couples tend to use about five positive behaviors for every one negative behavior in their interactions, whereas unhappy couples have a ratio that is closer to 1:1, and given these cue ratios happier couples trust one another more.

Couples whose relationships are ending are marked by more negative affect, less time spent together, and less nonverbal involvement, and Gottman and Silver's Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling, predict relational demise, with contempt often revealed through sighing or rolling one's eyes and stonewalling occurring through spatial distancing and silence.

Nonverbal forms of forgiveness, such as showing affection by giving a hug and acting normal toward the person again, are one of two preferred forms of forgiveness for people in dating relationships, and males in friendships reported nonverbal forgiveness as a primary reaction over time to their friends' transgressions.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Relational Messages: Power, Dominance, and Status

assets.topic: Scrub the Definitions: Power, Dominance, and Status
assets.visual_frame_description: A definitional workbench with five power-flavor vials labeled coercive, reward, legitimate, expert and referent pouring into a perception meter that only moves when a subordinate reacts; a hierarchy pyramid lights up a figurehead at its apex while the camera notes the raw jeans that once meant poverty but now signal affluence.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the chapter's conceptual core: how power is the broadest term and refers to the capacity to produce intended effects, how it splits into coercive, reward, legitimate, expert, and referent power, why power is ultimately a perception and relative to another person, why dominance is the interactive set of behaviors that accomplish power and only counts when someone answers with submissiveness, and how status places people in a social hierarchy, down to the cost signaling of luxury clothing and the figurehead president who has status but no real power.
key_concepts: Power is generally regarded as the broadest term among these concepts, referring to the capacity to produce intended effects, in particular the ability to influence the behavior of another person.

Power has been defined in terms of three specific abilities: the ability to do what one wants without interference from others, the ability to influence other people, and the ability to resist the influence attempts of others.

Coercive power occurs when a person has the ability to punish others or take away something they value, as when a boss can demote an employee, a parent can ground a child, or a teacher can take off points for a late paper.

Reward power is the ability to provide someone with valued resources or outcomes, such as raises and promotions from a supervisor, good grades from a teacher, or love and material goods from a parent.
People in high-status positions such as superiors, parents, and teachers typically have legitimate power, which is based on the perception that they have the right or authority to be in charge.

Expert power is rooted in a person's level of specialized knowledge, so a teenage computer whiz may hold expert power over his father even though the father retains the authority power that makes the son comply with requests.

Referent power relates to how dynamic and likeable a person is, and people gravitate toward and pay attention to individuals with referent power because they like, respect, and admire them or find them exciting to be around.

Although some people possess objective power because they own or control certain resources, power is ultimately a perception: for actual power to occur, other people must value the resources someone controls and be influenced by the person who controls them.
Relative power refers to the amount of power that a person possesses in relation to another person.
Whereas power can be held and expressed personally, dominance is more interactive, referring to the actual interactional behaviors by which power and influence can be accomplished.

Communication only qualifies as dominant if someone responds with submissiveness, so if a person tries to dominate others but no one responds with submissiveness, the attempts become merely domineering.
Status refers to one's position in a social hierarchy, and people may signal social status by wearing clothes that others will know cost a lot, a process known as cost signaling.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Physical Potency: Threat, Size, Strength, Invigoration, and Relaxation
assets.visual_frame_description: A debating hall where a raised fist faces a threat stare that freezes a black bear mid-frame; a height ruler stretches a candidate over an opponent behind a debate dais; side-by-side masks show a furrowed mature face and a babyish smiling face; a voice wave rises deep and loud then drops to a loaded silence; a walker with a quick, deliberate gait passes a slumped, eyes-downcast one.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on how bodies signal potency without fighting: debate the threat stare that stops a bear, the scowls and unsmiling faces read as dominant, why taller candidates win elections 84% of the time and taller salesmen earn 25% more, how babyish faces and high voices read as weak while mature faces and deep voices read as strong, why both loudness and the silent treatment can intimidate, how vigor and a brisk gait signal power, and why moderate relaxation rather than extremes is the mark of someone in control.
key_concepts: The principle of threat holds that the most obvious way all animate species signal physical potency is to show willingness to fight, with the threat stare being such a universal signal that it can keep even a black bear at bay.

Scowls and steady, extended gaze are generally perceived as dominant and threatening, especially when used by a high-status or powerful person, and these cues can effectively cause another to keep their distance.

Angry faces are rated as more dominant than sad or fearful faces, and non-smiling faces are perceived as more dominant than smiling faces, while smiling is overall associated with less dominance and more likely to invite approach or engagement.

The same nonverbal signal can produce opposite interpretations, as with face masks, which for many were a sign of protecting one's family during the COVID-19 pandemic but for others became a symbol of weakness and infringement on personal freedom.

Taller is usually better in terms of power, with taller people more likely to be seen as powerful than short people, and in the last 100 years the tallest US presidential candidate has won 84% of the time.

The power bias toward height is deeply embedded in the visual grammar of many cultures, as taller salesmen in the United Kingdom earn about 25% more than their short colleagues and taller people generally earn higher salaries.
When people were assigned taller avatars in a virtual environment, they acted more confident than did people who were assigned shorter avatars, showing that height can change behavior even virtually.

Faces thought to be mature have squarer jaws, larger noses, more prominent eyebrows, thinner lips, and a smaller ratio of eye size to face size, and mature unsmiling faces with a furrowed brow are seen as more dominant and aggressive than babyish, smiling faces.

Deep-pitched, louder, and more resonant voices are considered mature, whereas high-pitched, thin voices are considered babyish, and people who want to assert their relative strength and higher social ranking may lower their pitch while those signaling lesser rank may raise theirs.

Two seemingly opposite types of vocalic behavior can be intimidating: loudness and silence, with loud voices often heard as dominant and intimidating, but the silent treatment also serving as a potent reminder of a parent's power.

The principle of invigoration holds that any nonverbal action entailing a high degree of intensity and dynamic action is likely to connote greater power, while lethargy and torpidity are typically associated with weakness and ineffectualness.

Moderate postural and vocal relaxation connotes power, dominance, and status, as powerful individuals typically appear more relaxed than their less powerful counterparts and higher-status people are freer to drop their guard and deviate from norms for proper behavior.

assets.topic: Audit the Resource Control Ledger: Territory, Valued Resources, and Time
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger unrolls across an office tower: floor by floor, the president's guarded corner office shrinks into a professor's office, then a shared windowless grad-student cubby; a stamp machine stamps luxury labels onto jeans and cars while a clock turns into a one-way arrow pointing upward; a briefcase rides home in a subordinate's hand while the CEO leaves empty-handed.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how material resources signal power: check the territorial ledger, from the university president's largest hardest-to-access office down to the graduate student's shared windowless room, the military's rank-specific desks and wastebaskets, the brass name plates, gatekeepers, and the powerful person's easy access to anyone; then price the status symbols, the expensive brands, the deference paid to well-dressed shoppers, and the way time itself becomes a one-way resource that the powerful command but do not give; close the books on the expectation advantage that leaders display before they ever perform.
key_concepts: The principle of territorial possession and access holds that those in power are typically given access to more space and larger, more luxurious territories, so office space decreases along with a person's status within an organization.

In one example from the chapter, a university president's office is the largest and hardest to access, followed by a professor's office, while graduate students may share the smallest spaces, which sometimes have no windows at all.
People who have larger, more private territories typically have more room to display status symbols such as luxurious furnishings, expensive cars, artwork, framed diplomas, and awards.
In the military, rank specifically determines the size of an office, the size of a desk, the number of filing cabinets, and even the type of wastebasket, whether metal or wood.

The spaces of powerful people are more likely to be protected by territorial markers and gatekeepers, such as brass name plates on European residences, name plaques on private offices, and assistants who block off access to the most senior people.

Whereas it is usually difficult for a subordinate to gain access to a superior, a powerful person generally has easy access to a wide variety of people and places, and the president of a corporation does not need an appointment or a knock on the door.

In addition to having more private office space, powerful individuals communicate dominance by taking up more physical space, sitting in more open body positions, using more expansive gestures, and being given more space around them by others at tables.

One of the most obvious ways to signal dominance and power is through status symbols, and the billions of dollars of consumer spending on nonessentials testifies to how much people the world over value possession of the right athletic shoes, clothing lines, phones, and automobiles.
People infer a person's status from clothing that they know is expensive, though they may not see those wearing expensive clothing positively even if they judge them to have more status.

Passersby are less likely to intrude on a group of well-dressed shoppers, and anyone buying a new car realizes the deference paid to customers in direct proportion to the formality and expensiveness of what they are wearing.

Time is a valued resource that those in power tend to control: people in power set schedules, determine the duration and frequency of contact with others, and can command others' time but not vice versa, making the relationship one-way and nonreciprocal.

In decision-making situations, individuals expecting to influence group task performance exhibit more cues indicative of their status as a leader and their task-related ability, a phenomenon known as an expectation advantage in expectation states theory.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Six Principles of Interaction Control
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with six cells; into each cell a live scene locks in: a summit table on an island in the Azores, a parent's silent treatment freezing a child, the head of a boardroom table glowing at its end, a penthouse floating above a judge's bench above a row of bowing figures, two leaders wrestling over a doorway, and a salesperson sweeping behind an executive's desk while the clock shows a publisher arriving an hour late.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a six-cell matrix for interaction control: drop each principle into its cell, TERRITORIAL IMPERATIVE with the Azores summit and the Zelensky White House lobbying, APPROACH AND AVOIDANCE with silence as a symbolic weapon and the stare-power of eye contact, CENTRALITY with the CEO at the head of the table and the visual dominance ratio, ELEVATION with the penthouse office, the raised judge's bench, and the depth of a bow, INITIATION with who enters first, talks first, and interrupts most, and the PREROGATIVE OF VIOLATION with the late publisher, the casual-dressing boss, and the territory-intruding salesperson who took over the executive's desk.
key_concepts: The principle of the territorial imperative holds that one way to reinforce power through interaction control is to insist that important negotiations occur within one's own territory, because people entering someone else's domain tend to become more deferent and submissive automatically.

The recognized territorial advantage is the reason for insisting on a neutral locale for summit meetings, as when US President G. W. Bush, British Prime Minister Blair, and Spanish Prime Minister Aznar met in the Azores before the second Gulf War was launched in 2003.

Silence can be used as a symbolic weapon that intimidates subordinates and keeps them in their low-status positions, and because the silent treatment often causes frustration, it can provoke behavior that reinforces power.

One of the most effective ways to control who can approach and who cannot is through eye contact, as people in positions of power or status are more likely to be recipients of more eye contact and are also freer to engage in unwavering, direct looks or stares.

The principle of centrality holds that dominance and status are signaled by centrality of position, with leaders usually sitting or standing in more central positions in a group wherever visual access to the most people is maximized, such as CEOs at the head of the table.

According to the visual dominance ratio, powerful people look more at others when speaking than when listening, whereas submissive or low-status individuals look at superiors more when they are listening, as a sign of attention and respect, than when they are speaking.

The principle of elevation holds that location in vertical space conveys power, as when high-ranking members have offices on upper floors, the judge's bench is higher than the rest of the courtroom, and rulers across cultures and generations have been seated on elevated thrones.

The principle of elevation applies in non-US cultures as well, as in many Asian cultures people bow to show respect and the higher your partner's status in comparison to your own, the lower you are expected to bow.

The principle of initiation holds that dominant and powerful individuals are typically the first to enter a room, the first to sit, the first to talk, and the first to start a conversational thread, and people who are the talkers are often perceived as the leader of a group.

Touch becomes a dominance signal when the initiator of the touch is someone of higher status, especially if the touch is nonreciprocal, though people of lower status can neutralize the power asymmetry by engaging in more formal touch such as a handshake.

The principle of the prerogative of violation holds that once a person has achieved high status and power within an organization, the need to follow organizational norms often fades, and a powerful person has the prerogative to dress casually or show up late without being questioned or scrutinized.

Dominance can be exerted through violations of personal space, as when people approach others' territory in a rapid and deliberate fashion they display dominance, whereas people display submission when they hesitantly approach others.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Dyadic Power Theory and the Fine Line Between Intimidation and Social Skill
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like the dominance quadrants grid, where couples' silhouettes trade cues while a power scale tips: equal-power partners flash more dominance displays, a silent partner withholds a complaint, and a low-power man's fist clenches; behind them a manager's intimidation tactics detonate into lower job satisfaction, a stare drives a helper away, and a parent's skilled, calm request plants a habit that lasts.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the puzzle of power in close relationships: hold dyadic power theory up to the light and see why equal-power couples display more dominance cues than unequal ones, why the powerful have less need to demonstrate their power, why the chilling effect silences the less powerful partner, and why low-power men explode with aggressiveness when their situational power also fails; then walk the subordination hypothesis and the finding that women in equal-power heterosexual relationships use more dominant cues than their male partners; finish against the cost of dominance, the intimidation strategies that backfire, the staring that kills helping, and the skilled balance between friendliness and dominance that makes influence endure.
key_concepts: Dyadic power theory proposes that power is an integral part of any relationship but is especially important in close romantic relationships because it determines how the partners relate to each other and how decisions are made.
Dyadic power theory predicts that more equal power relationships will include more nonverbal and verbal dominance displays than will those with a larger power imbalance.
The chilling effect holds that the less powerful person in a relationship often hesitates to communicate grievances to her or his partner.

In relationships where one person has more power, the person with greater power has less need to demonstrate it because their relative position can be assumed, and it is in relationships where two people sometimes need to vie for more power that dominance cues will occur more frequently.
