In a study of interactions between strangers, those with less power were least likely to act dominantly, those with equal power acted the most dominant, and those with the most power were somewhat less likely to act dominant.

Dominance displays are more common in romantic relationships than in friendships, and women are more likely to act dominant (with more open body positions and less self-touching) in heterosexual relationships than men, contrary to stereotypes.
Women in heterosexual relationships defined by equal power use more dominant cues than do their male partners, at least when they are interacting about a conflict.

Low-power partners do not always act submissively, and particularly when they also have lower situational power, low-power men are more likely to display aggressiveness in their interactions with their partner than are those who had power.
Intimidation strategies often backfire because they alienate employees, increase status differentials, and lead to less job satisfaction.

When dominance is communicated using social skill rather than intimidation, a person's influence is likely to be more enduring, as a parent who engages in dominant yet socially skilled communication is more likely to convince their child to do homework and instill good long-term studying habits.

Skillful communication often entails striking a balance between appearing friendly and approachable and acting dominant and self-confident, because individuals who come off as overly friendly may not be perceived to have the leadership skills to accomplish certain goals.

The subordination hypothesis proposes that women's nonverbal behavior is characterized by submissiveness whereas men's nonverbal behavior is characterized by dominance, and research supporting it shows that men talk more often, in louder voices, and interrupt more while women are more vocally and facially expressive and smile more.

assets.topic: Scrub the Choosing: Propinquity, Gaze, Attractiveness, and Setting the Stage for Interaction
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over an apartment hallway where neighbors meet, lands on a Maryland classroom where alphabetically seated police trainees cluster into Andersons with Andersons, then zooms into a sidewalk where two passersby cast their eyes down as they cross; a photo of a 1960s soda-date flips up, and a dinner table sets itself with seating, candles, and music while a caption reads telling the context.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the forces that decide whether interaction happens at all: how propinquity, or geographic proximity, pushes neighbors, classmates, and coworkers into conversation and even marriage, how our spatial schemata make us feel we belong with those physically near us, and how the sheer force of proximity can erode racial prejudice. Then track the gaze: civil inattention in unfocused situations, the eye contact that invites interaction, and the passing encounters where people glance down to stay disengaged. Weigh physical attractiveness from the 1960s computer dating studies, then scrub on to how nonverbal cues frame and set the stage for interaction, from dinner party decisions about seating and music to telling the context.
key_concepts: Propinquity, or geographic proximity, exerts strong pressure on people to interact, and workers in businesses and medical offices who are seated within 12 feet of each other are more likely to seek interaction with one another than are those seated further away.

Researchers in the mid-1900s found that people in residences, classrooms, or military bunk quarters were much more likely to interact, develop friendships, and even marry those who were physically closest to them.

In a study of Maryland police trainees assigned classroom seats and living quarters alphabetically, after six weeks of training the Andersons and Bakers preferred each other to the Youngs and Zimmermans.

Our expectancies about propinquity, called spatial schemata, are closely related to our belong schemata, so we tend to feel we belong with those physically close to us and use communication to create and then express that bond.

Mann attempted to determine if increased contact could decrease racial prejudice and found, after Black and White students interacted in leaderless groups for three weeks, that interracial exposure reduced the tendency to use race as a criterion for choosing friends.

In unfocused social situations the rule is to engage in civil inattention, such as casting the eyes down as the other passes, and the mere act of making eye contact creates a temporary union between people and serves as an invitation to interact.

In passing encounters, most people walking by strangers glance down or away as a way not to engage with others, a pattern that is more apparent in some cultures such as Japan than in others such as the United States.
Attractive people are often viewed as more curious, confident, happy, active, and perceptive than unattractive people, which may be why we are more willing to interact with attractive strangers.

The first-ever computer dating studies of the 1960s showed that students were much more attracted to their date if the date was physically attractive, and they were more inclined to see the partner again at the end of the semester.
How people interact nonverbally can also make them seem more physically attractive, so the relationship between interaction and attractiveness goes both ways.

Nonverbal cues set the stage for interaction by framing what kind of interaction it will be, such as formal or informal, intimate or non-intimate, and equal or unequal, and these decisions can affect the quality of the interaction that occurs within the setting.

Erickson and Schultz refer to the process of cuing the appropriate behavioral programs as telling the context, and some ways of telling the context seem to be present in all instances of face-to-face interaction among humans.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Case of Privacy: Four Dimensions of Control and the Backstage
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table splits into four seats labeled PHYSICAL, SOCIAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL and INFORMATIONAL privacy; a door swings like a fire is struck behind it, a Starbucks table gets walled off with books, tablets, and a computer, and a clock face spins from morning shower to midnight park bench while a dancer lets down her mask in a curtained backstage.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on privacy as a defining feature of situations: debate the four dimensions of privacy, physical, social, psychological, and informational, and how each is managed nonverbally, then walk the sociofugal-sociopetal continuum, the doors Schwartz ranked with the discovery of fire, the dorm room posters that predict staying in school, and the nonimmediacy behaviors that carve private pockets out of public space. Hold the floor on time as a privacy tool, from showering after roommates leave to the living room that becomes a bedroom at night, then take the stage backstage, where letting down the mask and wearing uniforms mark front stage from backstage life.
key_concepts: Most definitions of privacy stress that it includes the ability to exert control over self, objects, spaces, information, and behavior, to regulate interactions with others, and to deny unwanted access to or influence by others.
Burgoon identifies four major types or dimensions of privacy: physical, social, psychological, and informational.

Physical privacy refers to the degree to which an individual, dyad, or group is physically accessible or inaccessible to others, and the more nonverbal sensory channels through which a person is accessible, the less privacy they presumably have.

Social privacy refers to the ability of individuals, dyads, and groups to control the who, when, and where of communication, and when the number of social contacts becomes excessive, the amount of stimulation overloads the system, creating stress and a desire to withdraw.
Psychological privacy refers to the ability to control affective and cognitive inputs and outputs so as to prevent intrusions on one's intellectual and emotional private property.
Sociofugal environments move people apart, creating more privacy, whereas sociopetal ones bring them together and encourage interaction, creating less privacy.
Schwartz referred to doors as a human event of significance equal to the discovery of fire, because they can be used deliberately and selectively to regulate physical and social intrusion.
The more spatial divisions there are in a setting, and the smaller the volume of space in each, the greater the sense of physical and psychological privacy and social intimacy.
People use nonimmediacy behaviors such as indirect body orientation, gaze avoidance, and extreme sideways or backward lean to signal their desire for individual privacy in public places.

When people feel their sense of privacy is threatened, they may compensate by increasing nonimmediacy, erect body and artifact barriers, or resort to flight, freeze, or, rarely, fight to retain their privacy.

Time can be managed in at least three ways to regulate privacy: segregating use of a setting by time, being in interactional or public territories during non-peak hours, and assigning different functions to a place by time.

Goffman distinguishes front stage behavior, appropriate to a given role, from backstage behavior, which includes behaviors that occur when one lets down the mask, so to engage in backstage behavior is to view a situation as private.

assets.topic: Audit the Conversation: Speaker Cues, Listener Cues, and the Rules of Turn-Taking
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with two columns, SPEAKER and LISTENER, stamps entries: breath, gesture, intonation, fillers on one side; gaze, nods, forward leans, raised index finger on the other; a backchannel line ticks off mmm-hmm and wincing, while a stamp of a meerkat and a gorilla marks rule-bound turn-taking and a Turkish politician stamps SILENCE.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how conversations are managed turn by turn: check the six-second average turn, the speaker's five turn-suppressing cues from audible breath to fillers like hmmm and uhhh, and the turn-yielding cues that hand the floor over, then check the listener's ledger of turn-requesting cues, backchannel cues both generic and specific, and turn-denying cues like silence with illocutionary force. Close the books on the rules of conversational management, from the greeting that precedes talk to listeners who must signal attention, and tally the cross-cultural evidence from Australians, Mandarin speakers, Turkish politicians, meerkats, and gorillas.
key_concepts: Cappella claimed that coordination of interpersonal behavior is the defining feature of interpersonal communication, and if the ability of nonverbal cues to manage, regulate, or coordinate conversations were taken away, it would be impossible to have conversations at all.
A conversation is composed of turns, or times during which one speaker has sole possession of the speaking floor, and the average turn length is, surprisingly, only six seconds.

A speaking turn begins when one interlocutor starts solo talking and ends when a different interlocutor starts solo talking, and interactants constantly enter and exit the roles of speaker and listener as they engage in conversation.

When people listen, they are not only working on information cognitively but also acting toward another, and Yu and colleagues found that empathic listening included the ability to notice and respond to a speaker's nonverbal affect cues.

Turn-suppressing cues that speakers use to keep possession of the floor include audible inhalation of breath, continuation of a gesture, facing away from the listener, sustained intonation, and fillers such as hmmm and uhhh.

Turn-yielding cues such as termination of gesturing, facing the listener, making eye contact, falling or rising intonation, and silence signal giving up the floor, and floor exchanges are smoothest when speakers display many turn-yielding cues.
In conversations among three or more people, eye contact, gesturing, and head nodding in the direction of a given listener all serve to increase the probability of that person being the next speaker.

Wiemann and Knapp found that US American listeners use gaze directed at the speaker, head nods, forward leans, a raised index finger, and an inhalation of breath coupled with a straightened back to gain the floor.

Backchannel cues are behaviors the listener uses to communicate messages to the speaker without attempting to gain access to the conversational floor, and Bavelas and colleagues observed two primary forms, generic cues like nodding and mmm-hmm and specific cues like wincing in reaction to a part of a speaker's story.
Speakers expect listeners to display cues that show involvement and typically find it disconcerting when listeners fail to signal attentiveness by smiling, leaning toward the speaker, or gazing.

Turn-denying cues include relaxed posture, silence, and staring away from the speaker, and Alagozlu and Sahin found that Turkish politicians used silence rather than take a turn-at-talk when it helped the flow of the ideas being discussed.

Conversational management is rule bound, and among the basic unstated rules in many cultures are that conversations are preceded by a greeting, only one speaker may speak at a time, and listeners must signal that they are paying attention to the speaker.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Beginnings, Boundaries, Endings, and the Models of Turn Exchange
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled BEGINNINGS, CHANGES, ENDINGS and TURN EXCHANGE; an eyebrow flash blinks one-sixth of a second into the first cell, a phone check and throat clear drop into the second, a ranked list from breaking eye contact to handshake fills the third, and three gear-models, one rule-bound, one open and flexible, one resource-based, settle into the fourth.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for the life cycle of a conversation: drop the greeting cards into BEGINNINGS, from Goffman's access ritual and Morris's gestural debt to the universal eyebrow flash and Kendon's four greeting stages with their sex and status differences, then drop the boundary markers into CHANGES, the proxemic shifts, extrainteractional activities, silences, and vocalic cues that mark episode and position boundaries. Fill ENDINGS with leave-taking, the politeness maxim, the Knapp study's termination cues ranked from breaking eye contact to the handshake, and then close the matrix with TURN EXCHANGE, sorting the signaling approach, the sequential production approach, and the resource model into their cells.
key_concepts: Greeting cues are highly ritualized and habitual, producing what Goffman called an access ritual.

Morris captures the importance of the greeting ritual by noting that friends meeting after a long separation amplify their friendly signals to super-friendly signals because they have built up a backlog of signals, a gestural debt that must be repaid without delay.
The eyebrow flash, a quick raising of the eyebrows held for about one-sixth of a second before lowering, is part of greetings among a wide range of cultures and may be universal.

Kendon describes greeting stages that include sighting and salutation, the head dip, approach with increased gazing and grooming, and a final approach within ten feet in which mutual gazing and smiling resume and outstretched arms may signal an intention to embrace.

Cultural prescriptions govern greetings, as when a commoner hugged Queen Elizabeth II and the British press was appalled because royalty are not to be touched unless the touch is invited, and business travelers ignorant of Japan's customs may confound their hosts by failing to exchange business cards.

Nonverbal cues help segment and organize topics by marking the boundaries between episodes, periods when discussion focuses on a particular topic, and positions, segments of interaction during which a person maintains a consistent disposition toward the topic.

Four classes of nonverbal cues serve as interactional boundary markers: proxemic shifts, extrainteractional activities such as checking one's phone or rearranging articles, silences, and vocalic cues such as sighs, gasps, and clearing the throat.

Leave-taking rituals may look like greeting rituals in reverse, and people typically prefer to leave conversations on a positive note, conforming to a politeness maxim of avoiding offensive language and projecting mutual support.

In the Knapp and colleagues study, paid interviewers who wanted to end interviews quickly displayed termination cues ranked from most to least frequent that included breaking eye contact, left positioning, forward lean, nodding, and smiling behavior.

The signaling approach to the turn exchange process presumes that turn-taking cues are discrete, independent signals that call up rules, so interruptions are a rule violation that may incur some sanction or penalty.

The sequential production approach, identified with Sacks and colleagues, views conversation as an open, flexible process in which silences and simultaneous speech are expected parts of conversation rather than breakdowns or rule violations.

The resource model developed by Wilson and colleagues treats turn-taking cues as resources within people's behavioral repertoires whose meaning and function vary systematically across different contexts and situations.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Interaction Adaptation Patterns, Theories, Effects, and Self-Synchrony
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a mirrored dance floor where two dancers fall into identical postures while a chameleon changes color on one wall; theory cards flip past, equilibrium scales, arousal labels, expectancy bolts, and a required-expected-desired stack forming an interaction position, while a hand gestures grow point into speech and a winking emoticon punctuates a caption on the screen.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the puzzle of how partners fall into step with one another: name the patterns, matching, mirroring, convergence, reciprocity, motor mimicry, the chameleon effect, and interactional synchrony, then confront their opposites, complementarity, divergence, compensation, dissynchrony, and under- and overaccommodation. Walk the evidence from the microscopic, convergence within milliseconds and neonates syncing to mother's voice, to the macroscopic, hostile reciprocity breeding hostility, then face the theory gauntlet: affiliative conflict theory, the arousal-labeling model, discrepancy-arousal and expectancy violations theories, cognitive valence theory, communication accommodation theory, and the required-expected-desired logic of interaction adaptation theory. Finish with the effects, rapport, persuasion, and stepchildren's satisfaction, and coordinate your own behavior with self-synchrony, growth point theory, and emoticons as illocutionary forces.
key_concepts: When two people display similar behavior, such as pause lengths, gesturing rates, or linguistic elaboration, they are said to match one another, and when the matching takes the form of identical physical behavior, such as adopting the same posture, it is called mirroring or sometimes postural congruence.

If one person's behavior becomes increasingly like another's over the course of an interaction, the pattern is described as convergence, whereas reciprocity refers to contingent behavior that is directed toward and in exchange for the other's behavior.

Motor mimicry is a special form of contingent behavior in which a person displays an empathic behavior in response to another's actual or imagined circumstance, such as wincing when a friend recounts accidentally running into a low-hanging tree branch.

Chartrand and Bargh cite what they call the chameleon effect, people's tendency to unconsciously mimic the nonverbal behaviors of others, and they demonstrated that participants liked a confederate who mimicked their mannerisms more and rated the interaction quality higher.

Interactional synchrony exists when behavioral similarity is based on communicators coordinating dynamic behaviors temporally and rhythmically, and it may occur simultaneously or concatenously, as when a first speaker's baton gestures are echoed by the next speaker.

The opposites of these patterns include complementarity, in which behaviors are dissimilar or opposite, divergence, in which behaviors become increasingly dissimilar, compensation, dissynchrony, underaccommodation, and overaccommodation, when people overstep the level of adjustment appropriate for smooth interaction.

From the microscopic level comes evidence that humans can converge toward or diverge from another's speech within milliseconds, and Condon's high-speed film work revealed not only that adults entrain their communication but that neonates synchronize their movements to the mother's voice.

At the macroscopic level there is a strong preponderance of convergence, matching, and reciprocity, and the degree of people's behavioral synchrony is higher in positive conversations than in negative ones, but it is observed in both.

Argyle and Dean's affiliative conflict theory, also called equilibrium theory, states that humans seek to bring competing drives to approach and to avoid others into balance, and deviations from the equilibrium point cause arousal and a resultant compensatory effort.

Patterson's arousal-labeling model proposes that deviations from a comfortable interaction level create nonspecific arousal that we label as pleasant or unpleasant by examining the situation, so positive arousal is predicted to produce reciprocity and negative arousal to produce compensation.

Interaction adaptation theory proposes that people bring required, expected, and desired levels to interactions that combine into an interaction position, and if the partner's actual behavior is more positively valenced than the interaction position, people should converge toward it, producing reciprocity.
Self-synchrony involves individuals coordinating their own kinesic behavior with their verbal-vocal stream, as when people use hand and vocal cues to indicate just how important a point is.

assets.topic: Scrub the Roots of Influence: Motives, Estimates, and Analogic Power
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a courtroom where a plea is being made, then lands on a weighing scale tipped heavily toward a face and voice icon while a stack of word bubbles labeled 12x slides off; a spectrum strip shows the continuous rainbow of an analogic code snapping into five discrete grade boxes, and a lone spectator's silhouette looms over a golfer whose performance surges and dips.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the foundations of social influence: how influence is defined as preserving or changing thoughts, feelings, attitudes, or behaviors, how the three motives of self-presentational, relational, and instrumental goals drive influence attempts, and how researchers estimate the sheer weight of nonverbal signals, from Segrin's verdict on compliance-gaining to Argyle's failed attempts to overpower face and voice with words made 12 times stronger. Then weigh Birdwhistell's 65% claim, the bias toward negative and vocal signals, the analogic-versus-digital code distinction, and the arou sing force of compresence.
key_concepts: Social influence, sometimes called persuasion, is defined as preserving or changing an individual's thoughts, feelings, attitudes, or behaviors that result from interaction with another individual or a group.

Three general motives for social influence are self-presentational goals, which revolve around our identities and the images we present to others, relational goals, which focus on the establishment, maintenance, and sometimes termination of particular relationships, and instrumental goals, which involve trying to accomplish specific tasks.

The three influence motives are present in most attempts at social influence, although each fluctuates in importance and will play out differently based on the cultural code in which it occurs, and at times they compete, complement, or are irrelevant to one another.

After summarizing the compliance-gaining literature, Segrin concluded that nonverbal behaviors are as powerful as, and in some cases more powerful than, verbal communication in determining the outcome of influence attempts.

In experiments combining varying degrees of friendly and hostile verbal, kinesic, and vocalic signals, the nonverbal signals of face and voice were more powerful than the words, and even making the verbal message 12 times as strong was not enough to overpower the nonverbal signals.
Birdwhistell, one of the pioneers in this area, contended that nonverbal signals account for up to 65% of the social meaning in human interactions.

Negative signals have been found to carry more weight than positive signals in persuasion, and vocal cues carry more weight than visual or verbal ones for certain speech acts like warnings, threats, and contentious disagreements.

Certain kinds of communication, such as informative messages, rely more on verbal signals, and verbal signals become increasingly significant when the content of the message is cognitive rather than affective.

An analogic code is composed of an infinite, continuous range of naturally occurring values, whereas a digital code consists of a finite set of discrete and arbitrarily defined units, such as an A-to-E grading system.

Among the nonverbal behaviors that have a continuum of values are conversational distance, length of eye gaze, touch intensity and frequency, colors used in clothing, chronemic messages of promptness or tardiness, emotional expressions, and most vocal features.

Because nonverbal signals can be intrinsic, natural, spontaneous, and infinite, they may be what humans instinctively recognize and use, and we may be more receptive to messages that utilize nonverbal signals when they take an analogic form.

Compresence is the mere physical presence of another human being that is arousing and can alter our behavior even in a nonconscious way, causing social facilitation of well-learned routines and impairment of weakly learned ones.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Source: Appearance, Attractiveness, and the Faces of Credibility
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-stage debate table: one side holds up a babyish face labeled sincere but naive while a courtroom gavel falls less often on it, and the other side shows a beauty meter swinging votes 44 to 56; above the table a credibility pentagon glows with eye contact, a tailored suit, a poised posture, a warm smile, and an expansive gesture, while a small ticker reads women lead in 84% of measured competencies.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the two source factors of influence that matter most: physical appearance and credibility. Defend both sides of the beauty ledger, from babyish faces that read as sincere, to manipulated political flyers that swung votes from 44% to 56%, to the halo effect and its limits when beautiful women are passed over for management. Then walk the five dimensions of credibility, character and trustworthiness, competence, composure, sociability, and dynamism, and weigh which nonverbal profiles build each one, from eye contact and formal dress to tension-release adaptors and charismatic display.
key_concepts: People with babyish facial features are more likely to be judged as honest, sincere, and warm compared to people with mature facial features, though they may also be perceived as somewhat unintelligent or unsophisticated.

In a simulated courtroom, people with babyish facial features were convicted less often of intentional crimes that involved the perpetrator's manipulation, whereas people with mature faces were convicted less often for unintentional crimes that involved negligence.

In a study of women in politics, a make-up artist manipulated images on political flyers, and in three elections candidates presented with the favorable image received 56% of the vote compared to 44% when presented unfavorably.

The what is beautiful is good hypothesis holds that people assume physically attractive individuals are good on the inside because they look good on the outside, and this is one form of the halo effect in which a trait such as beauty becomes linked to other irrelevant traits.

A person's attractiveness transfers to others, since a group's attractiveness may be judged by its most physically attractive member, and the attractiveness of our Facebook friends influences others' judgments of our own attractiveness.

Some research suggests that attractiveness is only likely to be persuasive when the person being persuaded is not highly motivated to process other information that may be available, so that persuadees focus on peripheral cues rather than the verbal message.

Physically attractive women were less likely to be selected for managerial positions than less attractive women, possibly because beautiful women are sometimes perceived as too feminine to possess leadership qualities such as dominance.

Physical attractiveness is more of an asset when people are interviewing for jobs that specifically require interpersonal skills, such as positions in sales or counseling, as opposed to jobs where people spend much of their time alone behind a desk.

Credibility refers to a set of perceptions held by a receiver about a communicator, with the most credible individuals perceived as having high levels of expertise, authority, and status (competence) as well as being trustworthy and having integrity (character).

In the Burgoon et al. investigation, all five aspects of credibility, character and trustworthiness, competence, composure, sociability and likeability, and dynamism, correlated with persuasion, with perceptions of competence associated most strongly.

People are usually judged as more trustworthy and sincere when they maintain eye contact with listeners and less when they do not, and trust increases with direct eye contact when it is unclear whether a statement is true.

In a study of the U.S. Senate, politicians whose coded behaviors displayed virtues became more influential once elected, whereas those with vice cues either kept their level of influence or went down, suggesting a virtuous character seems to have persuasive impact in politics.

assets.topic: Audit the Message: Attention, Elaboration, Expectations, and Appeals
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger spread across a control room: a checklist ticks eye contact and fast tempo as attention-grabbing while a distraction gauge swings between enhance and impede; a fork in the road shows central route deep thought versus peripheral route fast lane with an attractive face as the exit sign; a horse stamps out answers to a man's tiny head movements, and a guard uniform at a bus stop stamps COMPLIED on passersby.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the message factors of persuasion: check off how immediacy and rapid speech capture attention, how distraction can both help and hurt a persuasive appeal, and how the elaboration likelihood model splits processing into central and peripheral routes, where nonverbal cues work as peripheral cues or as paralinguistic persuasion. Then tick through expectation effects, from Clever Hans to Rosenthal's 30-second expectancy transmission and the self-fulfilling prophecy, stamp the ledger of expectancy violations and proxemic violations by rewarding versus non-rewarding senders, and close the books on appeals to authority, Milgram's lab coat, Bickman's guard uniform, and gaze and touch in requests for help.
key_concepts: Since the 1950s, researchers have acknowledged that gaining a receiver's attention is the first step toward creating enduring change in beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors.

Immediacy behaviors such as smiling, standing close to someone, and looking someone straight in the eye are often arousing, leading to increased attention, and vocal expressiveness and varied tempo can also help secure and maintain attention.

In an experiment, students who watched a sped-up version of the CBS show 60 Minutes were better able to recall the content of the program two days later than those who watched the normal version, suggesting the human brain is equipped to handle rapid-tempo speech.

Distractions that are relevant to judgments of a sender, such as their level of attractiveness or credibility, can either enhance or impede persuasion, since senders judged attractive or credible benefited from distraction while low-attractiveness or low-credibility senders had difficulty persuading regardless of their arguments.

The elaboration likelihood model holds that people process persuasive information through a central route of careful, thoughtful consideration of the true merits of the information, or through a peripheral route that focuses on some simple cue in the persuasion context such as the attractiveness of the sender.

Van Zant and Berger's concept of paralinguistic persuasion holds that because recipients are less likely to think of vocal cues, particularly loudness, as a persuasion attempt, such cues can be more influential and work as indicators of confidence without affecting judgments of the would-be persuader's sincerity.

Experimenter expectancy effects were first discovered with Clever Hans, a horse that appeared to solve math problems by tapping his hoof but was actually responding to minute head and eye movements of questioners who signaled when the correct answer neared.

Rosenthal and his colleagues found that expectations were communicated in the first 30 seconds of an experiment, before the participant had made any response, through cues such as amount of eye contact, vocal loudness, vocal stress, and length of interaction.

The self-fulfilling prophecy effect occurs when expectations are transmitted subconsciously from the person holding the expectancy and the target of those expectations conforms to them, as when teachers who hold high expectations give students more time, attention, and feedback and those students perform better.

According to expectancy violations theory, people hold expectations about how people will and should behave in a given situation, and when a sender violates these expectations, receivers try to make sense of the violation by evaluating both the behavior and the person who committed the violation.

In early EVT research on proxemic violations in a simulated murder trial, the highly rewarding confederates were most persuasive when they violated distance norms, especially by staying farther away than expected, while the non-rewarding confederates were most persuasive when they stayed within proxemic norms.

In Milgram's famous experiments at Yale, 65% of participants continued to administer electric shocks when the experimenter wearing a gray technician's lab coat told them to, even when told the level was dangerous, with the prestigious setting and the experimenter's high-status appearance likely contributing to compliance.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Voice, Touch, Proximity, and the Compliance Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled VOICE, TOUCH, PROXIMITY and COMPLIANCE; cards fly into place, a voiceprint with tempo dial at 375, a bar chart showing tips of 31% versus 11% when touched, a petition sheet stamped 81% against 50%, a close-standing figure triggering a helping hand, and a mimic mirroring a target's posture while a fake badge and repair kit open a door; below, a color wheel of green and blue versus red, black and navy.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of the mechanics of compliance: drop each evidence card into its cell, the four vocal cues of persuasion and the tempo ceiling into VOICE, the tipping and petition-signing numbers of touch into TOUCH, the proxemic violations that win or lose help into PROXIMITY, and the legitimacy rules, social engineering charades, and behavioral mimicry into COMPLIANCE. Then close the ledger with Dunbar and Burgoon's profile of the requestor people comply with, and check the service-industry color and speech propositions that tip customer perceptions.
key_concepts: Mehrabian and Williams identified four vocal cues that are both encoded and decoded as persuasive: louder amplitude, more intonation, greater fluency, and faster tempo.

Research on nonfluencies such as sentence corrections, slips of the tongue, repetitions, vocalized pauses, and stutters indicates that nonfluent speech results in lower ratings of a speaker's competence, and this reduction in credibility often translates into being less persuasive.

Faster tempos generally produce higher assessments of the speaker's expertise and competence, but there is an upper limit to tempo, around 375 syllables per minute, after which judgments of competence plateau or even decrease.

Similarity in tempo appears to enhance perceptions of the persuader's sociability, likeability, and general social attractiveness, so matching a partner's tempo might be the best bet for persuasion when influence is based on character or social attractiveness.

In bar-style restaurants, Hubbard and her colleagues found that men tipped female servers an average of 31% when touched versus 24% when touched by a male server, and about 11% when not touched at all.

In Willis and Hamm's studies, 81% of the people who were touched signed a petition compared to only 50% of those not touched, and 60% of those touched completed a questionnaire compared to only 40% of those not touched.

People were most likely to comply with a request to sign a petition when requesters moved closer, and helping behavior was more likely when the person requesting help violated spatial norms by standing closer than is customary.

In Baron's study, people who violated spatial norms by moving close to someone were more likely to receive help, but only when their apparent need for assistance was high, and when the need was low, getting close actually decreased the likelihood of receiving help.

Staring and prolonged gaze are most likely to be effective when used by a high-status or powerful person, when a request is considered legitimate, and when receivers agree with the persuader's position, and requests pressed too assertively are evaluated as less legitimate.

Social engineering combines setting false expectations with appeals to authority and requests for help, tricking targets into making snap judgments, and the success of the hack relies on the nonverbal performance of the attacker and accomplices pulling off the charade.

Behavioral mimicry promotes compliance, since mimicked targets were more likely to comply with a request for help critiquing an essay, and mimicry also promotes helping behaviors such as picking up dropped pens, as long as it is seen to be sincere.

According to Dunbar and Burgoon's summary of compliance-gaining research, people are more likely to comply when the person making the request is immediate, uses a visual dominance ratio and direct gaze, engages in positive and appropriate forms of touch, has a professional, well-groomed appearance, and stands close, but not too close.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Likeability, Reward and Punishment, and the New Channels of Influence
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena split into three rings: in the first, a smiling face and an angry face duel over a dominance meter while a direct effects beam fires from an immediate teacher; in the second, a school corridor with carpeting calms students while a cramped prison cell box squeezes a prisoner and a long dorm hallway drops a letter nobody mails; in the third, a video screen beats a text page in persuasion, a humanoid robot crosses toward the uncanny valley edge, and a deep-fake face flickers as a counter-forensic scanner sweeps it.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the remaining strategies and frontiers of influence: hold the direct effects model of immediacy up to the light and untangle the smiling contradiction, intimidation versus likeability, then walk the appeals that evoke pleasure or pain, from carpeted schools and soothing music to Solzhenitsyn's space-deprived prison cells and the corridor dorm that kills helping. Finish with the channel gauntlet: videotape over text, vivid online formats, charity faces, hyper-personal communication, and the embodied conversational agents, uncanny valley, and deep fakes of the AI frontier, before landing on the two-thirds claim that sums up the chapter.
key_concepts: Andersen's direct effects model proposes that both single-channeled immediacy increases, such as increased eye contact, and multi-channeled immediacy increases are associated with increased persuasion.

Angry, non-smiling faces are most likely when power or authority is communicated via intimidation, whereas smiling and facial pleasantness are most likely when dominance is wielded through likeability, and both angry and happy faces are rated as more dominant than sad or fearful faces.

A person who smiles too much, especially in response to others, may be viewed as submissive or insincere, while a person who smiles occasionally and at appropriate times may be perceived as more personable and likeable.

In a classic study, college students who were lightly and inconspicuously touched by librarians when checking out their books reported more positive feelings about the library and its staff than students who were not touched.

Carpeting at school helps create the impression that school is a desirable place to be by making it comfortable and aesthetically appealing, and as a result students are quieter in the halls and less rowdy and restless in class, while music can soothe nerves or stimulate buying.

Prisons make extensive use of space deprivation, as Solzhenitsyn wrote that Russian prisons maintained submissive behavior by denying prisoners adequate physical space, and Ramsey noted that new inmates in the Pennsylvania system lived in cells half the size of the regular population, with space deprivation one of the greatest causes of prison riots.

Students who live in dormitory rooms off a long corridor feel more crowded and are less apt to help others than those who live in dorms with a suite arrangement, being less likely to mail a letter ostensibly dropped by accident in the hallway and less likely to save milk cartons for charity.

Cancer patients' stories were more persuasive when people viewed them on videotape rather than just as text, in large part because the visual and vocal cues in the video version allowed viewers to feel more involved in the person's story.

Online formats need to be as vivid as possible to be persuasive, since consumers are more likely to be persuaded to buy items face to face when they can touch them, and charities needed to show faces and facial expressions of possible recipients for people to be persuaded to donate online.

According to Walther's principle of hyper-personal communication, in the absence of visual information users of online communication may be especially disclosive, and mediated communication affords more opportunity for selective impression management and a better chance to craft a more successful, persuasive presentation.

Newer AI technologies are building embodied conversational agents, humanoid robots that can interact with the nonverbal voices and gestures like real humans use, and among the challenges are emulating the multimodal head, eye, face, posture, voice, and proxemics of the human without crossing the uncanny valley where the artificial becomes creepy.

Nonverbal signals are potent sources of social influence, accounting for as much as two-thirds of the social meaning in human interactions, and the mere presence of others, compresence, causes our antennae to go up, so that nonverbal signals serve to reinforce or change another's thoughts, feelings, attitudes, and behaviors.

assets.topic: Scrub the History: From Ancient Ordeals and the Polygraph to the Pervasiveness of Everyday Lies
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead sweeps across a timeline of lie detection: ancient Chinese suspects chewing dry rice, a medieval suspect cast into a pond, John Larson's needle-drum polygraph, and a modern robot interviewer in a kiosk; a bar chart tilts showing 40% lying in email against 26% face to face while a stack of 2.4 million resumes glows with a 44% fabrications stamp.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the long history of catching liars: how the ancient Chinese used dry rice, Hindus watched for flushing, and Medieval England drowned suspects to test guilt, how John Larson's polygraph brought psychophysiological measurement into the early 1900s, and how the Army added a voice stress analyzer. Then audit the definition of deception, weigh the numbers on its pervasiveness, from the 92% who lied in the last week and the 1.65 lies per day to the 44% of resumes with fabrications, and trace how lying rises to 40% in email while dropping to 26% face to face, ending with the Madoff and Peter Foster cases.
key_concepts: In ancient times, the Chinese made suspects chew a grain of rice while being questioned, because a dry mouth that produced no saliva would mark them as guilty of whatever offense they were accused of.
In Medieval England, suspects were bound and cast into a pond, so that if they sank they were declared innocent but if they floated they were declared guilty and executed.

In the early 1900s, a medical student named John Larson invented the polygraph, which measured three psychophysiological signals, blood pressure, respiration, and pulse, to register a suspect's innocence or guilt.

Over the course of the twentieth century the polygraph underwent many improvements, including the addition of galvanic skin conductance, but it still relies on vital signs as indicators of verisimilitude.
Deception includes senders knowingly transmitting messages, verbal or nonverbal, to mislead another by fostering false impressions, beliefs, or understandings or actively concealing the truth.

The definition of deception rules out self-deception, intentionally transparent lies such as sarcasm, joking, polite comments, tall tales, and role-playing, and mistaken information the sender believes is true.

A national survey conducted with nonstudents and another with students reported that 92% or more had told a lie in the last week, and 24% had told a falsehood just the day before they took the survey.
The investigation by Serota and colleagues found that those in a nonstudent sample averaged 1.65 lies per day, whereas those in the student sample averaged 1.75 lies per day.
Students in diary studies reported that they told lies in 66% of their interactions with strangers, 44% of their interactions with acquaintances, and 36% to 38% with friends.

The rate of lying was far higher with email (40%), phone (39%), or instant messages (34%) than during face-to-face communication (26%), suggesting people are more uncomfortable lying to someone's face.
A background checking company called Avert studied 2.4 million resumes and purportedly found that 44% contained fabrications or embellishments.

Mayew and Venkatachalam discovered that a manager's voice can predict a firm's future performance, as executives who exhibited negative emotions signaled bad news while those who conveyed positive affect and excitement signaled positive future performance.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Theories: Physiognomy, Evolution, Leakage, Four Factors, IDT and Self-Presentation
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table under a holographic theory tree: a phrenology head with labeled bumps faces a Darwin portrait with a chameleon, a body diagram glows showing the face least leaky and the voice most leaky, four glowing jars labeled AROUSAL, AFFECT, COGNITION, CONTROL spill microexpressions, while two puppeteers exchange strings labeled moves and countermoves.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a debate among the perspectives on why deceivers leak and detectors read: argue against the phrenologist's physiognomic reading of heads and faces with the verdict that no scientific data support it, champion Darwin's lineage in the evolutionary view that deception and detection both carried selective advantage, then walk Ekman and Friesen's leakage hypothesis from the limbic system to the leakage hierarchy, ending with the strange truth that the face is least leaky but most watched while the voice is the most diagnostic channel. Finish by weighing four-factor theory's arousal, affect, cognition, and control against the Othello error, and let interpersonal deception theory and self-presentation theory argue that deception is dynamic, interdependent, and hard to tell apart from truth telling.
key_concepts: More than a century ago, Vaught's Character Reader promised to identify who could be trusted as honest and forthright and who could not on the basis of the shapes of their heads, ears, and eyes, a process referred to as phrenology.
According to the physiognomic view, deceptiveness or truthfulness is an inborn trait that will be revealed through one's outward appearance, yet no scientific data support this perspective.

An evolutionary perspective holds that deception evolved as an effective means of aiding the ablest tricksters and manipulators to gain goods, resources, and mates through illicit means and thus perpetuated the bloodlines of those skilled at deception.

Bond and Robinson wrote that deception has evolved under natural selection, as has the capacity to detect deceit, so that liars leave behind more offspring and the progeny inherit their parents' advantage.

Many of the most successful spies in history were masters of disguise, changing every feature of their physical appearance, from eyebrows, eye color, and hairstyle to clothing, accessories, and gait, to prevent their true identity being uncovered.

The voice of conman Peter Foster was as distinctive as his fingerprints, and a prospective investor recognized him within the first word or two of a radio interview because his intonation, pitch, and rhythm of speech could not be revamped.

Ekman and Friesen's leakage hypothesis holds that the act of deception is associated with a host of internal physiological, emotional, and cognitive responses that give rise to external displays which leak out of the body unbidden.

According to the leakage hypothesis, leaked emotions are under the control of the lower parts of the brain, the limbic system, and include difficult-to-inhibit expressions such as eyebrow raises that show fear, lip presses that show anger, or cheek raises that show enjoyment.

Ekman proposed that facial cues are the least likely to leak information about deception, yet people pay closer attention to the face than to body or voice cues, which is why they are misled by fake smiles known as the Duchenne smile.

Empirical evidence indicates that the voice is at least as leaky as the body and may actually be the most diagnostic channel as to a sender's veracity, while the verbal channel is considered the least likely to reveal deception.
Four-factor theory groups the internal events that cause outward deception displays into four classes: arousal, negative affect, cognitive processing, and attempted control.

Interpersonal deception theory views deception as dynamic and iterative rather than static, so that displays and judgments change as senders read receivers' signals as feedback and adjust what they say and do in ongoing moves and countermoves.

assets.topic: Audit the Indicators: Stereotypical Versus Actual Cues and the Moderators That Bend Them
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with two columns, STEREOTYPED and ACTUAL: a red pencil strikes out the averted gaze row whose actual correlation is near zero, while a row of combined cue constellations stamps 68% accurate; moderator cards flip past, a world map with Resistance players, a first-grader's face beside a seventh-grader's, a Machiavellian mask, and a liar's calendar showing planned versus spontaneous lies.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit what really gives liars away: tick off the world's favorite stereotype, that liars look away, then open the ledger showing the eyes are not a reliable indicator and no single cue is valid, and weigh the meta-analytic findings, the Brunswikian lens model, the 68% accuracy of combined cue constellations, and Porter's microexpressions in fake pleaders. Then take the moderator columns one by one, culture, sex, age, demeanor bias, personality, motivation, incentives, planning, interactivity, and suspicion, and check how each bends deceptive displays and detection accuracy.
key_concepts: In the 58 countries surveyed by the Global Deception Research Team, the number-one answer from 64% of the respondents to how you can tell when people are lying was that people look away.
In reality, the eyes are not a reliable indicator, and there are no single cues that by themselves are valid and produce consistent results across all circumstances and people.

Using the Brunswikian lens model, Hartwig and Bond found that, although behaviors correlated more strongly with perceived than actual deception, the cues people were relying on were valid and both perceived and actual cues successfully predicted deception.

When researchers stopped analyzing cues one at a time and instead looked at constellations of cues, they found a strong correlation between multiple cues and deception, allowing lies and truths to be detected with nearly 68% accuracy.
The DePaulo and colleagues meta-analysis reported the results of 1338 estimates of 158 cues from 120 different reports comparing truthful to deceptive verbal and nonverbal behavior.
Porter and colleagues found that fake pleaders for the return of missing children lacked certain muscle movements around the eyes but introduced into their smiles something akin to a smirk.

The correlations in the indicators table show that although people tend to see averted gaze or looking away as stereotypically associated with deception, the relationship between this behavior and actual deception is close to zero.

Women tell more polite lies while men tell more self-serving ones, and women's lies are more easily detected than lies by men, in part because males cover their distress with smiles more than females do.

First-graders are more easily detected than seventh-graders or college students, so deceit is partly an acquired skill, although children's lies are often indistinguishable from truths in low-stakes situations.
Some people are viewed consistently as sincere or trustworthy and others as lacking credibility no matter what they do, a phenomenon researchers have coined as honest demeanor bias.

Compared with lies that receive little or no forethought, planned lies are characterized by increased pupil dilation, fewer unfilled pauses, shorter response latencies, and faster speech, so planned speech appears credible and unimpaired.

When receivers are suspicious, deceivers tend to change their demeanor, sometimes becoming more dominant and smiling longer, but a common feature is that they make adjustments over time toward adapting to the receiver's nonverbal behavior.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Accuracy, Stereotypes, Biases and Heuristics in the Lie-Catching Judgment Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled ACCURACY, BIAS, DEMEANOR and SUSPICION: cards fly into place, a coin flip hovering at 54%, a scales tilting toward truth judgments, a baby-faced adult stamped truthful, and a fishy-looking liar card with a red X; beneath it a thermometer shows confidence uncorrelated with accuracy while an ear icon outranks an eye icon.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell judgment matrix for why lie catching fails: drop the 54% overall accuracy and the 47% deception-detection rate into the ACCURACY cell, the truth bias, lie bias, and visual bias into the BIAS cell, the demeanor bias and baby-faced credibility into the DEMEANOR cell, and expectancy violations and nonverbal conspicuousness into the SUSPICION cell. Then audit the moderators of detection: confidence that is unrelated to accuracy, audio that beats video, baseline familiarity that helps while relational closeness blinds, bogus training's placebo effect, and the suspicious receiver whose accuracy is undermined rather than aided.
key_concepts: Bond and DePaulo found that, on average, people are accurate in detecting deception at an overall rate of about 54%, which is only slightly better than chance, equivalent to flipping a coin.
Detection of deception, as compared to detection of truth, is far worse, averaging 47%, and this poor performance generally holds true for both experts and nonexperts.

A meta-analysis of 108 studies covering 16,537 subjects concluded that professional lie catchers such as police officers, detectives, judges, and psychologists were no more accurate than students and citizens, with experts averaging 55% accuracy and lay subjects 54%.

The truth bias, also called the honesty bias, is the tendency to overestimate the truthfulness of others, while the opposite lie bias reflects an underestimate of the truthfulness of others' communication and is more likely among professionals who ferret out bad guys.

The visual bias refers to the tendency to assign primacy to visual information over other forms of nonverbal and verbal information, even though facial cues are typically the least diagnostic in identifying deception because senders can control them.

In one experiment, fully 82% of interviewees were judged as truthful when observers had access to visual information, compared to 71% for those with only words and voice and 47% for those who received only the text presentation.

Baby-faced adults are judged to be more truthful and credible than more mature-faced individuals, and demeanor bias generalizes across situations, so individuals judged as truthful and sincere in one situation earn the same ratings in another.

The expectancy violations bias, also called the nonverbal conspicuousness bias, is the tendency to infer deception from abnormal, fishy-looking, or atypical behavior, which unduly influences judgments in the direction of judging the person as deceptive.

Time and again, research has documented that confidence is totally unrelated to accuracy, with the correlation between accuracy and confidence near zero, and overconfidence can actually lead to more error.

Accuracy in detecting deception was poorest when only the visual information was available and best when audio information was available, so receivers are more accurate in distinguishing lies from truths when hearing rather than seeing or reading lies.

Unlike behavioral familiarity with a sender's baseline behavior, which improves detection accuracy, relational familiarity can be detrimental to accurate detection because people put on blinders with those to whom they are close.

Bogus training has been found to improve detection accuracy, which raises doubts about whether training is truly making a difference or is just a placebo effect that makes people pay closer attention.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Motivation Impairment, Cognitive Load, Truth Default and the Machines That Would Replace Human Judgment
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a security checkpoint: a motivated liar freezes mid-gesture under a freeze-frame of decreased blinking, a cognitive load gauge spikes while an fMRI brain scan lights up across activation, decision, and construction phases, and a wall of machines, thermal cameras, laser vibrometers, and computer vision trackers scan a crowd while a polygraph needle draws its familiar trace.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of whether anyone can reliably detect a lie: hold the motivated liar up to the light and catch the freeze pattern, then walk the motivation impairment effect into the choking-under-pressure trap where only extreme jeopardy damages performance. Next, load cognitive load theory's working memory budget and the activation-decision-construction model into the scanner, then challenge Levine's truth-default theory, which dismisses nonverbal cue theories altogether. Finish in the machine room: the polygraph, fMRI, thermal imaging, laser Doppler vibrometry, layered voice analysis, computer vision, SPOT screening, and Project Hostile Intent, and decide whether they beat the 54% human average or simply automate suspicion.
key_concepts: The motivation impairment effect states that the lies of motivated deceivers will be more detectable when told in channels that include nonverbal cues than in verbal-only channels, meaning the harder people try, the more they will fail nonverbally.

Participants who are given incentives to deceive tend to show a freeze pattern of decreased blinking, less facial animation, fewer head movements, adaptors, and postural shifts, and more reticence with shorter responses and slower speaking.
Only under extreme motivation or jeopardy does impairment occur, a pattern that better fits a choking-under-pressure explanation because both verbal and nonverbal behaviors suffer under high stakes.

Moderate motivation appears to be more beneficial than harmful, and motivated deceivers whose deception went undetected were judged by observers to be more credible than those reporting moderate to low motivation.

Cognitive load theory holds that working memory has limited capacity and that deception can cause an overload that leads deceivers to give off telltale physiological and behavioral signals of the additional mental workload.

In Walczyk's activation-decision-construction model of deception, the activation phase retrieves information from long-term memory, the decision phase chooses truth or lie, and the construction phase builds a plausible lie while inhibiting the truth, with each phase producing longer response latencies.

Tests using fMRI, PET, EEG, and other neuroimaging and autonomic nervous system measures are amassing indications such as reaction time, hesitations, holding one's breath, pupil dilation, and blinks that a communicator is working hard.

Truth-default theory embraces truth-bias, so when the base rate of truths and deceptions is 50-50 judges will be more accurate judging truths but less accurate in judging lies, and the fewer the lies to be detected, the worse the rate of deception detection.

Levine dismisses nonverbal and other cue theories as unhelpful in accurately predicting deceit, so truth-default theory tells us little about nonverbal displays that relate to deception and their ability to accurately identify deceit.

The polygraph measures respiratory, cardiac, and electrodermal responses, while other devices like fMRI, event-related potentials, thermal imaging, laser Doppler vibrometry, and near-infrared spectroscopy measure physiological responses predicated on deception causing stress.

An alternative approach that is emerging is to measure outward nonverbal behavior using computer vision techniques that automatically identify and track body movements, gestures, and facial expressions.

Project Hostile Intent is intended to use an array of lasers, sensors, cameras, microphones, and other remote sensing devices to identify facial expressions, gait, blood pressure, pulse, and perspiration rates that are characteristic of hostility or the desire to deceive.
